Ce verset appelle les croyants à la patience, à la constance face à l'ennemi, à l'occupation des frontières et à la crainte de Dieu, afin de réussir. Les commentateurs divergent sur le sens des trois termes. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Juraydj et al-Dahhak entendent : patientez dans l'obéissance à Dieu et dans la religion, soyez plus constants que l'ennemi dans le combat, et tenez les frontières, ce que retient aussi al-Tabari. Zayd ibn Aslam comprend la patience comme la persévérance dans le jihad, et Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi comprend la constance comme l'attente patiente de la promesse divine de victoire. Le mot rabat désigne à l'origine l'attache des chevaux pour la guerre, puis la présence dans les places fortes, Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn Kathir précisant que celui qui y réside en permanence n'est pas à proprement parler un mourabit. Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, relayé par al-Razi, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir, rapporte au contraire, d'après Abu Hurayra, que le verset vise l'attente de la prière après la prière, car il n'y avait pas de guerre de frontière du temps du Prophète, et il s'appuie sur le hadith qui range parmi le rabat l'ablution parfaite malgré le froid, la marche vers les mosquées et l'attente de la prière. Ibn Kathir estime aussi que le sens peut englober le combat. Al-Razi montre que le verset couvre la patience dans les actes, dans les épreuves et contre les passions, et qu'il peut se comprendre dans tous ces sens à la fois. La crainte de Dieu s'étend à toute la conduite, et le mot la'alla, selon plusieurs, marque la finalité plutôt que l'espérance. Le fawz désigne l'obtention du bien désiré et la sauvegarde du mal redouté.
en: This commentary opens with the disjointed letters (Alif Lam Mim), whose meaning most exegetes leave to God alone, and then treats the following verse (God, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting) as a self-standing sentence. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the opening of the surah was revealed concerning the Christian delegation of Najran, who came to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ about Jesus, so the opening affirms God's oneness and denies divinity to anything besides Him. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy hold that 'the Living, the Self-Subsisting' answers the Christians who made Jesus divine, since he was born, ate, drank and died, which cannot belong to the Living and Self-Subsisting. Al-Mawardi and al-Sam'ani offer several readings of the letters and of the verse's place in the surah without deciding between them. On 'He has sent down to you the Book with truth, confirming what came before it', most commentators say the Book is the Quran, and that its confirmation means it agrees with earlier scriptures on monotheism and prophethood. On the Torah and the Gospel, the Basrans derive the words from Arabic roots, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan consider them foreign names whose Arabic derivations are unconvincing. As for al-Furqan, Qatada, al-Rabi' and al-Tabari take it to mean the Quran, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as anything that distinguishes truth from falsehood. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain that the Quran was sent down gradually, hence the verb 'nazzala', while the Torah and Gospel came all at once, hence 'anzala'. The commentators conclude that those who reject God's signs will face a severe punishment, for God is Mighty and able to take vengeance.

This verse declares that God alone is the true deity, that no one deserves worship but Him, that He is the Living, whose life is complete and never ends, and that He is al-Qayyum, the One who sustains and manages all things. The commentators explain that this opening of the surah answers the Christians of Najran who claimed that Jesus was God: a divinity must be living and self-subsisting, whereas Jesus, by their own account, died.

The commentators agree that al-Hayy al-Qayyum together gather the attributes of perfection. They differ on the meaning of al-Qayyum. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and al-Rabi' take it to mean the One who takes charge of everything, guarding, providing for and directing it, while others understand it as the One whose existence is permanent and who neither moves nor changes. Al-Tabari adopts the first meaning and explains the grammatical form of the word. Umar and Ibn Mas'ud are reported to have read al-Hayy al-Qayyam, a reading that is not among the accepted canonical readings, and al-Tabari prefers the common reading.

On the disconnected letters at the start of the surah, al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that some leave their meaning to God alone, while others see in them a sign of the Qur'an's inimitability, composed from the very letters of the Arabic language. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also discuss the vowelling of the letter mim, which the grammarians of Basra and Kufa debated. The early commentators link the revelation of these verses to the delegation of Najran, and Ibn Kathir notes that they arrived in Medina in the ninth year after the Hijra.

This verse states that God sent down the Qur'an to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with truth, meaning accuracy in its reports and justice in its rulings, and that it confirms the scriptures and messengers before it. Most commentators understand the Book as the Qur'an and the verb nazzala as a gradual sending down, while the Torah and the Gospel were sent down all at once, as al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note. On the phrase confirming what is before it, al-Tabari and Mujahid take it to mean the earlier books and messengers, whereas Abu Muslim, reported by al-Razi, sees it as proof of the Qur'an's divine origin, since a text from any other source would not agree with the earlier scriptures. Most exegetes describe the Torah and the Gospel as guidance for people; al-Baydawi and Ibn Atiyya note that 'people' may mean the Children of Israel or extend to all who follow them, and al-Ka'bi argues from the general scope of the guidance. The Furqan is taken by some as the Qur'an, by others as the scriptures collectively, the miracles, or the signs that distinguish truth from falsehood, and al-Tabari takes it as the act of distinguishing itself. All tie the warning of a severe punishment for those who reject God's signs to the debate with the Najran delegation, and they stress that God is mighty and takes revenge. On the origin of the words Torah and Injil, the grammarians of Basra and Kufa offered different Arabic derivations, but several scholars, including Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi, consider such attempts unconvincing because the words are foreign.

This verse states that God sent down the Book to the Prophet ﷺ with the truth, confirming what came before it. It adds that the Torah and the Gospel were revealed earlier as guidance for people, and that the Criterion, meaning that which distinguishes truth from falsehood, was also sent down. It then warns that those who reject God's signs will face a severe punishment, for God is mighty and able to take vengeance. The commentators, such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi, agree that the Book refers to the Quran and that the Torah and the Gospel were genuine guidance for those who followed them before they were abrogated. They differ, however, on the meaning of the word al-Furqan. Al-Tabari and Qatada, among others, take it to be the Quran itself. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi understand it as anything that separates truth from falsehood in the scriptures and laws. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it to mean the revealed scriptures in general, al-Razi takes it to mean the miracles that accompanied the revelations, and some take it to be the Psalms. As for the occasion of revelation, Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that these verses were revealed about the Christian delegation of Najran, who came to dispute with the Prophet about Jesus. On the scope of the threat, some limit it to those Christians, while others, such as al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur, extend it to all disbelievers. The commentators set out these views without judging between them.

This verse states that nothing is hidden from God, neither on earth nor in heaven, and that His knowledge encompasses everything in the world, including the outward and inward deeds of people. The commentators explain that it was revealed in response to the Christian delegation of Najran, who came to debate with the Prophet ﷺ about Jesus and claimed divinity for him. The verse thus implies that a god must know all things, which Jesus did not. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that the following phrase, 'He forms you in the wombs as He wills', is further proof: Jesus himself was shaped in Mary's womb like any human being, so he cannot be God. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan read 'earth and heaven' as a way of naming the whole universe, since they are its two extremes, while Ibn 'Ashur explains that mentioning the earth first allows a gradual move toward what is more distant. Al-Razi argues that God's complete knowledge and power are the basis of His role as the one who sustains and governs all things, and shows how these attributes answer the Christian arguments based on Jesus's knowledge of hidden matters and his power to heal and raise the dead. Ibn al-Jawzi gives a similar reading. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress the moral lesson: the believer should avoid disobedience to God both in private and in public. No legal ruling is drawn from this verse; its main purpose is to refute the divinity of Jesus and to affirm God's perfect knowledge.

This verse states that Allah alone shapes human beings in their mothers' wombs as He wills, male or female, handsome or plain, tall or short, white or black, happy or unhappy. There is no god but Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise. The commentators agree that the verse denies any partner or likeness to God. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi connect it to the debate with the Christian delegation of Najran, who claimed that Jesus was the son of God. For them, if God formed Jesus in Mary's womb, he was a created being like all other humans and could be neither God nor His son.

Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi develop this answer. According to al-Razi, the verse responds to two Christian arguments: the first concerning knowledge, since Jesus foretold certain hidden things, and the second concerning power, since he raised the dead and healed the blind and the leper. Al-Razi holds that these acts do not prove divinity, because Jesus' knowledge and power were limited. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir describe the stages of the embryo's formation, drawing on reports transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Zamakhshari adds that the mention of God's comprehensive knowledge serves as a warning to those who oppose Him.

Opinions differ on the meaning of "as He wills". Al-Tabari understands it as the variety of physical traits, while Ibn 'Ashur reads "kayfa" as indicating manner. Ibn 'Uthaymin links this divine will to questions of medical intervention, which he discusses at length, though the other commentators draw no legal ruling from the verse.

The commentators explain that God sent down the Book, with some verses clear and forming its foundation, and others ambiguous, whose meaning becomes certain only when read in light of the clear ones. Those whose hearts incline toward deviation follow the ambiguous verses, seeking discord and twisting their meaning to suit their desires. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed about the Christians of Najran or the Jews, while others, such as al-Baghawi and al-Wahidi, extend it to all innovators, including the Kharijites. The scholars differ on where to pause after "except God". Most of the early authorities, including Aisha, Urwa, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz and Malik, hold that only God knows the reality of the ambiguous verses, and that the firmly grounded in knowledge say simply: we believe in it, all of it comes from our Lord. Mujahid, al-Rabi ibn Anas and another report from Ibn Abbas hold that the firmly grounded also know its interpretation. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya set out these views, and Ibn Atiyya distinguishes what God alone knows from what can be reached by reflection. Ibn Taymiyya, quoted by al-Qasimi, argues that the verse is about the meaning of the ambiguous words, not their ultimate reality. All agree that the firmly grounded pray not to be made to swerve after being guided, and that only people of sound reason truly take heed.

The people firm in knowledge pray to their Lord not to let their hearts swerve after He has guided them, and to grant them mercy from Himself, for He is the Ever-Bestowing. Al-Tabari explains that zaygh means inclining away from the truth, and he reports from al-Dahhak that mercy here means forgiveness and pardon, while others understand it as the grace of steadfastness in guidance. Al-Tha'labi and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as a request for firmness in faith. The Mu'tazilites, as al-Razi and al-Qurtubi report, refuse to attribute the swerving to God and interpret the verse as asking not to be tested beyond one's strength or deprived of divine favours, whereas the Sunni commentators see in it proof that both guidance and misguidance come from God, and al-Razi cites the saying that the heart lies between two of the fingers of the Merciful. Traditions transmitted through Umm Salama, Anas and Abu Hurayra report that the Prophet often prayed, 'O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm in Your religion,' and Ibn Kathir reports that Abu Bakr recited this verse in prayer during the apostasy wars. The commentators agree on the general meaning of the supplication, and differ mainly over the definition of zaygh and rahma and over the role of divine creation in deviation.

In this verse, those firmly rooted in knowledge call upon their Lord, affirming that God will gather people for a Day about which there is no doubt, since He never breaks His promise. Al-Tabari explains that although the wording is that of a statement, its meaning is a supplication and a plea to God, asking Him to forgive the believers on that day, for He does not break His promise to those who believe in Him and follow His messenger. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take the lam to mean 'for the reckoning of' or 'for the recompense of' that day. Ibn Kathir and others explain that the word 'rayb' means doubt. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur see in the verse a prayer taught to believers at a time of deviation, and the request not to let the heart turn aside is a protection against it. As for the phrase 'God does not break His promise', some, such as al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi, regard it as God's own speech or as a reason for rejecting doubt, since divinity is incompatible with breaking a promise. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari attach it to the words of the believers. The Mu'tazilites used the verse to argue that the punishment of sinners is certain, but the Sunni scholars answered that this threat is conditional on the absence of pardon. Commentators also differ on how this verse links with what precedes it, especially on whether the pause falls after the divine name or after 'those firmly rooted in knowledge'.

This verse states that those who rejected the truth after recognising it will gain nothing from their wealth or children before God, and that they will be the fuel of the Fire. The commentators take "those who disbelieved" to mean disbelievers in general, though al-Wahidi and others name the Jews of Qurayza and al-Nadir, the delegation of Najran, or the Arab polytheists. They agree that neither wealth nor offspring will shield the disbeliever from punishment, either in this world or the next, and that "wuqud" is what fuel is burned with. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud read the particle "min" as meaning "in place of", that is, in exchange for God's mercy or obedience, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Mubarrad take it to mean a starting point, and Abu 'Ubayda takes it as "near", a view Abu Hayyan finds weak. On the word "da'b", Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid understand it as conduct and practice, al-Nadr ibn Shumayl as habit, and al-Zajjaj as circumstance. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the comparison with the conduct of Pharaoh's people in denial, and the seizing for their sins as a punishment already inflicted. Al-Razi explains that the fullness of torment is the loss of every means of protection followed by the gathering of every cause of pain. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the threat here is probably worldly punishment, since it is compared to the fate of Pharaoh's family, with the punishment of the Hereafter added after it.

This part of the verse says that the fate of those who disbelieve, whose wealth and children will avail them nothing against God, is like that of the family of Pharaoh and the peoples before them: they denied God's signs, so God seized them for their sins, and God is severe in punishment. The commentators gave several readings of the word 'da’b'. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid and al-Dahhak understood it as the deed or conduct, the way the family of Pharaoh acted in disbelief and denial. al-Rabi', Abu 'Ubayda and al-Kisa'i took it as custom or practice, al-Akhfash as affair or condition, and al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari as persistent striving in disbelief and in opposing the Prophet together. Lexicographers note that the root means sustained effort in work, which later came to mean habit or manner, and al-Tabari quotes a line of Imru al-Qays to illustrate this.

The commentators agree that being seized for sins means the punishment that struck the deniers, and that the signs include miracles and revealed scriptures. They differ on who the disbelievers are. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and others name the Banu Qurayza and the Banu al-Nadir, others name the delegation of Najran or the Arab polytheists, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi refer to the Jews of Medina, and Ibn 'Ashur reads it as all disbelievers with emphasis on the Jews. On the particle 'ka' (like), grammarians proposed several analyses: al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan attach it to an implied subject or to the preceding verb, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi take it as a comparison of conduct, which most of them find the strongest reading.

This verse tells the disbelievers that they will be overcome in this world and then gathered into Hell on the Day of Resurrection, which is described as a wretched resting place. The commentators differ on who is addressed. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Kathir report that the Jews of Medina are meant, since the Prophet gathered them in the market of Banu Qaynuqa after Badr and they answered with threats; Muqatil and others take the polytheists of Mecca, while al-Kalbi links the revelation to the events after Uhud. Al-Tabari prefers the Jewish reading because the next verse addresses them directly with 'you have had a sign'. On recitation, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read the verb in the second person, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the third person, which Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari explain as a faithful report of what God said. Regarding 'al-mihad', Mujahid takes it as what they prepared for themselves, while al-Hasan takes it simply as their final abode. The scholars agree that the verse is a promise to the believers and a warning to the disbelievers, and that the defeat of the polytheists at Badr was its fulfilment.

This verse recalls that the victory of a small force over a larger one at the battle of Badr was a sign and a lesson for those who reflect. Two groups met: one fought in the way of God, the other was unbelieving. The commentators generally identify the two sides as the Muslims and the Quraysh at Badr, though they differ on who is addressed by "you": some say the Jews of Medina, others the polytheists or the believers themselves. The phrase "they see them as twice their number" has been read in several ways. Ibn Mas'ud reports that the Muslims first saw the enemy at its true size and then were made to see them as fewer; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God made the enemy appear smaller and then larger at different moments, which does not contradict the verse in al-Anfal. Al-Farra' holds that "twice" may mean a larger multiple, and Nafi' read the verb in the second person. All agree that victory comes from God's support alone, given to whom He wills, and that the event is a lesson for those with insight. A few, such as Ibn Juzayy, see the example as illustrative rather than a single historical event.

This verse states that God has made the desires of people appealing to them: women, children, heaped piles of gold and silver, branded horses, livestock and tilled land. It describes all of this as the passing enjoyment of the life of this world, while with God is the finest return. The commentators differ on who makes these things attractive. Umar ibn al-Khattab and most exegetes say it is God Himself, as a test for His servants; al-Hasan al-Basri attributes it to Satan. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qadi distinguish a praiseworthy adornment from God and a blameworthy one from Satan, while al-Jubba'i separates what is permitted from what is forbidden. Women are named first because they are Satan's snares and the greatest trial, and sons are mentioned without daughters because the Arabs took pride in them. As for the qanatir, the scholars disagree on their measure: Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Umar and Abu Hurayra put it at twelve hundred ounces, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak at twelve hundred dinars, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab at eighty thousand, Mujahid at seventy thousand dinars, and Abu Nadra at a bull's hide filled with gold, while al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu Ubayda regard it as great wealth without fixed measure. On al-muqantara, Qatada says it means doubled, al-Suddi minted into coins, and Ibn Kaysan gathered and secured. For the branded horses, Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say grazing horses, Mujahid and Ikrima say fine and noble ones, Qatada and Ibn Abbas in another report say marked with blazes, and Ibn Zayd say readied for war. Most commentators regard horses, livestock and crops as passing goods, the purpose of the verse being to turn people away from the world and toward the good return with God.

God instructs His Prophet to tell people of something better than the worldly pleasures just mentioned: for those who are mindful of God there are gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will dwell forever, with purified spouses and God's good pleasure, and God sees His servants and will recompense them. The commentators agree that this reward far surpasses worldly goods and that God's pleasure is the greatest part of it, often citing the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri in which God says He will bestow His pleasure and never be displeased with them again. They also agree that taqwa means guarding oneself against polytheism and sins while doing what God commands, and that the purified spouses are free from menstruation, childbirth bleeding and every blemish, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi extending this to both body and character.

The grammarians differ on where the sentence is to be paused: al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi end the question at « than that », whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and others hold that the statement ends at « with their Lord ». The reading of « ridwan » with a kasra or a damma is a matter of dialect and does not change the meaning. Regarding the qintar, opinions vary: twelve thousand ounces according to one reported hadith, a hundred pounds of gold according to others, or a bull's hide filled with gold according to Abu Nadra. As for the hours before dawn, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take them to be the last part of the night, when prayer and seeking forgiveness are recommended, while others read them as the dawn prayer in congregation. Al-Shawkani notes that the adornment of desires is attributed by some to God and by others to Satan, al-Hasan holding the latter.

This verse describes the God-fearing, to whom gardens are promised with their Lord, who pray: 'Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the torment of the Fire.' The commentators agree that forgiveness means concealing and erasing sins, and that protection from the Fire means averting punishment, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn explain. Grammatically the phrase may be a qualifier, an apposition, or a praise, in the genitive, nominative or accusative, as al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note. Al-Razi argues from this that faith alone is enough to ask for forgiveness, and that the qualities listed afterwards are not conditions for pardon but marks of higher ranks, a view that al-Maturidi is also said to hold according to Abu Hayyan. Ibn Ashur instead sees a supplication accompanied by deeds that make it more likely to be answered. As for the pre-dawn hours (al-asḥar), al-Zajjaj places them just before dawn, Ibn Zayd in the last sixth of the night, and others in the last third, a view Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi support by the hadith of the Lord's descent. Opinions differ on who 'seek forgiveness': some say they are those who pray, such as Qatada and Mujahid, others those who pray the dawn prayer in congregation, as Zayd ibn Aslam says, and others those who ask forgiveness aloud, as Ibn Mas'ud and Anas report. The commentators agree that the verse lists the qualities of the pious: patience, truthfulness, devotion, generosity and seeking forgiveness at dawn.

This verse describes the qualities of those who guard against God's displeasure, for whom gardens, purified spouses and God's good pleasure are prepared. They are patient in obedience, in turning away from sin and in facing painful decrees; truthful in speech, deed and intention; devoted to constant obedience with humility; generous in spending their wealth; and they seek forgiveness at the hour before dawn. The commentators differ on what seeking forgiveness at dawn means. Qatada, Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi and Mujahid take it to mean those who pray at that hour; Anas ibn Malik, Ibn Umar and Ibn Mas'ud take it to mean those who ask God for forgiveness; and Zayd ibn Aslam takes it to mean those who attend the dawn prayer in congregation. Al-Tabari judges that the meaning of asking forgiveness through supplication is the most apparent, while allowing that it may also mean seeking forgiveness through action and prayer. The word as-sahar refers to the last part of the night just before dawn. It is singled out because, as several hadiths report, God descends to the lowest heaven at that time, and because worship then is harder and the soul is purer. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the conjunction 'and' between the qualities shows that each is complete and stands on its own, a principle Abu Hayyan does not accept as general. The explanations of patience, truthfulness, devotion and spending largely overlap without contradiction, and together they portray the conduct of the God-fearing.

God bears witness, with the angels and those of knowledge, that there is no deity but Him, standing firm in justice. Al-Tabari explains that witness here means declaration and making clear, rejecting Abu 'Ubayda's reading of it as decree. Al-Mawardi offers several meanings, including informing with certainty and establishing proofs. The angels' testimony is affirmation. Those possessing knowledge are understood by commentators as the prophets, the emigrants and helpers, the believing scholars of the People of the Book, or more broadly all believing scholars; al-Qurtubi and al-Shawkani prefer the last view for its generality. The phrase standing in justice is an attribute of God for most exegetes, while some take it as an epithet or a praise. The repetition of the declaration of Oneness is read by al-Baydawi as a stress, and by Ibn Qayyim as a means of tying the sentence to the attribute of justice. Ibn Kathir and others report the occasion of revelation as the two rabbis from Syria or the Najran delegation. Scholars differ on the vowelling of the hamza in inna: most read it with a kasra, making the reading an affirmation, while other readings with a fatha yield different constructions. Ibn Kathir stresses that the religion accepted by God is islam, the path of all prophets, and that the People of the Book split only after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves.

This verse states that the religion accepted by God is Islam, meaning submission to God alone through obedience, monotheism and following what the messengers brought, and that any other path is not accepted. Commentators agree that Islam here covers both faith and deeds, though they word it differently: al-Rabi', Abu al-'Aliya and Qatada take it as the testimony that there is no god but God and acceptance of what comes from Him, al-Tabari as submission and obedience, Ibn 'Atiyya and most theologians as faith together with works, while Ibn Kathir describes it as following the prophets up to Muhammad, the last of them. On the phrase 'and those given the Book did not differ except after knowledge had come to them,' opinions vary about who is meant: al-Rabi' ibn Anas says the Jews, with the division occurring after Moses, Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr says the Christians concerning Jesus, while Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Kathir apply it to the People of the Book in general. Most explain 'baghy' as envy and the desire for leadership and worldly gain rather than honest doubt, since they knew the truth. All agree that whoever denies God's signs will be swiftly reckoned with, that is, God counts and recompenses quickly. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan report al-Kisa'i's reading with a fatha on the hamza of 'anna al-din', while the majority reading uses a kasra, which they consider more natural as the start of a new clause. Commentators link the passage to the dispute with the Christian delegation of Najran and note the command to the Prophet to say: 'I have submitted my face to God.'

In this verse God instructs His Prophet that if the People of the Book dispute with him about the religion after the proof has been set before them, he should say that he has surrendered his face, meaning his whole self, to God alone, as have those who follow him. He then addresses the Jews, the Christians and the Arab polytheists, asking whether they have submitted, and states that whoever submits is rightly guided, while whoever turns away bears no burden on the Prophet beyond delivering the message. God is All-Seeing of His servants. Most commentators report that the verse concerns the Christian delegation of Najran, and that the dispute was about Jesus and the truth of religion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain "I have submitted my face" as surrendering in heart, tongue and all limbs, the face being singled out for its honour; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir understand it as pure monotheism, the religion of all the prophets. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan offer several ways of understanding the argument, including reasoning from points the opponents already accept, such as their esteem for Abraham. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the debate ends with an invitation to Islam rather than with war. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi read the question "have you submitted?" as a threat or a command, and Ibn 'Atiyya favours the threat reading. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that some scholars consider the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others hold it to be final. Ibn Kathir, al-Suyuti and al-Tha'alibi relate reports about the occasion of revelation. All agree on the essential meaning: the Prophet is charged only with delivering the message, and guidance belongs to God.

This verse announces a painful punishment for those who deny the signs of God, kill the prophets without right, and kill those who call people to justice; their deeds come to nothing in this life and the next, and no one can help them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that the address first concerns the Jews of the Prophet's time, who approved of what their forefathers had done; al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi add that these crimes are attributed to them because they followed the same path and were pleased with it. All agree that those who call to justice are people who enjoin good and forbid evil, whether scholars or rulers; al-Hasan al-Basri, quoted by al-Qurtubi, holds that their rank is close to that of the prophets. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the report of Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah about forty-three prophets slain in a single morning, though Ibn Kathir notes that one of its transmitters is unknown. On recitation, Hamza reads “wa yuqatilun” while the majority reads “wa yaqtulun”; al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi prefer the majority reading, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see no conflict between them. Commentators differ on “bashshir-hum”: al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi take it as irony, al-Razi as metaphor, and others as a visible change in the skin. The meaning of “habitat a'maluhum” also varies: al-Tabari speaks of lasting blame and curse in this world, Ibn Kathir of loss of reward, and Ibn 'Ashur explains it through the image of a camel that dies from bloating. Grammarians debate whether the fa' may enter the predicate of inna: some allow it because the subject carries a conditional sense, while Sibawayh and al-Akhfash reject it.

This part of the verse states that those who combine denying God's signs with killing prophets and those who enjoin justice see their deeds rendered void both in this world and in the Hereafter, and that they have no helpers to save them from God's punishment. The commentators explain that habita, the voiding of deeds, means their loss and disappearance. Al-Tabari says that in this world it means they gain no praise and bear a lasting curse, and in the Hereafter their deeds become worthless, with no reward. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi take a similar view. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the voiding in this life is the lasting blame, and in the next life the deeds become scattered dust, with punishment for them. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di hold that in this world the deeds are not accepted, and in the next they are not rewarded. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari cite the hadith of Abu 'Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah about the people most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection, though al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Hajar regard its chain as weak. Some take the verse as addressed to Jews and Christians of the Prophet's time, while al-Alusi and Ibn Sa'di read it as a general rule covering every disbeliever. The plural form of 'helpers' is explained by Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan as matching the verse endings, and Abu Hayyan adds that the negation covers any help that would bring benefit. There is agreement that the verse is a severe warning; the scholars differ on the precise meaning of the voiding and its scope.

God addresses the Prophet with astonishment about a group of People of the Book who were given a share of the Scripture: when they are called to the Book of God to settle their disputes, a faction of them turns away, though they know they are being called to the truth. The commentators generally take this to refer mainly to the Jews. As to which Book is meant, Ibn Abbas and most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, identify it as the Torah, while al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Juraij identify it as the Quran, which they recognised as God's word. Several accounts of the occasion of revelation exist: the best known, transmitted by Ibn Ishaq from Ibn Abbas, tells of the Prophet calling Jews in their house of study to the Torah and their refusal; the story of the stoning of an adulterous couple from Khaybar, given by al-Kalbi, is more doubtful, and al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note its weakness. Opinions differ on what the judgement concerns: al-Tabari says it could be the Prophet's mission, the religion of Abraham, Islam, or a legal penalty, while al-Mawardi and al-Razi mention prophethood, Abraham's religion and a penalty. Several commentators report that their claim that the Fire would touch them only for a few counted days rested, according to Qatada and al-Rabi, on the forty days of worshipping the calf, or, according to al-Hasan, on seven days. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari conclude that on the Day of Judgement, about which there is no doubt, every soul will be paid in full for what it earned, without injustice.

This passage describes how Jewish rabbis, who had been given a share of the Book, turned away when they were called to judge by God's Book. The commentators explain that what led them to turn away was their delusion that the Fire would touch them only for a few counted days. They differ on how long those days were. Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Kathir say they were the forty days during which their forefathers worshipped the calf, while al-Hasan says seven days, and some later scholars take them to be scattered periods after which the punishment ends. As for what deceived them in their religion, Qatada identifies their claim that they are God's sons and beloved ones, while Mujahid identifies their claim that the Fire would touch them only for a few days. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and others add that they claimed God had promised their father Ya'qub that He would punish his descendants only for the length of an oath's fulfilment, and al-Baydawi and al-Alusi repeat these possibilities. The point of the verse, most agree, is that this illusion made them despise both punishment and truth. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur read the question 'how will it be' as a way of expressing the terror of the Day when all will be gathered and every soul repaid for what it earned without wrong. Al-Zamakhshari compares this belief to what the Jabriyya and the Hashwiyya hope for, and Abu Hayyan follows him, while al-Alusi and others answer such criticism. Al-Razi draws an argument from the verse in the debate over threat and eternal punishment, and each school keeps its own reading of it.

This verse expresses an awe-filled warning about the fate of those who fabricate lies against God and are deceived by their own wishful thinking. It asks what their state will be when God gathers them on the Day about which there is no doubt, when every soul will be paid in full for what it has earned, and no one will be wronged. The commentators connect the verse to the claim of the Jews that the Fire would touch them only for a few counted days, a claim they regard as false. Al-Tabari explains that the phrase 'how then' is a rhetorical question of magnification that needs no answer, and that the lam in 'for a day' means 'in' according to al-Kisa'i, while the Basran grammarians read it as 'for the reckoning of a day', and al-Tabari takes it as 'for what will happen on a day'. On 'there is no doubt in it', al-Tabari reads it as no doubt about its coming, while al-Razi reads it as no doubt about its occurrence. Ibn Kathir and others understand that each soul receives the recompense of its deeds, good or bad. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the pronoun 'they' refers to the sense of 'each soul', which covers all people. Al-Razi and other theologians used the verse in the debate over threat and the eternity of punishment for major sins: the Mu'tazilites took it to confirm punishment, while the Sunnis maintained that the believer does not remain in the Fire forever, and al-Razi answered that the verse is a general statement. Scholars differed on the length of the 'counted days': forty days according to Qatada and al-Rabi', seven days according to al-Hasan, and the days of Adam's creation according to Mujahid. Ibn Kathir reports that these days were the period during which the calf was worshipped.

The verse instructs the Prophet to address God with this supplication: O God, Owner of all sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and take it from whom You will, You honour whom You will and humble whom You will, in Your hand is the good, and You are powerful over all things. The commentators agree that the verse affirms God's sole sovereignty and His exclusive control over power and good. They differ on the occasion of its revelation. Ibn Abbas and Anas, as reported by al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi, say that after the conquest of Mecca the Prophet promised his community the lands of Persia and Byzantium, which the hypocrites and Jews mocked as impossible; Qatada reports instead that the Prophet asked God for this. On the meaning of 'sovereignty', Mujahid takes it to mean prophethood, while others understand political power, wealth, or dominion. Al-Hasan and others explain honour and humiliation as victory and defeat, wealth and poverty, or obedience and disobedience. Regarding 'in Your hand is the good', several scholars hold that evil is implied, while others, rejecting that evil is ascribed to God, see the mention of good alone as a matter of courtesy in address. The insertion of night into day is understood by most as the changing length of days and nights through the seasons. The bringing forth of the living from the dead varies: a living creature from a drop of semen, a believer from an unbeliever, grain from the ear, or a chick from the egg. Providing without reckoning means giving abundantly, without measure or return.

The commentators explain that the verse describes God's absolute power over the order of the cosmos: He makes the night enter the day and the day enter the night, that is, He adds to one what the other loses, so that one lengthens while the other shortens; He brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living; and He grants provision to whom He wills without measure. Most agree that the interpenetration refers to the variation in the length of day and night, as reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, and al-Tabari notes that one may reach fifteen hours while the other has nine. As for bringing the living from the dead, the majority take it literally: the human or animal from the drop of seed and the seed from the living being, the chick from the egg and the egg from the bird, the plant from the grain and the grain from the plant, as held by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ikrima and al-Suddi. Al-Hasan and Ata' understood it as the believer coming out of the unbeliever and the reverse, a figurative sense supported by a report about the pious woman Khalida bint al-Aswad. Al-Tabari prefers the literal meaning as the more common usage. Readers differ on the shadda of al-mayyit: the Kufans distinguish the dead from one who will die, while the Basrans consider the two forms equivalent, and al-Tabari favours the emphatic form. The verse ends with provision without reckoning, a boundless gift. Some report that it was revealed in response to the Jews and hypocrites who doubted that the Muslims would conquer Persia and Byzantium, and that it shows that the One who does such things can transfer dominion.

This verse forbids believers from taking disbelievers as allies in place of the believers, and states that whoever does so has no connection with God. It makes an exception for real fear, allowing outward friendliness in speech while the heart stays firm in faith. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand the prohibition to cover religious allegiance, support against Muslims and disclosing their weaknesses, with taqiyya permitted only under compulsion. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Dahhak restrict it to speech, while al-Tabari reports views that extend it to some actions. Qatada reads the exception as permitting kinship ties with a disbelieving relative, but al-Tabari considers this far from the apparent meaning. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya report that Mujahid and Mu'adh ibn Jabal held taqiyya to belong to the early period of Islam, whereas al-Hasan held it valid until the Day of Judgment. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that taqiyya does not extend to killing, and al-Razi and Ibn Kathir consider enduring until death more meritorious, citing 'Ammar ibn Yasir. Several scholars link the occasion of revelation to Jews in Medina, to hypocrites, or to Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a. The verse ends by warning of God's punishment and of the return to Him.

This verse states that God knows what hearts conceal and what tongues and deeds reveal, so nothing hidden or open escapes Him. Most commentators understand concealing and showing as inner inclination toward the disbelievers and alliance with them, either kept secret or expressed in word and act, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi explain. Al-Sudi and al-Kalbi add that it also refers to hostility toward the Prophet, whether kept hidden or turned into open fighting.

The exegetes agree that the clause "and He knows what is in the heavens and the earth" is a new sentence, not a continuation of the condition. It stresses the breadth of God's knowledge after the particular case has been named. The closing phrase, "God is capable of all things", completes the warning. Al-Zamakhshari sees the verse as explaining God's warning of Himself, and Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur stress that a threat cannot be evaded either through ignorance or through weakness.

Opinions differ on whether God knows things in time or eternally. Al-Razi answers that the change lies in relations and not in the essence of knowledge, while Ibn Uthaymin distinguishes God's prior knowledge of what will be from His knowledge after the event, which is the basis of reward and punishment. Commentators also discuss the wording "in your breasts", which al-Razi and Ibn Ashur explain as referring to the heart, the seat of inner thought.

Earlier verses are linked to this one in the discussion of taqiyya. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Shawkani and al-Jaza'iri allow outward friendliness under fear while the heart remains firm in faith, and they cite Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mu'adh ibn Jabal hold that taqiyya applies only in a situation of fear from an enemy at war.

This verse says that on the Day of Resurrection every soul will find present what it did of good and what it did of evil, and will wish that a vast distance lay between it and that evil. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, agree that finding refers to the presence of the records of deeds or of their recompense, and that the wish expresses a longing to be far from the evil. The word amad means a limit or term; al-Suddi and Muqatil take it as a physical distance, like that between east and west, while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir also link it to a span of time or the end of life. Al-Hasan al-Basri explains that a person would wish never to meet his deed, though in this world he enjoyed his sin. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that deeds do not endure, so the verb must be understood as the presence of their records or their rewards. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud prefer the reading in which the phrase about evil deeds begins a new sentence, since the familiar recitation uses the nominative. Commentators differ on what the pronoun in 'between them' refers to: al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take it to be the Day, while others take it to be the evil deed, the nearer noun. The repeated warning that God cautions you against Himself is explained as emphasis and reminder, and the closing mention of God's compassion is taken by al-Hasan and al-Baydawi to show that the warning itself is an act of mercy.

This verse states that a servant's love for God is proven by following the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and its fruit is that God loves the believer and forgives his sins, for God is Forgiving and Merciful. The commentators report several occasions of revelation. Al-Hasan and Ibn Juraij relate that some people in the Prophet's time claimed to love their Lord, and God made following the Prophet the sign of that love. Ibn Ishaq, quoting Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, says it was revealed about the Christian delegation of Najran who claimed to exalt the Messiah out of love for God; al-Tabari prefers this view because the whole surah deals with the Christians of Najran. Others say it concerns the Quraysh who prostrated to idols claiming to worship them out of love for God, or the Jews who said they were God's sons and beloved. Commentators agree that the servant's love means preferring obedience to God and seeking His pleasure, and that God's love means His approval, favour and pardon. Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Sa'di treat the verse as a criterion: whoever claims to love God without following the Prophet's Sunna is a liar. Al-Razi gives two lines of argument: the miracles oblige following him, and whoever wants God to love him must obey. Al-Zamakhshari reads love as the desire to reserve worship for God alone, while Ibn al-Qayyim calls it the verse of the trial and makes it the sign of mutual love. Al-Shawkani and al-Alusi note that many later scholars understand God's love as approval and drawing near.

This verse tells the Prophet to say: obey God and the Messenger; if you turn away, God does not love the disbelievers. Most commentators take it as addressed first to the Christian delegation of Najran. Al-Tabari explains that the Prophet reminds them they know his mission and find it written in their Gospel, so turning away from it is disbelief, a point al-Tabari transmits through Ibn Ishaq. Many link it to the verse before, where love of God is shown by following the Prophet. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir state that whoever claims to love God while opposing the Prophet's way is lying in his claim. Several accounts of the occasion of revelation are given: Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj mention people who said they loved God, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi cite Jews, idolaters, or the Christians of Najran, and a report attributes the words to Abdullah ibn Ubayy. Commentators agree that denying God's love expresses displeasure and refusal of approval, and that the disbelievers are those who turn away from obedience. The verb tawallaw can be read as past or present; al-Tabari favours the past. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that repeating the divine name and using the term disbelievers signal generality and cause. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as the conclusion of an extended exhortation to the People of the Book.

In this verse God declares that He chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of Imran, preferring them over the people of their time. The commentators agree that the choosing (istifa') refers to their selection for religion, prophethood or mission. Al-Tabari says He chose their religion, while al-Zajjaj holds that He chose them for prophethood. Adam is the father of mankind, and Noah, according to most, is the first messenger sent to the people of the earth, as Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report. Most exegetes take the family of Abraham to be Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes, and the prophets descended from them, and most include the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ among them. Al-Tabari, and Ibn 'Abbas in one report, understand it to mean the believers among them. On 'Imran, Muqatil identifies him as the father of Moses and Aaron, while al-Hasan, Wahb, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take him to be the father of Mary, mother of Jesus, relying on the context of the passage. The phrase 'offspring, one of another' is understood either as a real lineage or as a shared bond of faith. The closing words, 'God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing', are explained by al-Razi as His knowledge of who deserves to be chosen, and by al-Tabari as His hearing of the words of 'Imran's wife and His knowledge of her intention.

This verse states that God chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of Imran over the worlds, and then describes them as one descent, some of whom come from others. Commentators read the word "descendants" as an accusative, either in apposition to the two families or as a circumstantial complement.

Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir take this as a genealogical link: Moses and Aaron descend from Imran, Jesus is the son of Mary, daughter of Imran, and all the prophets come from this line. Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the word dhurriyya can mean both ancestors and offspring, since it derives from the root meaning to create. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi stress a continuous line of one stock.

Others, including al-Tabari, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya, explain that they are bound by religion, mutual support and belief in the divine oneness, in the same way the verse on the hypocrites uses the phrase. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud combine both meanings, presenting the link as both lineage and shared faith.

Scholars differ on who Imran is. Muqatil, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi identify him as Mary's father, while Muqatil in another report and Ibn Kathir elsewhere mention the father of Moses and Aaron. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi, and several others, favour Mary's father, since the following story concerns his wife.

As for the closing words, al-Tabari and al-Nasafi understand them as God hearing the words of Imran's wife and knowing her intention, while others read them as God's knowledge of who deserves to be chosen.

This verse recounts the wife of Imran, Hannah, the mother of Mary, who vowed to God the child in her womb as muharrar, that is, freed from worldly concerns and wholly devoted to worship and to the service of the sanctuary. The commentators agree on the general sense: she hoped for a boy, since such a vow was customarily made for sons who served places of worship. According to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, the vow came after a long period of barrenness: seeing a bird feeding its young beneath a tree, she longed for a child and prayed, and her husband Imran then died while she was pregnant.

On the meaning of muharran, al-Sha'bi gives "devoted to worship", Mujahid "a servant of the church", and Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr "freed from the things of this world". Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the mother was hoping for a son, which is why she spoke in those terms, and that a daughter was not accepted for this service under their custom. Al-Baghawi reports that such vows were made among the Children of Israel and that the child could, upon reaching maturity, choose to stay or leave.

As for "fa-taqabbal minni", all understand it as a request that the vow be accepted with favour, and "as-Sami' al-'Alim" as an affirmation that God hears her and knows her intention. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the phrase "God knows best what she has borne", depending on the reading, may be God's words or the mother's, and several commentators read it as an apology addressed to God. The shared conclusions are that the vow is a valid pious commitment and that one should trust in God's answering of prayer.

This verse tells how Hanna, the wife of 'Imran and mother of Mary, gave birth to a daughter after having dedicated the child in her womb, thinking it would be a boy, to serve the Temple in Jerusalem. Her words express disappointment and an apology to God, since a girl was not fit for that service as a boy would be, given menstruation and postpartum bleeding. The commentators largely agree that the words convey regret more than mere information. They differ on the phrase "God knows best what she gave birth to": al-Tabari reads it as God's own statement, following the majority reading, while others, including al-Zamakhshari, take it as the mother's words of consolation. Several, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, explain the name Mary as meaning servant or worshipper in their language, and the mother's plea to protect her and her offspring from Satan is explained as a request for divine protection. The hadith of Abu Hurayra that every newborn is touched by Satan except Mary and her son is widely cited, though some, such as al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar, reject it, while al-Zamakhshari accepts it in a figurative sense. The later verses, which the commentators also discuss, describe God accepting Mary graciously, Zakariyya taking charge of her, and the food he found with her out of season, which she attributed to God.

This verse tells that God graciously accepted Mary, whom her mother Hanna had dedicated as a free servant of the Temple in Jerusalem, caused her to grow in a goodly growth, and entrusted her to Zechariah. The commentators agree that the acceptance means God was pleased with her in place of the boy the vow had sought, and that her goodly growth refers to an upbringing marked by righteousness and chastity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that Zechariah took her under his care, in some accounts after a drawing of lots among the scholars at the river Jordan. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi report that Zechariah found with her fruit out of season, summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer, and asked her where it came from; she answered that it was from God. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi take this as a sign of the dignity of God's chosen servants, whereas the Mu'tazilite al-Jubba'i considered it a miracle granted to Zechariah or a prelude to Jesus's mission. The readings differ on the verb for her guardianship: the doubled form makes God the one who assigned Zechariah, while the simple form makes Zechariah the actor, and al-Tabari preferred the doubled reading. These variants do not change the overall meaning of the passage.

The commentators explain that Zakariyya, seeing that Marium had summer fruits in winter and winter fruits in summer, understood that God gives beyond ordinary causes. Despite his old age and his wife's barrenness, he hoped for a child and prayed: grant me from You a good offspring, meaning a pious and blessed son, for You are the Hearer of supplication. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir say he prayed at that very moment and place, while Ibn 'Ashur holds that the prayer was made in that place. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud argue that the desire for a child already existed and the scene only stirred it. The Mu'tazilites, as al-Razi reports, attribute the impulse solely to Marium's virtue, a view most commentators reject. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi note that dhurriyya can mean one child or many, and that the feminine tayyiba follows the word's form. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain tayyiba as blessed or obedient to God. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that asking for a righteous offspring is the practice of prophets and the righteous, and al-Qurtubi cites several hadiths on seeking children. Ibn Kathir notes the answer came quickly, while others place an interval between the prayer and the glad tidings. The commentators conclude that the passage shows the value of supplication and that God gives without measure to whom He wills.

This passage tells how the angels called out to Zechariah while he stood praying in the sanctuary, to give him the good news that God would grant him a son named Yahya. Most commentators hold that the caller was Gabriel alone, and that the plural is permitted in Arabic, either out of honour or because he was the chief of the angels. They agree that Yahya would confirm a word from God, namely Jesus son of Mary, who was called the Word of God because he was created by God's command

Zakariyya asks in wonder how he can have a son when old age has overtaken him and his wife is barren. God answers that He does what He wills. The commentators agree that Zakariyya did not doubt God's power; he sought assurance or expressed amazement. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report the account in which Satan tried to unsettle him by casting doubt on the call, while al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan understood the question as asking how the child would come about: whether they would return to youth or remain as they were. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the word anna can mean either 'how' or 'from where', and al-Razi holds that the astonishment came from a joy so great that it bewildered him. Opinions differ on their ages: Ibn 'Abbas gives one hundred and twenty for Zakariyya and ninety-eight for his wife, while others give other figures. Al-Razi explains that mentioning both his old age and his wife's barrenness intensifies the sense of improbability. As for 'thus God does what He wills', most take it to mean extraordinary acts beyond the usual order; some see the particle as pointing to a child born of an aged man and a barren woman, and al-Tabari adds that God can grant a child to one who had despaired, just as He created Zakariyya himself before.

The commentators explain that after the angels brought Zakariya the good news of Yahya while he was praying in the sanctuary, he asked God for a sign that his wife was pregnant. He was told that the sign would be that he could not speak to people for three days except by gestures, while remaining able to remember and glorify God morning and evening. The exegetes agree that the purpose of the sign was to free this time for remembering God and giving thanks, and that glorifying God here means prayer for some, that the evening runs from midday to sunset, and that the morning runs from dawn to mid-morning. They differ on the reason for his silence. Qatada and most exegetes, as al-Qurtubi reports, held it to be a punishment for asking for the sign after the angels had spoken to him directly. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya say there was no defect in his tongue but only a prohibition from speaking with people, while Jubayr ibn Nufayr says his tongue swelled until it filled his mouth. They also differ on the meaning of ramz: Mujahid and Ibn 'Atiyya say it is moving the lips, al-Dahhak and al-Hasan a gesture of hand or head, Qatada a sign, and al-Farra' a quiet murmur. On grammar, most treat the exception as disconnected, since a gesture is not speech, while others take it as connected because a gesture conveys meaning. Some note that jurists treat gestures as speech in oaths and similar matters, and cite the hadith of the Ansari slave-girl whose gesture the Prophet accepted. As for the remembrance, some read it as remembrance of the heart and others as remembrance aloud, and Ibn Kathir sees it as an order to give thanks for the blessing of a child.

This verse records the angels' words to Mary: God has chosen you, purified you, and preferred you above the women of the worlds. The commentators agree that it is an honour for Mary, but they differ on the meaning of some terms. Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Abbas understand the purification as deliverance from disbelief or sins; al-Suddi takes it to mean freedom from menstruation and postnatal bleeding; Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that many hold it to be a general purification from every physical, moral and religious defect. As for the second choosing, al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj restrict it to the women of her own time, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi take it as the miraculous birth of Jesus without a father, a unique privilege. Al-Zajjaj extends the preference to all women until the Day of Resurrection. Several hadiths are cited to rank women: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate that Mary, Khadija, Fatima and Asiya are among the best, and opinions differ on whether Mary is the foremost of all women or only the best of her age. Some read the two choosings as two distinct selections, others as an emphasis on one selection. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi also report that the angels addressed her directly, which many regard as an honour while others see it as inspiration.

In this verse, God speaks through the angels to Mary, commanding her to remain constantly devoted and humble before her Lord, to prostrate and to bow with those who bow, in gratitude for the choosing and purification she has received. The commentators agree that qunut means continuous obedience and worship, but they differ on its precise sense. Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, al-Rabi' and al-Awza'i take it as prolonging the standing in prayer, al-Awza'i even reporting that her feet swelled and pus ran from them from standing so long. Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd read it as obedience, al-Hasan as worship, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as sincerity toward God. As for prostration and bowing, most scholars see them as naming two pillars of prayer, some taking the phrase as referring to prayer itself. On bowing with those who bow, some understand congregational prayer, while Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes her private prayer at home from her prayer with the community. Regarding why prostration comes first, some say this was the order in their law, others argue that the particle wa does not imply sequence, and al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim note that prostration is the closest a servant comes to his Lord. The first choosing is generally explained as God accepting her mother's vow and dedicating her to worship, the second as the birth of Jesus without a father; Ibn Jarir takes "the women of the worlds" to mean the women of her own time, while others read it generally, supported by hadiths comparing her with Khadija, Asiya and Fatima. Scholars disagree on whether she was a prophet, since the angels addressed her: most reject this. The commentaries on the following verse describe the dispute over her guardianship and the drawing of lots with pens or arrows.

This verse refers to accounts of the unseen that can only be known through revelation: the stories of the family of Imran, Mary, Zakariya, Yahya and Isa. God revealed them to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who was not present when Zakariya's people cast their pens or lots to decide who would take charge of Mary, nor when they disputed over it. Most commentators understand the word aqlam as arrows or lots used for drawing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report, following Ibn Abbas and Qatada, that the lots were thrown into flowing water and Zakariya's stayed fixed against the current, so he was given her care. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy add that these pens may have been the ones used to copy the Torah, chosen for their blessing, while Ibn Ashur notes that Jews used their writing pens for such drawings. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi say that scholars cite the verse to justify casting lots when rights are equal, a view Abu Hanifa rejected. Al-Qurtubi adds that the maternal aunt has priority in custody. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the denial of his presence is said in mocking reply to those who rejected revelation, since neither hearing nor reading could have supplied the knowledge. Ibn Ashur sees in the passage a hint that the books of the People of the Book may omit such details, and al-Alusi notes that the double negation strengthens the proof of prophethood.

This verse from Surah Al Imran records the angels' announcement to Maryam that God gives her good news of a son who is a word from Him, whose name is al-Masih Isa son of Maryam, honoured in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near to God. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, understand the speaker to be Gabriel, and note that calling him the son of his mother rather than of a father signals that he will be born without a father. On the word 'word', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the creative command 'Be', while al-Razi and al-Biqa'i add that he is called so because his existence came from God's word alone, outside the usual causes. Regarding the name al-Masih, Ibn Kathir reports several explanations: that he was anointed with blessing, that he was cleansed of sins, or that he healed whoever he touched, and al-Zamakhshari and others connect it to a term meaning 'blessed'. Honour (wajaha) is explained by al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya as prophethood and standing among people in this life, and as intercession and high rank in the next. His speaking in the cradle is taken as a sign, and his speaking in maturity as a call to God. Scholars differ on details of grammar and lexicon in this verse, and the commentators do not decide between these readings.

In this verse, delivered through the angels, God tells Mary that He gives her good news of a son, born by a word from Him, whose name will be the Messiah Jesus son of Mary. The commentators explain that he will speak in the cradle, meaning in infancy, and will also speak as a grown man, which means he addresses people in both stages without difference, as the prophets do. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others see in his speech in the cradle a sign proving his mother's innocence against the accusations made against her. They also agree that his speech as an adult is a call and teaching, and that 'mahd' refers to the infant's cradle. On the meaning of 'kahl' (middle age), opinions differ: Mujahid understands it as forbearance, while most scholars take it as the stage between youth and old age, placed by some around thirty and by others around forty. Muqatil and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl link this speech to the moment he will be raised to heaven or to after his descent. Ibn Zayd sees in it a reference to his return at the end of time, when he will speak as an adult after killing the Dajjal. Some commentators, including al-Razi, hold that he was already a prophet when he spoke in the cradle, while others consider it a foundation for his prophethood. Finally, being among the righteous is understood by al-Tabari as belonging to their company and ranks, and by al-Razi as the highest of qualities.

Maryam is astonished that she could have a child when no man has touched her, and God replies that it is so: He creates what He wills as He wills, and when He decides a matter He says to it "Be" and it is. The commentators agree that her question expresses natural wonder and not doubt. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the answer announces a child created without a father, and Ibn Kathir notes that the verb "create" is used here, unlike "do" in the story of Zachariah, because a virgin birth is more extraordinary. Al-Zamakhshari sees the question as a denial mixed with wonder, while al-Baydawi and al-Razi take it as astonishment at something beyond custom, and al-Baydawi also allows that she may be asking how it will happen, through marriage or otherwise. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi relate that she asks about the means rather than the possibility. Regarding the word "my Lord" in her address, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi take it as addressed to Gabriel in the sense of "my master", whereas al-Zamakhshari considers this an odd reading and holds that she is calling upon God. As for "fayakun", Ibn Amir reads it in the subjunctive and the rest in the indicative; Ibn Atiyya judges the first reading less suitable. Nearly all agree that the formula "Be, and it is" expresses God's absolute power and the immediacy of creation, without any audible word.

This verse, spoken by the angels, reports that God will teach Jesus the Book, wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel. Commentators differ on the meaning of "the Book": Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Juraij and several others understand it as writing, the skill of forming letters by hand, which Ibn Kathir considers the apparent meaning, while al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take it as the category of divine scriptures or a book other than the Torah and the Gospel. "Wisdom" is read by Qatada as the Sunna, by Ibn 'Abbas as juristic understanding and the judgement of the prophets, by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi as a faculty combining knowledge and moral refinement, and by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir as soundness in speech and action. Nearly all agree that the Torah is the Book revealed to Moses, and note that the Gospel had not yet been revealed when Mary was addressed, but is named because it was known among the prophets and was destined to descend. The reading of Nafi', 'Asim and Ya'qub in the third person ("yu'allimuhu") is linked to the preceding context, while the first-person plural reading ("nu'allimuhu") expresses the same idea in another form; al-Tabari holds that the two readings carry the same meaning, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan find some grammatical connections too distant. The verse thus presents this divine teaching as a preparation for Jesus' mission to the Children of Israel.

The commentators explain that this verse describes ʿIsa's mission to the Children of Israel and the sign he brings from his Lord: he shapes from clay the form of a bird, breathes into it and it becomes a bird by God's permission, he heals the born-blind and the leper, raises the dead by God's permission, and tells them what they eat and what they store in their homes. The commentators agree that all of this happens by God's leave and not by any power of ʿIsa's own, and that these signs are a proof of his truthfulness for those who believe. Al-Tabari, then al-Razi, al-Baydawi and others explain that khalq here means shaping and determining a form, not creation from nothing; al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyya note that the pronoun in fa-anfukh may refer to the clay, the form, or the likeness. Readers differ on tayran and ta'iran: Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the plural as reflecting the many birds made, and the singular as referring to the bat alone, which the Children of Israel had asked for. On al-akmah, Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada say the man born blind, Mujahid one who sees by day but not by night, ʿIkrima one with weak sight, al-Hasan and al-Suddi a blind man in general. Al-Tabari notes that the common Arabic sense is blindness. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir report that ʿIsa healed many illnesses by invocation alone and that crowds came to him. On raising the dead, Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite accounts about Lazarus, the widow's son, the tax collector's daughter and Sam ibn Nuh, though Ibn Kathir disputes some details. As for telling what is eaten and stored, Mujahid takes it as what was eaten the day before and hidden, Qatada links it to the table sent down from heaven and its prohibition on storing, and al-Suddi to the schoolboys. All agree these signs are proof for the believer, and God knows best.

This verse records Jesus's words to the Children of Israel: he came confirming what was before him of the Torah, to make lawful for them some of what had been forbidden, bringing a sign from their Lord, and urging them to fear God and obey him. The commentators agree that Jesus affirmed the Torah and acted by it, and that his law lightened some of its burdens. Al-Tabari, citing Wahb ibn Munabbih, reports that he kept the Sabbath and faced Jerusalem in prayer. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others, the prohibitions he lifted included camel meat, certain fats, and some fish and birds. Abu 'Ubayda held that "some" here means "all", a view rejected by al-Qurtubi and others, who kept the word in its literal sense and noted that Jesus permitted neither murder nor theft. Al-Razi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir hold that he abrogated part of the Mosaic law, while others say he abrogated nothing and only clarified points of disagreement. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi argue that abrogation does not contradict confirmation, since it only marks the end of a ruling's period. As for the "sign", most identify it with the miracles Jesus performed, while Ibn Juzayy and others point to his words, "God is my Lord and your Lord". In sum, the verse calls to piety, obedience and monotheism, presenting Jesus as God's servant and messenger.

This verse records Jesus's words to the Children of Israel: God is his Lord and theirs, so they should worship Him, for this is the straight path. The commentators agree on this plain meaning: worship is due to God alone, and Jesus presents himself as a servant of God, not as a partner in divinity. Al-Tabari prefers the reading with a kasra on the hamza of 'inna' because it is the reading of the majority of reciters. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud mention a reading with a fatha, which makes the phrase an apposition to 'a sign', and they then see it as proof of his mission, since all the prophets proclaimed this same message. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi stress the call to monotheism and Jesus's humility in calling himself a servant. Al-Razi notes that the statement is meant to rule out any claim of divinity, and Ibn 'Ashur observes that 'inna' here gives the reason for the command to fear God and obey. The commentators agree on the general sense and do not settle the finer points of the sentence's construction.

The commentators explain that when Jesus sensed disbelief among the Children of Israel and their intent to kill him, he asked who would support him in God's cause. The disciples answered that they were God's helpers, declared their faith, and asked him to bear witness to their submission. The plain meaning is thus a call for support to spread the message and to protect the prophet from his enemies. On the preposition 'ila', al-Tabari, al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Kathir take it to mean 'along with', while al-Hasan, Abu 'Ubayda and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi read it as 'in' or as a goal. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer an implied sense of adding one's support to God's support.

The scholars differ on the origin of the name 'Hawariyyun'. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn 'Abbas say it was for the whiteness of their garments; Abu Arta'a and al-Dahhak say they were launderers; Qatada says they were the elite of the prophets. Al-Tabari finds the root meaning of intense whiteness most likely, while Ibn Kathir adopts the sense of 'helper', citing the Prophet's words about al-Zubayr. Some reports describe them as fishermen, others as kings.

There is agreement that the disciples declared their submission to God, and that faith here includes acceptance and surrender, not mere assent. As for 'the witnesses' they ask to be joined with, Ibn 'Abbas and others understand them as the community of Muhammad ﷺ, while others take it to mean all who testified to the truth of the messengers.

This verse records the prayer of Jesus's disciples, the hawariyyun, after Jesus sensed disbelief among his people and asked who would be his helpers. They say: we believe in what You have sent down and we follow the messenger, so write us among the witnesses. The commentators agree on the core meaning: faith in the revelation and loyalty to the messenger. They differ on who the witnesses are. Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, followed by Qurtubi and Baydawi, identify them as the community of Muhammad, who testify that the messengers delivered their message. Ata, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi take them to be the prophets, since each prophet testifies for his community. Muqatil calls them the truthful, al-Zajjaj those who attest to the prophets' truth, and al-Razi adds mystical readings such as those who witness divine unity. Al-Wahidi and Ibn Sa'di stress witnesses to God's oneness and to the prophets' mission. On the word hawariyyun, the explanations differ: launderers according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi Najih, fishermen according to al-Suddi, or the chosen intimates and helpers according to Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Juzayy. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the term became the name of Jesus's companions. Modern commentators such as Sayyid Qutb read the request as a commitment to bear witness to the faith through one's conduct and effort to establish its system.

The commentators explain that the "scheming" in this verse refers first to the scheme of the disbelieving Children of Israel against Jesus, who plotted to kill him secretly after he perceived their disbelief and sought helpers. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, Ibn Kathir and most others report that God's "scheming" is His requital of their scheme. The word for scheming is then applied to the requital by verbal correspondence, as in "God mocks them".
