Al-Suddi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir relate that God cast Jesus' likeness upon the man who betrayed him, or upon another, who was killed and crucified in his place, while Jesus was raised to heaven. According to al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, the one who received the likeness was a disciple; others say he was a hypocrite who guided them to Jesus.

The commentators agree on the basic meaning of scheming as secret deception, and that attributing it to God is, according to the majority, permissible only by verbal correspondence. Al-Razi and al-Alusi hold that it may be used in a sense befitting God's majesty, while Ibn 'Uthaymin says it applies to God only in the context of a response, since scheming out of place is a defect. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that "best of schemers" means the most powerful in scheming and the most effective in retaliation.

The details of the story and the meaning of "tawaffi" differ, but all agree that the schemers failed and that Jesus was saved.

This verse recounts how the people of Jesus plotted against him and how God outwitted their scheme. God tells Jesus that He will cause him to die or take him in full, raise him to Himself, purify him from those who disbelieved, place those who follow him above those who disbelieved until the Day of Resurrection, and that all will return to Him, who will judge between them concerning their disputes. The commentators agree that Jesus was raised to heaven, but differ on the meaning of 'mutawaffika'. Al-Tabari, al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd understand it as taking him from the earth and raising him to God without death. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas understands it as a sleep during which he was raised. Ibn 'Abbas, in one report, understands it as an actual death, and Wahb ibn Munabbih relates that God caused him to die for three hours before raising him, while Ibn Ishaq reports that the Christians speak of seven hours. Al-Farra' and others hold that the order is reversed, meaning that God raises him and then causes him to die after his descent. As for the superiority of his followers, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jurayj take it to mean the Muslims who follow his way, with proof and power, Ibn Zayd applies it to the Christians over the Jews, and al-Mawardi also mentions superiority through argument. Regarding the plot, the Jews planned to kill him, and God made his likeness fall upon another who was crucified in his place. Several commentators cite the sound hadith of Jesus's descent at the end of time to judge by the law of Muhammad, break the cross, kill the swine, and then die.

This verse from Al Imran describes the fate of both groups after God announces that He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning their disputes. Those who disbelieved will be punished with a severe punishment in this world and in the Hereafter, and no one will come to their aid. The commentators explain the worldly punishment as killing, captivity, the poll tax, humiliation and abasement, as al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir report. The punishment in the Hereafter is the Fire in all accounts. Abu Hayyan adds that someone who suffers none of these harms lives in constant apprehension, knowing that Islam seeks him out. Al-Razi, by contrast, holds that humiliation and poverty fall mainly on the Jews. The scholars differ on who the "disbelievers" are. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and others say they are those who rejected Jesus' prophethood, Jews, Christians and others, while Ibn Zayd says that the followers of Jesus are the Christians and the disbelievers are the Jews. As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, God will pay them their rewards in full. Hafs reads "yuwaffihim" in the third person, while the rest read "nuwaffihim" in the first person. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see the verse as a detailed account of the judgment mentioned earlier. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the closing phrase, "God does not love the wrongdoers," as meaning that God does not treat the obedient like the disobedient. Ibn 'Ashur considers that punishment in both worlds is a particular case rather than a general rule.

This verse states that those who believe and do righteous deeds will be given their rewards in full, and that God does not love the wrongdoers. The commentators explain that faith means acknowledging the prophethood and what the Messenger brought, and righteous deeds means performing the obligations and laws God prescribed, as al-Tabari reports from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tabari holds that the verse affirms God's freedom from injustice, since He does not treat the good doer like the wrongdoer, and that its declarative form contains both a warning to disbelievers and a promise to believers. Al-Mawardi, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and others connect it to the preceding account of 'Isa, and understand the full payment as the allotment of ranks in Paradise according to deeds, though Ibn 'Atiyya adds that entry into Paradise itself is by God's mercy. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the verse separates righteous deeds from faith and compares the reward to a worker's wage. The reading with the third-person verb is attributed to Hafs, while most readers use the first-person plural, which Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain as the plural of majesty. Al-Razi uses the verse in the debate over divine love and will: the Mu'tazilites take it as denying that God wills injustice, while Ash'ari scholars define love as willing good to reach someone. Ibn 'Uthaymin remarks that denying love for wrongdoers implies affirming it for others, and that the injustice meant includes disbelief along with other sins. The sources agree that the verse closes the discussion of 'Isa and promises believers their full reward.

The commentators explain that the demonstrative "that" refers to the preceding account of Jesus, Mary, Zechariah, John and the disciples, which God recites to the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Tabari adds that this recitation comes through Gabriel, and that God attributes it to Himself as an honour. Nearly all agree that the "signs" are proofs and lessons confirming prophethood, since these reports could not be known to an unlettered man who neither reads nor mixes with the People of the Book. Al-Razi and others also allow that the signs may mean the verses of the Quran itself.

As for the "wise reminder", Ibn Abbas and the majority take it to mean the Quran. Ibn Atiyya and others note that "wise" may mean perfected and free from any flaw, or possessing wisdom, or even judging; al-Razi says its wisdom is so abundant that it seems to speak wisdom.

A different view, reported by al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, identifies the reminder with the Preserved Tablet, from which all revealed books were said to have been copied. This is presented as a minority reading, and al-Razi and others prefer the Quran as the primary meaning.

Finally, many commentators place the verse in its context: it closes the account of Jesus and leads into the dispute with the Najran delegation, whose answer is the statement that Jesus is like Adam.

This verse states that Jesus's extraordinary case before God is like that of Adam: both were created without a father, and Adam more remarkably without a father or a mother. God formed him from dust and then said to him, Be, and he was. The commentators report that it was revealed in answer to the Christian delegation of Najran, who objected that Jesus could not be God's servant since he had no father. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Jalalayn agree that the comparison concerns birth without a father, and that the clause he created him from dust explains Adam's case. They also note that thumma may signal a gap in the report rather than in the event, and that fa-yakunu describes a past situation. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the more astonishing case is used to silence the opponent, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that one shared feature is enough for the comparison. Ibn 'Atiyya takes mathal here to mean the condition or description, a reading Abu Hayyan discusses without deciding. Al-Biqa'i stresses that every birth depends on God's will alone. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi draw from the verse the validity of reasoning by analogy. Ibn 'Ashur says the pronoun in he created him refers to Adam. The commentators link the passage to the mutual invocation of curse (mubahala) that follows, without judging between the scholars.

This verse states that what has been told to the Prophet ﷺ about 'Isa (Jesus) is the truth from his Lord, and forbids him to be among those who doubt. Most commentators take al-haqq as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning 'this is the truth', with 'from your Lord' as a complement, though al-Baydawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and others allow al-haqq to be the subject. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy understand the truth to be the reality of 'Isa as a servant of God, His messenger and His word. Al-Razi says it distinguishes this truth from what the Christians and Jews claimed about Mary, while others see the truth as the example of Adam. The word al-imtira' means doubt, and the commentators differ over whom the address targets. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi take it as an address to the Prophet ﷺ intended to strengthen his certainty, while al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi say he never doubted and that the address concerns his community or any listener. Ibn 'Uthaymin explains that it is an indirect rebuke of the doubters rather than a suggestion that the Prophet could doubt. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the argument refutes the divinity of 'Isa, since Adam, created without father or mother, was not worshipped. The commentators also report that the passage was revealed about the Christian delegation of Najran.

The verse addresses the Prophet after the Christian delegation of Najran disputed about Jesus, once knowledge had come to him: he is commanded to invite them to mubahala, that is, to gather their sons, their women and themselves, then to pray together for God's curse upon the liars. Commentators agree that the verse was revealed concerning the Najran delegation and that the dispute concerned Jesus as a servant and messenger of God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the Prophet invited them to the mubahala, that they refused it and agreed to pay the jizya, al-Aqib fearing total destruction. Opinions differ on who is meant by the family: Ibn Abbas, Jabir and al-Sha'bi name al-Hasan, al-Husayn, Fatima and Ali, a view followed by al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, whereas al-Tabari keeps the sense broader, and Rashid Rida, cited by Ibn Uthaymin, considers this identification at odds with the apparent wording. On the meaning of nabtahil, al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir take it as earnest supplication, while al-Kisa'i and Abu Ubayda take it as mutual cursing, and al-Razi discusses both. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that bringing the children and women shows the Prophet's full confidence in his truth, and Ibn Atiyya notes that the Christians' refusal is itself a sign of his prophethood.

The commentators explain that the verse affirms that the account God has given about Jesus is the true report beyond doubt, that there is no true deity but Allah, and that He is the Mighty, the Wise. Most take "this" as referring to what precedes about Jesus, though some take it to refer to the Qur'an. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir connect the verse to the dispute with the Najran delegation and the call to mutual invocation of curse (mubahala), which they refused, as reported in the narrations of Ibn Ishaq. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Atiyya explain "qasas" as a connected narrative, and Ibn Atiyya holds that although it was revealed concerning Najran, its address extends to the People of the Book in general. Most read the "min" in "min ilah" as an emphatic particle of total negation, a rebuttal of the Christian Trinity. Al-Razi sees in it an answer to the argument from Jesus raising the dead and shows that power and wisdom belong to God alone. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn explain that "tawallaw" means turning away, and that God knows those who corrupt by departing from the truth. Ibn Ashur sees the sentence as a parenthesis that establishes Jesus' servanthood after denying his divinity. The commentators do not decide between these readings and report them as they stand.

The commentators explain that this verse comes after the account of Jesus, who is the servant and messenger of God, the word He cast to Mary, and that there is no god but God. If those who dispute reject this truth, God is knowing of the corruptors: this is a warning of the punishment they deserve. Most exegetes agree that turning away means refusing the truth and faith, and that the corrupters are those who worship other than God and call people to worship other than Him, as al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir say.

Most report that the verse concerns the Najran delegation who argued with the Prophet about Jesus, then refused the mutual curse (mubahala) and asked for a settlement. Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti report that the Christians held back, knowing the Prophet was truthful and fearing ruin. Al-Tabari cites several reports but notes that most are incomplete transmissions, and that only the account from Ibn Abbas is continuous. Ibn Ashur sees the verse as a formal record against those who turn away, since they chose obstinacy over seeking the truth.

Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan explain turning away as rejecting monotheism or the acknowledgment of God's oneness, while Ibn al-Jawzi gives other meanings, including refusing the curse. Ibn Atiyya holds that the verse was revealed about the Najran delegation but that its wording covers all People of the Book. Al-Zamakhshari understands the corruption as belief in the Trinity.

God instructs His Prophet to call the People of the Book, meaning Jews and Christians according to the commentators, to a fair common word: worshipping God alone, associating nothing with Him, and not taking one another as lords besides God by obeying others in what God has neither permitted nor forbidden. If they turn away, the believers are to declare that they are submitting to God. The commentators agree that "sawa" means justice and equity. They differ over who is addressed. Al-Hasan, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd, followed by al-Tabari, say it was revealed concerning the Christian delegation of Najran, whereas Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jurayj say it concerns the Jews of Medina who disputed about Abraham. Al-Razi holds that it covers both groups, and al-Zamakhshari identifies the common word with the declaration of God's oneness. On taking lords, Ibn Jurayj understands obedience to leaders in disobedience, Ikrima understands prostration, and Muqatil and al-Zajjaj understand the deifying of Jesus and Ezra. Ibn Juzayy, Ibn 'Ashur and others note that God alone determines what is lawful and unlawful, and some cite a hadith of 'Adi ibn Hatim. The verb "tawallaw" means to turn away, and some read in it an implicit rebuke of their disbelief.

God addresses the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, and asks why they dispute about Abraham when each group claims he followed its religion. Yet the Torah and the Gospel were revealed only long after him, so he cannot have followed a faith that arose after his death. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baghawi report that the occasion was a dispute before the Prophet between the Christians of Najran and Jewish rabbis, each side claiming Abraham as its own. Al-Tabari also cites another account, transmitted from Qatada and Mujahid, that the verse concerns the Jewish claim that Abraham was one of them and died a Jew. Ibn Atiyya holds that the verse addresses both groups. The commentators agree on the plain sense: the claim is refuted by reason. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud mention roughly a thousand years between Abraham and Moses and another thousand between Moses and Jesus, although the figures reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Ishaq differ. Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur take the argument to address both parties, and read the dispute as being about attribution rather than religion alone. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baghawi add that Judaism and Christianity came into being after their respective scriptures were revealed. Ibn Kathir reads the verse as forbidding argument about what one has no knowledge of, while al-Jaza'iri and Ibn Sa'di stress that God knows Abraham's true state and they do not. Al-Shinqiti and Ibn Ashur show that the debate centers on the nature of the claim itself, whether to belong to Abraham or to attribute one's religion to him, and the verse answers both. The commentators conclude that Abraham was a pure monotheist, submitting to God, and not among the polytheists, and that the closest to him are those who followed him, then the Prophet and those who believed with him.

God addresses the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, rebuking them for disputing about Abraham. According to the commentators, they argued about what they had knowledge of, meaning what they found in their scriptures or what they had seen or heard from their prophets and laws, and then argued about what they had no knowledge of, namely Abraham and his religion, on which their books say nothing. Most commentators report that each side claimed Abraham as one of its own. God answers that the Torah and the Gospel were revealed long after Abraham, so he could not have followed a religion that did not yet exist. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Suddi explain that what they knew refers to what they had witnessed, or what was commanded or forbidden to them. Others, such as al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, read the phrase as describing a claim to knowledge rather than real knowledge, so the blame falls on arguing without knowledge. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi take the knowledge to mean the description of Muhammad found in their books, though this reading is not shared by all. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, note that disputation is not condemned when it rests on knowledge. All agree that God knows the truth and that the people of the Book do not.

This verse states that Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, and he was not among the polytheists, but a hanif and a Muslim, meaning one who turned away from false beliefs toward the upright religion and submitted to God's command. It rejects the claim of the People of the Book that Abraham belonged to their faith. The commentators agree that Judaism and Christianity arose long after Abraham, so they cannot be attributed to him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that this answered Jews and Christians who disputed about him in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Tabari explains that the hanif is one who follows God's command and stays on the path of guidance, and most read the Muslim here as one who submits humbly to God. Al-Samani, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi define the hanif as one who turns away from all religions toward the straight path, and al-Baghawi adds that he affirms God's oneness, performs the pilgrimage and sacrifice, and faces the Ka'ba. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan record that the word derives from straightness or from inclination, while others take it to mean a pilgrim. Al-Razi distinguishes whether the denial concerns fundamentals or details of the law. Al-Alusi lists two meanings of Islam here, and Ibn 'Ashur judges that the phrase about not being among the polytheists refutes all three claims together. As for the rest of the verse, most commentators hold that the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him, then the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, as Ibn Kathir and others report from a hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn 'Abbas relates that the revelation came over the dispute of the rabbis and the Christians of Najran, while al-Wahidi and al-Mawardi recount the episode of the migration to Abyssinia. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that the negation precedes the affirmation in this verse.

The commentators explain that this verse establishes that the people most worthy of Abraham, peace be upon him, and closest to him are those who followed his religion in his own time, then the Prophet Muhammad and those who believed with him, since they share his monotheism and much of his law, and that God is the protector of the believers through support, success and honour. Al-Tabari and Qatada take this to mean the believers among Abraham's followers and the Prophet's companions, and al-Tabari cites the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud in which the Prophet recites this verse and says that his own close friends among the prophets are Abraham. Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith is transmitted in divergent ways, with and without Masruq in the chain, and that several scholars regard the connected version as acceptable. On the occasion of revelation, Ibn 'Abbas and those who follow him report that Jewish leaders claimed Abraham was a Jew and that Muslims had no right to him, a story also recorded by Ibn Ishaq and al-Wahidi in the account of the emigrants to Abyssinia and the Negus. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Zamakhshari hold that the verse refutes the Jewish and Christian claims on Abraham, since Judaism and Christianity came after the Torah and the Gospel, about a thousand years after him. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi understand priority as nearness, support or argument. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see the mention of the Prophet after those who followed Abraham as a mark of honour. The readings differ: the accusative "wa-l-nabiyya" attaches to the pronoun in "ittaba'uhu", and the genitive attaches to "Ibrahim". Several modern commentaries, such as Ibn 'Uthaymin and Ibn Sa'di, hold that true closeness to Abraham is through adopting his way rather than by descent, and link God's special guardianship to the perfection of faith.

This verse reports that a group among the People of the Book, in most accounts the Jews, wished to lead the believers astray and turn them back to disbelief. The commentators differ on the meaning of misguiding. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take it to mean diverting Muslims from Islam and back to their own faith, while al-Tabari himself, citing a line of poetry by al-Akhtal, reads it as destruction, a view Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan judge unconvincing as a basis for the word's meaning. Abu Ali explains it as sowing doubt in the believers' minds through objections. On the phrase 'they mislead none but themselves', al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi hold that the burden of their misguidance falls only on them, since their punishment is multiplied, whereas al-Razi and Ibn Kathir see it as the consequence of their malice and rejection of guidance. On 'and they are unaware', most take it to mean they do not realise this harm recoils on them, and al-Qurtubi adds that they should have known Islam is true. The commentators also relate the occasion: Jewish men invited Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Hudhayfa and Ammar to their religion. Mujahid, al-Kalbi and others mention a scheme in which some would profess Islam at dawn and renounce it at dusk. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi link the verse to the wider passage, while Ibn Sa'di and Ibn Uthaymin read it as a warning about the enduring hostility of these people towards believers.

God addresses the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, rebuking them for disbelieving in God's signs, meaning what their scriptures say about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, even though they bear witness that these are true. Most commentators, including Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jurayj, explain that the Prophet's description is written in the Torah and the Gospel, that they find it there, and that they deny it while knowing it is true. Al-Mawardi gives a second reading: they witness similar signs in the miracles of prophets they accept. Al-Razi suggests that the denial may concern what the texts signify rather than the texts themselves, and that the witness may be given by the heart and reason. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi offer other readings, in which the signs are the Qur'an and its inimitability, or the Prophet's miracles. Ibn 'Ashur takes the signs to be miracles, and the concealment to cover both their acknowledgment of the Prophet and laws their scholars set aside. Ibn Juzayy links the verse to the plot of some rabbis to mislead believers, while Ibn Kathir and others read it as a rebuke of conduct the preceding verses already describe. The verse also condemns mixing truth with falsehood and concealing the truth while knowing it.

God rebukes the People of the Book for mixing truth with falsehood and for concealing the truth while knowing it. The commentators generally understand the truth to be the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and his description found in the Torah and the Gospel, which they hid. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the mixing consisted of blending Islam with Judaism and Christianity, professing faith outwardly while keeping their own religion in their hearts. Ibn Zayd understood the truth as the revealed Torah and the falsehood as what they wrote with their own hands. Ibn Abbas and Qatada report that they would accept Islam in the morning and reject it in the evening to sow doubt among the believers, a plot the preceding verses describe. Al-Razi distinguishes two tactics: rejecting the Prophet while knowing he is truthful, and spreading confusion and hiding the proofs. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya add that falsehood can also mean distorting the verses by misinterpreting them. Ibn Ashur notes that concealing the truth may refer to hiding the prophetic announcement or the laws they had abandoned. The commentators observe that the phrase 'while you know' is a clause emphasizing deliberate obstinacy rather than ignorance. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri draw from it a warning against concealing the truth and against falsification.

The verse describes a planned trick by some People of the Book: they pretend to believe in what was revealed to the believers at the start of the day, then deny it at its end, hoping to unsettle the believers and turn them back from their faith. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most early commentators read it as a deception meant to sow doubt among weaker Muslims. Qatada, al-Rabi' and Mujahid take 'the face of the day' to mean its beginning, and reading 'disbelieve at its end' as abandoning the outward faith. They also agree that the phrase 'believe only in those who follow your religion' is the Jews' own speech to one another, while 'Say: guidance is the guidance of God' is a divine answer that interrupts it. Accounts of the occasion of revelation differ. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that twelve rabbis plotted the scheme, and the best-known version links it to the change of the qibla: the Jews would pray toward the Ka'ba in the morning and toward the rock in the evening, as Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid relate. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi discuss the grammar and the variant readings. Ibn 'Atiyya records disagreement over the construction of 'an yu'ta ahad', including Ibn Kathir's reading as a question. Ibn al-Qayyim lists the scheme among Jewish tricks against the Prophet. Al-Razi sees the revelation of a secret plot as a proof of prophethood. Ibn 'Ashur reads the trick as an attempt to make it seem that the religion was tested and rejected.

This verse reports a scheme attributed by most commentators to some People of the Book, who proposed that some of them profess faith in the morning and reject it in the evening, so that the Muslims might doubt and turn back, and who told their followers to trust only those who share their religion. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the plot was aimed at unsettling the believers, and Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that it was attributed to Jewish leaders, some of whom were said to be from Khaybar. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya add that the scheme was linked by some transmitters to the change of the qibla.

The commentators agree that the reply, that guidance belongs to God alone, is a rebuttal of the scheme. They differ on whether this sentence is God's own speech inserted into the reported words, as al-Tabari and al-Baydawi suggest, or part of the Prophet's instruction, as al-Suyuti and al-Zamakhshari note. The phrase that a person may be given what you were given, or argue against you before your Lord, is the most debated part. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as the Jews' own words or as a rebuke of envy. Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi list several grammatical readings, including Ibn Kathir's interrogative reading. Al-Razi treats the verse as one of the most difficult in the chapter.

On the meaning of bounty, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj understand it as prophethood, the Book or Islam, while others take it more broadly as favour in general. The verse ends with the statements that God is all-encompassing and all-knowing and that He grants His mercy to whom He wills, on which the commentators are in agreement.

This verse states that God singles out whomever He wills for His mercy, and that His grace is immense. The commentators generally read it as the continuation of the words of a group of Jews, who wanted to keep their people in their own faith and turn them away from belief in what was sent down to the Muslims; God answers that guidance and grace are in His hand alone. As for the "mercy" meant, the early scholars differ: al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Rabi' take it to be prophethood, Ibn Jurayj the Qur'an and Islam, and Ibn 'Abbas religion, while others understand it as abundant remembrance of God. Al-Razi notes that the verse refutes those who would confine God's favour to fixed ranks or persons, and that grace is a matter of divine generosity rather than of earned desert.

On linguistic matters, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn 'Ashur regard the passage as one of the most difficult in the sura and offer several analyses of the phrases "that anyone should be given" and "that they should dispute with you before your Lord". Some read these as part of the Jewish speech, others as God's own reply; Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan discuss the readings, including Ibn Kathir's reading as an interrogative of reproach. Al-Shawkani reports that the group in question were the Banu al-Nadir, Qurayza and Qaynuqa, while others take it to mean the People of the Book in general.

The commentators agree that the verse rejects the Jewish claim and affirms that the source of guidance and favour belongs to God alone, who is vast in knowledge and knows who deserves His grace.

This verse distinguishes two kinds of People of the Book in matters of trust. Some, if entrusted with a great treasure, return it in full; others, if entrusted with a single dinar, deny it and return it only when pressed and repeatedly demanded. The commentators explain this conduct by a belief that it is permissible to take the property of the Arabs, called the Ummiyyun: 'There is no blame on us regarding the Ummiyyun,' they say, falsely attributing this to God while knowing it is a lie. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the Ummiyyun with the Arabs who did not follow a scripture, while Qatada and, in one report, Ibn Abbas understand them as the polytheists. Al-Razi and others note that the figures of a hundredweight and a dinar are examples of large and small sums rather than fixed amounts. The meaning of 'as long as you stand over him' is debated: Mujahid and Qatada take it as persistent demand, al-Sudi as physically standing over the debtor, and al-Tabari prefers the sense of insistent claiming. The verse then answers the claim with 'Yes indeed': whoever fulfils his covenant and fears God, God loves the God-fearing. Ibn Kathir and others cite a saying of the Prophet that a trust must be returned to the pious and the wicked alike. The commentators differ on who is meant: some name Abdullah ibn Salam as the faithful depositary and Finhas ibn Azura as the traitor, while others divide the categories between Christians and Jews.

The verse answers the claim of the People of the Book that there is no blame in taking the property of those who do not share their religion. It affirms that there is indeed a responsibility in this matter, and then states that whoever keeps his covenant with God, returns trusts, and fears God by refraining from betrayal and breaking of promises, God loves him. Commentators agree that "bala" is a rebuttal of their claim and that "man awfa" begins a new sentence that confirms what precedes it. They differ over what the pronoun in "bi-ahdihi" refers to. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it to refer to God, meaning the covenant He made in the Torah to believe in Muhammad, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya take it to refer back to the one who keeps the covenant; Ibn Atiyya considers that both readings come to the same meaning. As for piety, Ibn Abbas restricts it to avoiding associating partners with God, whereas al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir extend it to avoiding all sins and performing acts of obedience, a view also held by Ibn Sa'di. Several exegetes connect the preceding verses to Jews who betrayed trusts, and Ibn Kathir cites reports about Abdullah ibn Salam, who faithfully returned a sum entrusted to him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari also relay a prophetic saying about the trust being returned to the righteous and the wicked, and another on the property of protected non-Muslims taken during raids, which is lawful only with their consent. The commentators agree that the passage shows that keeping one's word and piety are causes of God's love.

This verse states that those who trade God's covenant and their oaths for a small worldly price will have no share in the good of the Hereafter; God will not speak to them in a way that pleases them, will not look upon them with mercy on the Day of Resurrection, will not purify them, and they will suffer a painful punishment. The commentators agree that the warning extends to anyone who breaks a pledge or swears falsely for material gain. On the occasion of revelation, the reports differ. Ikrima, Ibn Jurayj, al-Hasan and others say it concerns Jewish rabbis who concealed the description of the Prophet ﷺ and altered the Torah for bribes. Al-Bukhari and Muslim relate the case of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays, who disputed with a man over land or a well. Mujahid and al-Sha'bi mention a man who swore falsely in the market to sell his goods. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi consider the People of the Book the most likely context, while al-Razi holds that all these reports may be taken together. On the meaning of the punishment, opinions differ: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God will not speak to them in what pleases them, some take it as an expression of divine anger, and al-Razi clarifies that the denied look is one of favour rather than of the eyes. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari cite many hadiths on the false oath, and Ibn Kathir reports the hadith about the three people God will not address. Ibn al-Jawzi notes that the words may refer to disbelievers or to sinners, but in both cases the threat stands. The commentators do not judge between these views and present them as they are.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to a group among the People of the Book, namely the Jews of Medina in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, who twisted their tongues while reciting the Scripture. They presented their own words or alterations as if they were part of the revealed text, so that listeners would think them from God's Book, and then claimed outright that these came from God when they did not. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take the twisting to mean distortion, while Ibn Kathir understands it as altering both wording and meaning. Al-Tabari reads it as inventing what God had not sent down, in pursuit of leadership and worldly wealth. All agree that the phrase 'they speak falsehood about God while they know it' marks deliberate lying.

The scholars differ on the nature of the distortion. Wahb ibn Munabbih, cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi, held that the original books remained intact and that the corruption lay in the books they wrote themselves and in false interpretation. Al-Razi, by contrast, considered that the alteration may have touched the text itself, or at least that the Jews clouded the proofs of the Prophet's mission with doubts and objections, which he saw as the sense of the twisting, and he offered possible explanations of how such changes could have spread.

Some commentators relate the occasion of revelation: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions were said to have altered the description of the Prophet ﷺ in their writings and taken payment for it, a report that Ibn 'Abbas transmits through several chains. Exegetes also discuss the variant readings of the verb, and the grammatical justifications for them, but they largely agree on the meaning of twisting the tongue as falsification.

This verse states that it is not right for any human, to whom God has given the Book, wisdom and prophethood, to tell people to worship him instead of God. Instead, they should become rabbaniyyin, that is, scholars who act on their knowledge and guide people through it. The commentators agree that the negation expresses impossibility rather than mere prohibition, and that knowledge must be joined with action. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed in answer to those who asked the Prophet ﷺ whether he wanted them to worship him as the Christians worship Jesus; Ibn Kathir and others also read it as a rebuke to those who attributed such words to Jesus or to other prophets.

The meaning of rabbaniyyin is debated. Ibn Abbas, Ali, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Mas'ud take it as jurists and learned men; Abu Razin, Qatada and al-Suddi as wise and knowledgeable people; Sa'id ibn Jubayr as the pious sage or the one who acts on what he knows; and Ibn Zayd as the rulers who guide the community. Al-Tabari favours the sense of one who sets the affairs of people right, while Mujahid holds that they stand above the rabbis because they combine learning with political judgement.

The recitations of the words for teaching and studying differ. Most commentators hold that learning, teaching and study all together make a person rabbani. Al-Razi draws from this that knowledge without practice does not reach that rank, while Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan record the variant readings without preferring one.

This verse states that no human whom God has granted the Book, wisdom and prophethood could ever order people to worship him, or to take angels and prophets as lords besides God, since that would be disbelief after they have submitted. Most commentators read this as a rebuttal to those who wanted the Prophet ﷺ to be worshipped. Al-Tabari prefers the nominative reading, in which God is the subject, and rejects a report attributed to Ibn Mas'ud that would support it. Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir report that the occasion of revelation was a claim by Christians of Najran, or by Jews, that the Prophet ﷺ wanted to be worshipped, which he firmly denied. Ibn Kathir adds that the ignorant scholars who make lawful what God forbade fall under the same reproach.

For the accusative reading, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan offer two explanations: either the word "la" reinforces the negation, or it introduces a separate negation. Abu Hayyan rejects al-Tabari's view that this reading is an error. As for the word "rabbaniyyin", the commentators differ: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak take it to mean learned jurists, Mujahid means scholars above rabbis, Ibn Zayd means rulers who manage the affairs of people, and Sibawayh and al-Mubarrad derive it from the root for lordship or upbringing. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verbs "teach" and "study" imply a knowledge that should produce real devotion. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi conclude that study pursued without seeking God's pleasure is fruitless.

This verse tells that God took a binding covenant from all the prophets: whatever Book and wisdom He gives them, if a messenger comes confirming what they have, they must believe in him and support him. God asked them to acknowledge it, had them witness against one another, and Himself bore witness. The commentators agree that the covenant binds the prophets and that what is required of a leader is required of his followers. Ali, Ibn Abbas, Tawus, al-Suddi and Qatada, as well as Ibn Kathir, hold that the covenant was taken from the prophets themselves to believe in Muhammad, peace be upon him. Al-Tabari explains that the prophets pledged to confirm one another, and that this bound their peoples too. Mujahid and al-Rabi' held that the covenant concerned the People of the Book, relying on the readings of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, but most scholars rejected this in light of the Companions' consensus on the Uthmanic text. On the reading of the particle lamma, al-Tabari preferred the fatha reading, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi set out the kasra and tashdid readings, and Abu Hayyan analysed the grammar in detail. All agree that whoever turns away after this reminder is among the defiant. The following verse, questioning those who seek a religion other than God's, is read by the same exegetes as a rebuke: everything in the heavens and earth has submitted to God, willingly or by force, and to Him all will return.

This verse recalls that God took a solemn covenant from the prophets: that each would believe in the messenger who would come after them, confirming what they had, and support him. God had them affirm it, they acknowledged it, they bore witness against one another, and God Himself was a witness. The commentators agree that whoever turns away after this covenant is sealed is a rebellious transgressor who has left obedience to God. Ali, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir explain that each prophet was to believe in Muhammad if he lived to see him, and to command his people to do the same. Tawus, al-Hasan, Qatada and Sa'id ibn Jubayr hold that the covenant was that the prophets confirm one another. Mujahid and al-Rabi' take it to be imposed on the People of the Book themselves. Al-Razi adds that a covenant taken from the leaders binds the followers too, a reading supported by the recitations of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy. Al-Zamakhshari relates the dispute among the People of the Book over the religion of Abraham, in which the Prophet declared both sides innocent of it, provoking their anger. As for the phrase that all in the heavens and earth have submitted to Him, willingly or unwillingly, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid interpret it as the willing submission of the believer and the forced submission of the disbeliever, the prostration of shadows, or the acknowledgment of the Creator. Others see it as the submission of all creation to God's decree. The verse thus rebukes those who seek a religion other than God's, and reminds that all will return to Him.

In this verse God rebukes the People of the Book for seeking a religion other than God's, namely Islam, when everyone in the heavens and the earth has submitted to Him, willingly or unwillingly, and all will be returned to Him to be recompensed for their deeds. The commentators give several meanings to "willingly or unwillingly." Al-Hasan, Mutarrif al-Warraq and Qatada hold that the believer submitted willingly, while the disbeliever submits unwillingly at the moment he sees the punishment, when his faith no longer benefits him; al-Hasan adds that willing submission applies to the inhabitants of the heavens, while among the inhabitants of the earth some submitted willingly and others out of fear of the sword. Mujahid understands the unwilling submission as the prostration of the disbeliever's shadow, set against the willing prostration of the believer. Abu al-'Aliya says that every human has acknowledged by nature God's lordship: whoever associates others in worship has submitted unwillingly, whoever devotes sincere worship to Him has submitted willingly. Ibn 'Abbas holds that the unwilling submission occurred at the taking of the covenant, and al-Sha'bi that it is the seeking of refuge in God in distress. Al-Zajjaj understands submission as yielding to the decree of God's command in the nature of beings. The readings of "tabghun" and "yurja'un" vary between the second and third person; al-Tabari prefers the second person, since the preceding verse is addressed to its audience. Some also report an occasion of revelation linked to a dispute among the People of the Book over the religion of Abraham, though this report is open to question. The overall meaning is a warning against seeking any religion other than Islam, and a reminder that submission to God is universal in creation.

God instructs His Prophet to declare his faith and that of his community in God, in what was revealed to them, in what was revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes, and in what was given to Moses, Jesus and the prophets from their Lord, making no distinction among them, and submitting to God alone. The commentators explain the "submission" (islam) mentioned in the previous verse as surrender and obedience. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir say that all in the heavens and earth submitted to God, willingly or unwillingly, the believer willingly and the unbeliever sometimes under threat, as Qatada held. Mujahid understood it as the prostration of the believer's shadow willingly and the unbeliever's shadow unwillingly, while al-Sha'bi took it as seeking refuge in God in times of distress. As for "the tribes" (al-asbat), al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi take them to be the twelve sons of Jacob, whereas al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir understand them as the tribes of the Children of Israel, and say that believing in what was revealed to them means believing in what was revealed to their prophets. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain that making no distinction among the prophets means accepting all of them, unlike the Jews and Christians; al-Razi adds that it means not choosing between them by acceptance or rejection. As for the statement that whoever seeks a religion other than Islam will not be accepted, the commentators differ on its occasion of revelation: some link it to al-Harith ibn Suwayd and those who apostatized then repented, others to the People of the Book, and Ibn Atiyya considers it abrogating a verse of al-Baqara. Al-Razi specifies that Islam here means monotheism.

This verse states that whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will not be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers, meaning those who deprived themselves of their share of God's mercy, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain. The commentators agree that Islam here means monotheism and submission to God's command, and that any religion departing from this is rejected. Acceptance, according to al-Razi, means that God is pleased with the deed and rewards its doer. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud hold that whoever turns away from Islam lacks all benefit and falls into loss by abandoning the pure nature in which people were created. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a rebuke to the People of the Book who claimed to follow the religion of Abraham. Opinions differ on what Islam means: al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it as monotheism, while al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as the religion of Muhammad ﷺ, which agrees with the prophets on the foundations of belief. Al-Razi draws from the verse that faith is Islam, reconciling it with the verse in Surat al-Hujurat. Two accounts explain the occasion of revelation: that of Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Muqatil about al-Harith ibn Suwayd and his companions who apostatized then repented, and that of Ibn 'Abbas about the People of the Book who disputed over the religion of Abraham. Al-Tabari also reports that Muslims performed the pilgrimage while disbelievers stayed away. The commentators do not dispute that the verse announces loss in the Hereafter, though the images they give of that loss vary.

This verse asks, in a tone of reproach, how God could guide a people who disbelieved after having believed, after having testified that the Messenger was true and after clear proofs had come to them. Those who turn away from the truth after recognising it sink deeper into error, and God does not guide the wrongdoers, meaning those who put things in the wrong place by choosing disbelief over faith. The commentators broadly agree on this general sense. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the interrogative form expresses astonishment and the improbability of such guidance. Ibn Kathir and others specify that the threat concerns the one who dies in disbelief, whereas one who sincerely returns to faith is forgiven.

On the occasion of revelation, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid and al-Suddi report that it concerns al-Harith ibn Suwayd, an Ansari who apostatised, then regretted it and sent word through his people asking whether he could repent; he then returned to Islam. Others add Abu 'Amir the monk, Wahwah ibn al-Aslat and Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq. By contrast, al-Hasan, Qatada and Abu al-Aliya hold that it refers to Jews and Christians who recognised the description of the Prophet in their scriptures and then rejected him. Al-Tabari judged this second view closer to the apparent sense of the text, although most narrations support the first.

The scholars also differ on the scope of the statement in the following verse that repentance will never be accepted from them. Al-Hasan, Qatada and 'Ata' relate it to the moment of death, while Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Aliya relate it to those who persist in disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari reads the question as concerning divine favour: how could God grant them His guidance when they have persisted?

This verse from Al Imran states that the recompense of those who disbelieve after believing, and after the truth has been made clear to them, is to bear the curse of God, of the angels and of all people, meaning exclusion from God's mercy and His punishment. They remain in this curse and in the torment, which is neither lightened nor deferred. The commentators differ on the occasion of revelation. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ikrima, whom al-Tabari follows, say it was about al-Harith ibn Suwayd al-Ansari and others who apostatised and then repented, while al-Hasan, Qatada and Abu al-Aliya say it concerns the Jews and Christians who recognised the Prophet and then denied him. Al-Tabari prefers a general sense covering every apostate after faith, and whoever believed in the Prophet before his mission and then rejected him. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri stress that the exception, those who repent and make amends, opens the door to forgiveness, for God is Forgiving and Merciful. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi discuss the phrase that their repentance will not be accepted: al-Hasan, Qatada and Ata take it to mean repentance at the moment of death, Mujahid to mean one who dies in disbelief, and Ibn Abbas to mean one who holds back from Islam waiting for the Prophet to fail. Most agree that "the people" refers to believers or to all people, since the disbeliever himself curses whoever departs from the truth.

This verse describes those who disbelieve after having believed, having acknowledged that the Messenger is true and having received the clear proofs. The commentators agree that they incur the curse of God, the angels and all people, that they remain in that state for which they have earned punishment, that their torment will not be lightened, and that they will not be granted respite to make excuses. Scholars differ on the meaning of the word "abiding": al-Tabari takes it to mean the everlasting continuation of punishment without limit or relief, while some grammarians treat the clause as a circumstantial description of the people. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi report that the verse was revealed about al-Harith ibn Suwayd, an Ansari who apostatised and then repented and was forgiven. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Abu al-Aliya hold that it concerns Jews and Christians who recognised the Prophet from their scriptures and then rejected him out of envy. Al-Tabari suggests the verse includes all such cases. On the phrase about repentance not being accepted, al-Hasan and Qatada say it refers to the moment of death, Mujahid to dying in disbelief, and Ibn Abbas to a feigned repentance that conceals disbelief. The exception at the end is read by most as an opening of mercy for anyone who repents and makes amends, and Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur note that repentance alone is not enough without righting one's actions. Ibn 'Uthaymin lists the conditions of sincere repentance: sincerity, regret, giving up the sin, resolving not to return to it, and repenting before death.

This verse makes an exception to the punishment announced just before it: whoever disbelieves after faith, then repents and puts things right, will be forgiven and shown mercy by God. The commentators agree that repentance here means returning from apostasy to faith, and that setting things right means both repairing what the person corrupted by apostasy and doing good deeds afterwards. Some explain that it means entering into righteousness. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, al-Suddi, al-Kalbi and al-Baydawi report that it was revealed about al-Harith ibn Suwayd al-Ansari, who left Islam, joined the idolaters, then regretted it and sent word asking the Prophet whether he could still repent. The verse came down, he returned and embraced Islam sincerely.

Other reports, cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, speak of several men, or say the verses concern the People of the Book. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya hold that the verse refers to Jews and Christians who recognised the Prophet before his mission and then rejected him. Al-Tabari concludes that the verse covers both groups, the People of the Book and anyone who abandons Islam after accepting it.

On the meaning of setting things right, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note it may mean repairing what was spoiled or entering goodness. Al-Alusi adds that some scholars think mere regret and resolve are not enough without making amends for rights that were violated, though he answers that regret and resolve do suffice for a valid repentance. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi discuss how the verse's exception relates to what precedes it, and Ibn Juzayy notes that the forgiveness here is not the same as the fate of those who die in disbelief.

This verse states that those who disbelieve after believing, and then increase in disbelief, will not have their repentance accepted, and that they are the astray. The commentators differ on who is meant. Qatada, al-Hasan and 'Ata al-Khurasani take it to be the Jews, who disbelieved in Jesus and the Gospel after believing in Moses and the Torah, then disbelieved in Muhammad and the Qur'an. Abu al-'Aliya includes Jews and Christians who rejected Muhammad after recognising his description in their scriptures, then accumulated sins while still in disbelief. Mujahid and as-Suddi hold that it covers all who died in disbelief after having turned from faith. Ibn 'Abbas links the revelation to followers of al-Harith ibn Suwayd who apostatised and vowed to wait for misfortune to befall the Prophet.

On what it means that repentance is not accepted, the views vary. Al-Hasan, Qatada, 'Ata and as-Suddi refer it to repentance at the moment of death and the death rattle. Ibn 'Abbas holds that such repentance is not sincere, since disbelief remains in their hearts. Mujahid refers it to repentance after death. Az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as a figure of speech meaning that they will not repent at all. At-Tabari prefers that what is not accepted is repentance from sins committed while remaining in disbelief, whereas a return to Islam is accepted.

The statement that whoever dies in disbelief will not be ransomed, even with a earth full of gold, is read by most as meaning that no ransom will avail on the Day of Judgement, even of such wealth. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Anas about the man questioned in the Hereafter. Az-Zamakhshari discusses the particle wa-law ('even if') and its readings.

This verse states that whoever dies in disbelief will not be accepted on the Day of Judgment even if he offered the whole earth filled with gold as ransom, and even if he actually tried to ransom himself. Al-Tabari understands it to cover every disbeliever of every community, and cites a hadith from Anas about a man who is reminded that he was asked for something much easier and refused. The commentators agree that a disbeliever who dies in disbelief has no ransom and no helper, and that he will suffer a painful punishment. Opinions differ on the context of the preceding verse: Qatada and al-Hasan take it to be about the Jews who disbelieved in Jesus and then in Muhammad; Ibn 'Abbas takes it to be about apostates who pretended to repent in order to hide their condition; Abu al-'Aliya takes it to be about people who repented of particular sins while remaining in disbelief; and Mujahid takes it to be about anyone who persists in disbelief until death. On the particle waw in "even if he had ransomed himself", al-Tabari sees an implied clause, al-Zajjaj sees a rejection of every kind of offering, some see it as superfluous, and al-Zamakhshari explains it through the sense of the sentence. The word "dhahaban" is an accusative of specification according to al-Farra' and most grammarians, while al-Kisa'i takes it as elided "min", and a nominative reading is attributed to al-A'mash.

The commentators explain that the verse means believers will not attain true righteousness, the full measure of goodness and the rank of the righteous, nor receive God's reward, until they spend from what they love and cherish most of their wealth. There is disagreement over the meaning of al-Birr: Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi and 'Amr ibn Maymun take it to mean Paradise, while others cited by al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as obedience, piety, or the good deeds that earn reward, and al-Razi distinguishes between the righteousness produced by accepted deeds and the reward itself. As for what must be spent, al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to mean the obligatory zakat, Ibn 'Umar takes it to mean all charity, and al-Hasan in another report, along with al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, extends it to any spending sought for God's sake, even a single date. Al-Razi prefers that the verse concerns voluntary giving rather than obligatory zakat, while Mujahid and al-Kalbi hold that it was abrogated by the zakat verse, a view al-Razi considers far-fetched. The commentators recount how Abu Talha gave his beloved orchard of Bayruha, how Zayd ibn Haritha gave his favourite horse, and how Ibn 'Umar freed a slave-girl he loved, along with examples from the early pious. The verse ends by affirming that God knows whatever is spent, small or great, and will repay each giver according to it.

This verse explains that all food was permitted to the Children of Israel, the descendants of Jacob, before the Torah was revealed, except what Israel (Jacob) forbade himself. The commentators disagree about this prohibition. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most early exegetes, relying on Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak, say it was the sinew (al-'uruq), because Jacob suffered from sciatica and vowed not to eat sinews. Others, including al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Abu al-'Aliya, say it was camel meat and milk, which al-Tabari prefers because the Jews still observe that prohibition. Scholars also differ on whether Jacob acted by his own judgment or by divine permission, and al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that prophets may exercise independent judgment. As for the later prohibitions in the Torah, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi see them as punishment for Israelite wrongdoing, as stated in Surah An-Nisa' and Al-An'am. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read the verse as a rebuttal of Jews who claimed these laws were ancient. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir take it as evidence for the validity of abrogation. The Prophet tells the Jews to bring the Torah and recite it to prove their claim; they do not dare, which many commentators regard as proof of his prophethood.

This verse states that whoever fabricates a lie against God after the proof has been established is a wrongdoer to himself and to others. It belongs to the debate with the Jews, who claimed that prohibitions on certain foods went back to Abraham and Noah. The commentators explain that all food had been lawful to the children of Israel before the Torah, except what Israel (Jacob) forbade himself. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari agree that the lie is the claim that this prohibition was ancient, and that the wrongdoers are those who obstinately refuse the evident proof. On what Jacob forbade, opinions differ: Abu al-'Aliya, 'Ata', Muqatil and al-Kalbi name the flesh and milk of camels, while Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak name the sinews, linked to his sciatica. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi hold that this was Jacob's own choice rather than a divine permission. Al-Suddi says the Torah prohibited to the Israelites what they had forbidden themselves, whereas al-Kalbi holds that the Torah did not prohibit it and that later prohibitions came as punishment for their wrongdoing, citing the verse in Surat al-Nisa'. Several scholars, including al-Razi, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn 'Ashur, see in the passage evidence for abrogation (naskh). The challenge to bring the Torah is taken by many as proof of the Prophet's truthfulness.

This verse states that God has spoken the truth in reporting that all foods were lawful to the Children of Israel before the Torah was revealed, except what Israel (Jacob) forbade himself. The Prophet is therefore told to say to the People of the Book that their claims are false, and to call them to follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif who turned away from every false path and was not a polytheist. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari, agree that the intended meaning is pure monotheism and the rejection of associating partners with God, and that the verse implicitly refutes the Jews' lies while inviting them to Islam, which is in essence the religion of Abraham. Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Kathir relate the accounts of why Jacob forbade camel meat and milk, namely a vow made after an affliction of the sciatic nerve. On what followed, opinions differ. Al-Kalbi, al-Suddi and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that the Torah later forbade certain good things as punishment for Jewish wrongdoing, as Qur'an 4:160 recalls, while al-Razi sees it more as a clarification. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Juzayy treat this as a genuine case of abrogation, whereas Abu Hayyan limits the discussion to the historical moment of the command. Finally, Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Alusi stress that Abraham's religion concerns the oneness of God, not every legal detail.

This verse describes the Kaaba in Bakka (Makkah) as the first house built for worship, blessed and a guidance for all peoples. The commentators agree it was the first place of worship, but differ on what 'first' means. Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan and Ata' held that many houses existed before it and that it was the first built for the worship of God, citing the hadith of Abu Dharr that the Sacred Mosque was built first, forty years before al-Aqsa. Mujahid, Qatada, as-Suddi and Ibn Umar related that it was placed on the water before the earth, two thousand years earlier, and the earth was spread out beneath it; Ibn Kathir considered these reports weak. Ibn Attiya and al-Zamakhshari mention that Abraham built or rebuilt it on ancient foundations. Most say Bakka names the site of the house and the circumambulation, while Makka names the whole town; Ibn Abbas and others hold them to be two names for one place, the letters ba and mim interchanging in Arabic. Its blessing is taken as the multiplication of reward and forgiveness of sins for those who perform the hajj or umrah. The Station of Abraham is for many the stone on which he stood while building, and for Mujahid the whole sanctuary. Whoever enters the sacred precinct is safe, an idea some tie to the pre-Islamic period, while scholars divided over whether legal punishments are carried out inside it. The hajj is obligatory once in a lifetime for whoever is able, most taking ability as provision and mount; Malik added that a man able to walk and earn his way is also obliged. Those who neglect it are described as having disbelieved, and most scholars read this as a lesser kind of disbelief rather than outright apostasy.

The verse states that the Sacred House contains clear signs, the greatest of which is the Station of Abraham, the stone on which Abraham stood while raising the foundations of the Ka'ba and where his footprints remained. Al-Tabari and most exegetes take the plural 'signs' to include the Station and other signs, while Ibn Abbas and Mujahid regard the Station alone as the single sign, and others extend the sign to the whole sanctuary. All agree that whoever enters the sanctuary is safe, but they explain this differently: al-Hasan, Qatada, 'Ata' and others describe a safety that belonged to the pre-Islamic period, with punishments enforced inside the sanctuary in Islam; Ibn Abbas and Abu Hanifa hold that a wrongdoer who seeks refuge is not punished there but denied sale, purchase, food and shelter until he leaves; Malik and al-Shafi'i allow penalties to be carried out inside; Yahya ibn Ja'da understood it as safety from the Fire.

On the pilgrimage, scholars agree it is obligatory once in a lifetime for whoever is able, but differ on what ability means: Umar, Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata' and al-Shafi'i say provision and mount, Malik says physical capacity to walk or travel with earnings on the way, Abu Hanifa combines wealth and body, and Ibn al-Zubayr says it depends on one's strength. They also differ on the 'disbelief' mentioned at the end: for Ibn Abbas it is denying the obligation, for al-Hasan neglecting the pilgrimage while able is disbelief, for Ibn Umar and Mujahid it means disbelief in God and the Last Day; al-Tabari prefers rejecting the duty as an obligation.

God instructs His Prophet to rebuke the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, for rejecting the signs of God, meaning His proofs that confirm the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ. The commentators identify these signs as the Quran and the prophecies about the Prophet found in the Torah and the Gospel. The clause "and God is witness over what you do" is read as a circumstantial phrase that strengthens the rebuke and carries a warning, since God observes their deeds and will repay them. The exegetes agree that the reproach targets those who knew the truth yet denied it, and also those who followed their scholars without examination.

The next verse continues with a reproach for barring believers from the path of God, that is Islam, and for seeking to make it crooked. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the Jews claimed Muhammad was not described in their books, or stirred rivalry between the Aws and the Khazraj. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi consider several of these occasions plausible and do not choose among them. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari explain that crookedness means distorting the religion through doubt and falsification, while others distinguish between the forms 'iwaj for what is abstract and 'awaj for what is physical. As for "and you are witnesses," al-Tabari reads it as meaning sound minds, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as knowledge that Islam is true, and Abu Hayyan takes it as trusted witnesses among their own community.

God instructs His Prophet to rebuke the People of the Book for barring people from God's path, which is Islam, and for trying to make that path appear crooked to those who wish to enter it. The commentators agree that the verse reproaches them for leading believers astray, and that this obstruction took the form of denying that the Prophet ﷺ was described in their scriptures and of planting doubts among the weak. The phrase 'while you are witnesses' is a circumstantial clause: you know this path is true. Al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi understood it as addressed to Jewish and Christian scholars who told Muslims that Muhammad was not described in their books, and Ibn Abbas and Qatada report that the Torah itself states that God's religion is Islam. Ibn Zayd read the obstruction as stirring up discord between the Aws and the Khazraj to revive the feuds of the pre-Islamic age, and al-Tabari relates that the verse was revealed concerning Shas ibn Qays, who stirred up this strife. Al-Tabari and those who follow him take 'seeking crookedness in it' to mean seeking deviation for it, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya also see the spreading of doubts, such as the claim that Moses' law is not abrogated. Most scholars distinguish 'iwaj' with a kasra for abstract matters from 'awaj' with a fatha for physical objects. The verse closes with a warning that God is not unaware of what they do.

This verse warns believers against obeying a group of the People of the Book, who might turn them back into disbelief after their faith. The commentators agree that the address is to believers in general and that its origin lies with the Aws and Khazraj, when a Jew, named in many reports as Shas ibn Qays, stirred up old tribal grievances from the pre-Islamic period until two groups nearly fought. The Prophet ﷺ came and calmed the dispute. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi present this episode as the occasion of revelation, while al-Razi and al-Baydawi hold that the wording covers that episode and any other attempt by the People of the Book to mislead the believers. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan maintain that disbelief here does not mean outright unbelief but discord and disobedience, unless they were made lawful, and that misguidance can proceed gradually until people become true disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud read the command as a warning against the doubts raised by Jews and hypocrites, and as a call to refer each doubt to the Prophet ﷺ. The commentators stress that reciting God's signs and the presence of the Messenger protect against disbelief, and that holding fast to God leads to the straight path. Ibn Juzayy notes a disagreement over whether the verse 'fear God as He should be feared' was abrogated by 'fear God as much as you can', some saying it was and others saying there is no contradiction. Ibn Ashur finally extends the instruction to the whole community through the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

God rebukes the believers for disbelieving when God's signs are recited to them and the Messenger is among them, and He declares that whoever holds fast to God has already been guided to the straight path. The commentators generally agree that the question expresses that disbelief is unlikely for believers given these two safeguards, and that holding fast to God means adhering to His religion and obedience, according to Ibn Jurayj, faith in Him, and according to Abu al-'Aliya, trust and reliance on Him. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud add that the question may also express astonishment. Most cite the occasion of revelation: the Jew Shas ibn Qays stirred strife between the Aws and Khazraj by recalling the Battle of Bu'ath, and the Prophet intervened, reminding them of Islam, and they laid down their weapons. Al-Razi sees the verse as a warning against the seduction of the People of the Book, the Prophet's presence dispelling doubts. Qatada holds that the two safeguards are the Messenger and the Book, and that the Messenger has passed away while the Qur'an remains. On guidance, al-Razi reports the argument of those who hold that the servant's act is created by God, while the Mu'tazilites interpret it as an increase in divine favours or as guidance to Paradise. Ibn 'Ashur sees i'tisam here as a metaphor for adherence to the religion, and notes that the verse also addresses those who did not live in the Prophet's time.

In this verse God commands the believers to be mindful of Him as He truly deserves, that is, to strive to the utmost in obeying Him and avoiding what He forbids, and to remain Muslims until death. Ibn Mas'ud and others explain this true piety as being obeyed and not disobeyed, remembered and not forgotten, thanked and not ungrateful. Others, such as the report of Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas, understand it as striving in God's cause as is due, not fearing the blame of any blamer in standing for the truth, and upholding justice even against oneself and one's kin. Some relate it to sincerity of intention. Scholars differ on whether the verse is abrogated. Qatada, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil hold that it is abrogated by the verse saying to fear God as much as you are able, while Ibn Abbas and Tawus hold that it stands. Ibn Kathir and others consider it possible to reconcile the two verses by reading the second as an explanation of the first. The command to hold fast to God's rope is interpreted by commentators as the Qur'an, God's covenant, the community, or Islam, and it is accompanied by a prohibition of division, recalling the discord between the Aws and the Khazraj before Islam. God then reminds the believers of the blessing of joining hearts after enmity and of rescuing them from the brink of the fire through guidance, so that they may be grateful and remain rightly guided.

This verse calls the believers to hold fast together to the rope of God and not to split apart, and to remember God's favour in uniting their hearts after enmity, so that by Islam they became brothers, when they stood on the brink of a pit of Fire from which He rescued them. The commentators largely agree that the rope is the Book of God, according to Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada and al-Suddi, or the community, according to another report from Ibn Mas'ud, or the covenant of God, according to Mujahid and Ata, while Abu al-Aliya understood sincere devotion to God alone and Ibn Zayd understood Islam. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi consider these meanings close to one another. On division, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi take it to mean discord over the foundations of faith rather than legal differences, which were common among the Companions, whereas al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan also include the tribal wars of the pre-Islamic age. The occasion of revelation reported by Ibn Ishaq and others concerns the Aws and Khazraj, whose old quarrel was rekindled by a Jew who recalled the battle of Bu'ath, until the Prophet calmed them by reciting the verse. Al-Tabari reports that hostilities between the two tribes lasted one hundred and twenty years. Several commentators, including al-Razi, note that brotherhood through faith surpasses the ties of blood. Most treat the verse on fearing God as it is due (3:102) as not abrogated, meaning that one should exert the utmost effort within one's capacity. The verse concludes that God thus makes His signs clear so that people may be guided.

The verse calls for a group among the believers who call to good, meaning Islam and its laws, who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and it promises that they are the successful ones. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read the word "min" as partitive, so that this is a collective duty fulfilled by some on behalf of all, since these acts require knowledge of right and wrong and of how to carry them out. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy sometimes take it as explanatory, and al-Zajjaj, followed by others, sees the address as directed to the whole community. Most commentators hold that the call to good is general, while enjoining and forbidding are mentioned separately to honour them. The scholars agree that forbidding wrong is obligatory in full, and that enjoining good follows the status of what is enjoined. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes sincere advice from reproach. The next verse warns against division and discord like those who split after the clear signs came to them, and announces a great punishment. Ibn Kathir and others take these to be the people of innovation within this community, while al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas take them to be Jews and Christians. The commentators also differ on the faces that turn white and black on the Day of Resurrection, and on those who disbelieved after believing: hypocrites according to al-Hasan, apostates according to Mujahid, and others according to other views.

In this verse God warns believers against becoming like those who split apart and disagreed about their religion after clear proofs had come to them, and He promises them a great punishment. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, identify these people as the Jews and Christians, who broke into sects after their prophets; al-Tabari reports from al-Rabi' that the Muslims are being told not to do as they did. Others, such as Abu Umama, Qatada and al-Zamakhshari, take the reference to be the innovators of this community, the Kharijites, or the people of desires. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Wahidi widen the meaning to the earlier nations that divided. Al-Razi links the prohibition to the preceding verses: unity comes from holding fast to God's rope and remembering His favours, the rope being understood as the Book, the covenant, the religion or the community. Those who treat this verse within the context of enjoining good make the practice a means of preventing division, and neglecting it encourages division. The blamed disagreement is mostly seen as concerning the foundations of belief; al-Baydawi holds that it does not extend to matters of detail, while al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di understand it as deliberately turning away from the truth once it is clear, out of desire or envy. All agree that the faces of believers will be bright and those of disbelievers dark on the Day of Resurrection, though they differ on whether this is literal or figurative.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when some faces will turn white and others black. Those whose faces turn black will be addressed in rebuke: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Taste then the punishment for what you used to deny," while those whose faces turn white will be in the mercy of God, remaining in it forever. The commentators agree that the whiteness and blackness of faces express joy and distress, and that the verse concerns disbelievers and those who went astray. They differ, however, on who is meant by those who disbelieved after belief. Al-Tabari, following Ubayy ibn Ka'b, holds that it refers to all disbelievers who turned away from the covenant made when God asked, "Am I not your Lord?" and they answered yes. Al-Hasan identifies the hypocrites, who professed faith with their tongues while denying it in their hearts. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Zajjaj point to Jews and Christians who recognised the Prophet before his mission and then rejected him, while Abu Umama, Qatada and Malik think of innovators, the Kharijites or deviant sects. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi allow several of these readings. Some commentators, including Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, add that the verse warns believers against the division that struck earlier peoples.
