This part of the verse describes the fate of the people of reward on the Day of Judgment: their faces turn white with joy and radiance, and they are in the mercy of God, that is, in Paradise and its bounties, where they will remain forever without leaving or dying. Most commentators understand "the mercy" to mean Paradise itself. Al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi note that entry into Paradise comes through God's mercy and not by works alone, and that the word "mercy" reminds the believer that even the most devoted obedience does not earn Paradise without divine grace. All agree that this dwelling is eternal. Most explain the whiteness of the faces as a radiance of joy and happiness; Ibn 'Atiyya suggests it may also come from traces of ablution, citing the hadith of the radiant ones with bright limbs, which Ibn 'Uthaymin also mentions. The scholars do not differ on this part of the verse. Their disagreements concern who are meant by those whose faces turn black, discussed in the preceding phrase. This verse therefore sets clearly the fate of the believers against that of those who went astray.

This passage states that the preceding verses, which describe the reward of believers and the punishment of disbelievers, are the signs of God that the Prophet recites in truth, and that God does not desire injustice toward any of the worlds. The commentators explain that God does not punish anyone without fault, does not increase the punishment of a guilty person, and does not reduce the reward of a good doer; each receives what his deeds deserve. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read this as a denial of any intention of injustice, while Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the denial concerns injustice in God's judgment, and that the present tense and the indefinite noun express constancy and generality. Al-Zamakhshari sees it as a way of exonerating God from any desire for evil, and al-Samani and al-Baghawi stress that punishment is just when it is deserved.

The commentators agree that this verse concludes what precedes it, and that the following phrase, 'To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and on earth, and to God all matters are returned', affirms that sovereignty belongs entirely to God and that all affairs return to Him. Abu Hayyan says that the injustice in fact falls on the disbelievers who exposed themselves to eternal punishment, a point also made by al-Baydawi. Ibn 'Ashur sees a logical link: one who needs no one's harm and knows everything does not desire injustice. Al-Razi observes that the mention of severe punishment explains why divine justice is emphasized.

Linguistic points also receive attention. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that 'ma' here covers rational and non-rational beings, and that the preposition in 'bil-haqq' conveys truth or justice. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that denying the desire for injustice does not mean that injustice is impossible, but that divine wisdom refuses it. For all of them, the central meaning remains the complete justice of God.

This verse states that God alone owns whatever is in the heavens and on earth, through creation, governance and disposal, and that all matters return to Him. The commentators read it as a confirmation of divine justice: the one who owns everything has no need to wrong anyone, and He repays each person according to what He has promised or threatened. It comes after the passages on reward and punishment to show that this judgment proceeds from a Sovereign whom no one can challenge. The exegetes broadly agree on the idea of absolute sovereignty linked to the final return to God. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya connect the signs mentioned to the earlier passages on the two groups, and see in the denial of any intent to wrong a proof of divine perfection. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the sequence of three statements affirms that decision belongs to God in destiny, in law and in recompense. On the repetition of the divine name, al-Tabari reports the view of Basran grammarians who compared it to a common Arabic construction, while Kufan grammarians held the comparison inaccurate because the two clauses are independent; al-Tabari favoured the second view, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya explained the repetition as a device of emphasis. Ibn Sa'di notes that God governs through decrees, laws and judgments together, and al-Sha'rawi observes that human possession is only relative, with all affairs returning to God after having been run through causes in this world.

God declares that this community is the best nation ever brought forth for mankind, because it enjoins good, forbids evil and believes in God. The commentators differ on who is addressed. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Ibn Jurayj and Mujahid take it to mean the Companions, especially those who emigrated with the Prophet to Medina, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have said that it applied to the first of them only. Al-Hasan and others hold that the address covers the whole community in every age, a view supported by the prophetic reports that his community completes seventy nations and is the best of them. As for the word 'kuntum', some take it as the past tense, others as a statement of God's foreknowledge or of the Preserved Tablet, and others as the mere realisation of the quality without reference to time, a position defended by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya. Most explain the good as faith and obedience and the evil as disbelief and disobedience, while al-Hasan and Qatada include everything the law prescribes. Several explain why commanding good comes before faith: faith is shared by all nations, whereas enjoining good shows the excellence more clearly, and al-Razi adds that faith is its condition. God then says that had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them; some of them believe, such as 'Abdallah ibn Salam and the Negus, but most of them are transgressors. Some commentators note that this reassures the believers: the People of the Book can harm them only slightly, by words.

This verse states that the People of the Book, especially the wicked among them, cannot inflict real harm on the believers, only a minor hurt (adha), which most commentators understand as verbal: slander, distortion, threats, calls to misguidance and the uttering of disbelief in their hearing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi discuss whether the exception is continuous or discontinuous, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read it as a slight harm with no real effect. Muqatil and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the verse was revealed after Jewish leaders persecuted Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions for embracing Islam. The next clause, that if they fight you they will turn their backs, is taken by the commentators as a prediction of their defeat in battle, and the statement that they will not be helped is a lasting promise. Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud note that this came true with the Banu Qaynuqa, al-Nadir, Qurayza and Khaybar. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain why the verb is not put in the jussive: thumma signals a higher rank of tidings rather than a later time. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the promise applies to those who follow the guidance of the Prophet and his companions.

This verse states that humiliation has been imposed on the Jews wherever they are found, so they gain no security except by holding to a covenant from God or a covenant from people. The commentators generally explain the rope of God as a pact or the protection of dhimma, and the rope of people as a treaty or guarantee of safety. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as a covenant from God and a covenant from people, while al-Razi holds that the exception covers only protection: it removes killing, captivity, plunder and enslavement, but the poll tax and the mark of lowliness remain. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the exception as covering all circumstances, so that they find honour only when they seek the protection of God and of the Muslims.

The word miskana (misery) is usually understood as poverty and neediness, and Ibn Uthaymin reads it as a poverty of heart rooted in greed, while al-Razi mentions the view that a Jew shows poverty even when rich. The commentators agree that the cause of this punishment is their disbelief in the signs of God and their killing of the prophets without right, together with disobedience and transgression of limits. Al-Razi adds that persistent disobedience gradually leads to unbelief, and Ibn Sa'di stresses that God does not punish without fault.

On the scope of the verse, opinions differ. Al-Tabari and al-Razi connect it with the Jews of Medina, Khaybar, Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayza, Ibn Ashur sees it as a foretelling of their misery in this world, and Ibn Kathir extends its meaning to all times.

This verse draws a distinction among the People of the Book: they are not all alike, for among them is an upright community, steadfast in God's command, which recites His verses during the hours of the night while prostrating. The commentators differ on who this group is. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Juraij identify them with Jews who embraced Islam, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, and report that the revelation came in response to the rabbis' claim that only the worst of them had believed; Ibn Mas'ud and al-Suddi instead take it as a comparison between the Jews and the community of Muhammad. The meaning of 'upright' is given by Mujahid as just, by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada as steadfast upon God's Book and its obligations, and by al-Suddi as obedient; al-Tabari judges these meanings to be close. As for 'the hours of the night', Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Juraij take them as its periods, al-Suddi as its middle, while Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid understand the night prayer of 'atama (the 'isha prayer), and ath-Thawri the time between maghrib and 'isha. On 'and they prostrate', al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, followed by Muqatil, take it as a reference to prayer, since recitation is not made during prostration, whereas others understand the ritual prostration itself or humility before God. The verse then lists their qualities: faith in God and the Last Day, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and hastening to good deeds, which commentators link both to knowledge and to action. It concludes that whatever good they do will not be lost or denied, and that God knows the righteous well.

This verse describes a group among the People of the Book who remained upright in the truth and are not equal to those whom God has just condemned. They believe in God and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, hasten to good deeds, and are counted among the righteous. The commentators agree that this refers to those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam, and that the verse qualifies the general judgement passed on most of them. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Ishaq report that the occasion was the conversion of Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, after which the rabbis said that only their worst people had believed, and this verse answered them. The meaning of 'a upright community' is disputed: Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Juraij take it as a just community, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Rabi' as one steadfast upon the Book of God, and al-Suddi as an obedient one. Al-Zamakhshari understands reciting God's signs in the night as the night prayer, and reports that Ibn Mas'ud took it to mean the 'Isha' prayer, while al-Thawri placed it between maghrib and 'isha'. Al-Tabari reads the prostration as a separate clause, meaning they are also people of prostration, whereas most take it to mean prayer. Al-Razi links these qualities to the perfection of both practice and knowledge. Some commentators extend 'the righteous' to all Muslims, and al-Zamakhshari holds that uprightness goes beyond mere adherence to Islam. The readings differ on 'whatever good they do, it will not be denied them', between the yā' and the tā', but all agree that good is not lost and will be rewarded. The verse closes by affirming that God knows the God-fearing well.

According to the commentators, this verse means that every good deed done by the steadfast believers among the People of the Book, whether small or great, will not be lost and its reward will not be denied: it will be acknowledged and they will be repaid for it, for God knows well those who are mindful of Him. The exegetes see the verse as a conclusion to the description of the upright community that recites God's signs during the night while prostrating, believes in God and the Last Day, enjoins what is right, forbids what is wrong, and hastens to good works. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that this community refers to those Jewish rabbis who embraced Islam, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, while others, including Ibn Mas'ud, hold that it includes both the People of the Book and the community of Muhammad. Ibn 'Abbas read both verbs in the third person, a reading al-Tabari chose and Abu 'Ubayd preferred, whereas Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and 'Asim read them in the second person, and Abu 'Amr accepted both readings.

The meaning of the verb 'kafara' in 'fa-lan yukfarûhu' is also debated: al-Tabari and Qatada take it as being covered up or lost, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi understand it as the withholding of reward, the verb being construed with two objects by implication. All agree that God rewards obedience and repays it in full. Al-Razi draws from this verse an argument against the doctrine that good deeds are annulled. For most commentators, the good meant here is that which springs from faith and sincerity, and the closing mention of piety is a glad tidings to the God-fearing and a sign that only those who possess it succeed with God.

This verse states that those who disbelieve will not be spared God's punishment by their wealth or their children, and that they are the companions of the Fire, where they will remain forever. The commentators agree that wealth and children are named because wealth can be offered as ransom and children can defend a person, and that neither will avail. Al-Tabari explains that abiding there means an unbroken companionship, and Ibn Kathir adds that God's punishment cannot be averted when He wills it. Al-Razi draws from the verse that sinners among the believers will not remain in the Fire eternally, reading the phrase 'companions of the Fire' as restrictive, though this is his own reading. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that the verse follows a passage on righteous People of the Book, and that the disbelievers here are those who reject the truth. The next verse offers a comparison: what these people spend in this life is like a biting wind that destroys the crop of a people who wronged themselves. Most exegetes, including Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas, take this to refer to the spending of the polytheists, including Abu Sufyan's expenses at Badr. Ibn 'Atiyya widens it to all their deeds, and al-Sudi takes it to mean their words. Most define the sirr as an intense cold, while al-Zajjaj says it is the sound of fire carried on the wind. All agree that God did not wrong them, since they wronged themselves through disbelief and disobedience.

This verse compares what the disbelievers spend in this worldly life to a crop struck by a freezing wind that destroys it, so that its owners gain nothing from it although they had hoped for its harvest. The commentators agree that the word ṣirr means intense cold, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan, although al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari understood it as the sound of fire carried by the wind, and Ibn Kathir notes that such cold burns crops as fire would. They differ on what the spending refers to: Mujahid says it is all the disbelievers' expenditure and charity, Muqatil says the Jewish commoners' support of their scholars, others say the spending of Abu Sufyan and his companions at Badr and Uhud, al-Zamakhshari says spending done for show, pride and a good reputation, and Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as all deeds tainted by disbelief. All agree that the loss results from disbelief and from the lack of sincerity. The phrase 'God did not wrong them' means, according to al-Tabari, that God did not act unjustly; they wronged themselves through disbelief and disobedience. Ibn Kathir adds that the disbeliever will find no reward in the hereafter. Al-Razi reports that the Mu'tazilites cite this verse for the doctrine of the nullification of good deeds, while the Sunni scholars reply that reward is conditional on faith.

This verse forbids believers from taking as close confidants people outside their community, that is, intimates to whom one entrusts secrets and whom one consults. The commentators explain that bitana means the lining of a garment, which touches the body, and that it is applied to a person who is privy to one's inner affairs. Most of them say that these people spare no effort in harming the believers and wish them hardship, and their hostility shows in their speech, while what they hide in their hearts is even greater. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the enmity appears in words and in the face, and al-Razi notes that the inner feeling is stronger than what is expressed. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take 'anat to mean hardship or the loss of faith, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as distress and suffering. The scholars differ on who is meant. Ibn 'Abbas, in one report, speaks of Jews bound to some Muslims by old alliances, and Mujahid and Qatada identify the hypocrites, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur hold that the ruling is general to all disbelievers. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite 'Umar, who used this verse to refuse hiring a Christian as a scribe. On the phrase 'you love them but they do not love you', al-Zamakhshari sees a rebuke to the believers, since they believe in all the Books while these people do not believe in theirs. The commentators also report that hypocrites, when they meet believers, claim faith, but when alone they bite their fingertips in rage. For the final part, the exegetes explain that good that befalls the believers grieves those people, and harm that strikes them delights them, but patience and piety defeat their scheming, since God encompasses what they do.

God warns believers against taking non-believers as confidants, people to whom one entrusts secrets and whose counsel one seeks, because such people spare no effort to harm them and wish them hardship; their hatred has already shown in their speech, and what their breasts conceal is greater still. The verse then tells the believers that they love these people while those people do not love them, even though the believers accept all the scriptures and the others reject theirs. When they meet believers they profess faith out of hypocrisy, and when alone they bite their fingertips in rage at the unity and harmony of the Muslims. As for the phrase "Die in your rage," al-Tabari and most exegetes read it as a curse that wishes their anger to persist until it destroys them, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as an increase in what enrages them, namely the strength of Islam and the honour of its people. Others take it as a rebuke or a statement rather than a genuine prayer. Al-Tabari reports that Abu al-Jawza' named the Ibadiyya whenever he recited this verse, and Ibn 'Atiyya adds that such traits may recur among innovators until the Day of Resurrection. The verse closes by affirming God's knowledge of what the breasts hold, presented by some as a threat and by others as a reminder to the Prophet and the believers.

This verse describes the deep hostility that the hypocrites and the People of the Book bear towards the believers. When good befalls the Muslims, such as victory, spoils or unity, it grieves them; when harm strikes, such as defeat or discord among them, they rejoice. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the 'good' and the 'evil' cover whatever pleases or displeases, such as plenty or famine, victory or defeat, union or division, and that these examples are illustrations rather than a closed list. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud see the variation between 'touching' for good and 'striking' for evil as stylistic, the first being a figurative use of the second. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi instead find a deliberate point: even a slight good grieves them, while they rejoice only at a great harm. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that this envy-born hatred does not vanish in hardship. As for the call to patience and piety, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Baghawi take it as patience under their harm and avoidance of their alliance and of disobedience to God. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari add that whoever holds to these virtues is not harmed by their scheming. Readers differed over 'la yadurrukum', in the forms 'yadirkum' and 'yadurrukum', each with its grammatical justification, as al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya note. The verse ends by affirming that God encompasses what the disbelievers do, meaning He knows it and has power over it, and He will repay them for it.

The commentators explain the verse 'And [remember] when you set out early from your family to station the believers at their positions for battle' as referring to the Battle of Uhud. The Prophet ﷺ left his home in the morning and placed the believers in the positions he judged suitable for the fight. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and most exegetes adopt this reading, since the following verses speak of two groups of the Ansar, Banu Salama and Banu Haritha, who intended to withdraw, and this happened at Uhud. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Muqatil placed the event at Badr or at the Battle of the Confederates, an opinion the majority considers weak.

On the time of departure, opinions differ. Some say he set out after the Friday prayer, the phrase 'set out early' being used figuratively. Others say he left on Saturday morning. The reports agree that the Prophet consulted his companions about going out or staying in Medina. He preferred to stay, and Abd Allah ibn Ubayy agreed, but young believers insisted on going out. He then put on his armour and went out, saying it is not fitting for a prophet to remove his armour before he has fought. Abd Allah ibn Ubayy withdrew with about a third of the army, and two groups of the Ansar nearly turned back, but God strengthened them.

Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim note that mentioning Uhud and Badr together shows that victory accompanies patience and piety, while the defeat came from disobeying the Prophet's command. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di stress divine protection. The commentators thus agree on the essentials, while the disagreement concerns mainly the exact place, the precise moment of departure and the interpretation of certain details.

This verse refers to the battle of Uhud, when two groups of the Ansar, Banu Salama of the Khazraj and Banu Haritha of the Aws, almost lost heart and considered withdrawing. God preserved them, for He is their ally and protector, and He commands the believers to rely on Him alone. Commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that these two clans are meant and that the episode took place after Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew with about a third of the army. Fashal means cowardice or loss of resolve. Jabir ibn Abdullah, as transmitted in the Sahih, said the verse was revealed about them and that he would not wish it had not been revealed, because it shows God's protection of them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya hold that this was only a passing thought and not a firm decision, as the phrase 'and God is their ally' suggests. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan note that hamm can mean resolve, reflection or a fleeting impulse, and that the verse does not prove a grave sin. Views differ on the cause: al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj say it was Ibn Ubayy's call to turn back, while others say they had already disagreed about going out at all. Finally, the commentators stress that the believer must rely on God while also taking the necessary means, as al-Qurtubi and al-Razi explain.

In this verse God reminds the believers of His favour at the battle of Badr, where He gave them victory although they were few and poorly equipped, so that they would fear Him and be grateful. The commentators agree that Badr was a place, or a water source, between Mecca and Medina, but they differ on its name. Al-Sha'bi said it was a well belonging to a man called Badr, while al-Waqidi and his informants rejected this and held that it was simply the name of the site. Ibn Kathir reports that the battle took place on the seventeenth of Ramadan. The word 'adhilla' (humbled) is taken by most to mean weakness in number and equipment: the Muslims were about three hundred and some men, with one or two horses and some seventy camels they shared in turns, while their enemy numbered between nine hundred and a thousand, with a hundred horses and abundant weapons. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the plural of small number was chosen to show that they were few despite their humiliation, while al-Tabari sees the word simply as referring to their lack of numbers. Fear of God is understood by many as obedience to the Prophet's command and steadfastness in battle; Ibn Ishaq links it to giving thanks for the favour, and Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a call to remain firm after the defeat at Uhud. The commentators also differ on when the Prophet promised the believers three thousand angels: most say it was at Badr, while others, such as Mujahid, Ikrima and al-Dahhak, place that promise at Uhud, where it was not fulfilled because the believers lacked patience and piety. They largely agree that the angels fought only at Badr, but remain divided over exactly what they did.

God reminds the believers of the victory He gave them at Badr, when they were few and weak, and of the words the Prophet ﷺ spoke when he heard that Kurz ibn Jabir intended to reinforce the polytheists: would it not suffice you that your Lord support you with three thousand angels sent down? The verse then promises five thousand marked angels if they endure patiently, fear God, and the enemy comes at once. Commentators agree that angels took part in or were present at Badr, that this support was good news and a calming of hearts, and that victory comes from God alone. On the timing of the statement, opinions differ. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and most exegetes place it at Badr; Ibn Kathir reports this from al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and al-Rabi'. Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Dahhak and al-Zuhri place it at Uhud, where the promise, conditional on patience and piety, was not fulfilled because the Muslims neither endured nor feared God, so no angel was sent. The thousand angels in Surat al-Anfal are, for all, the aid of Badr; al-Tabari and others reconcile the numbers by describing a promise that grew from a thousand to three thousand to five thousand. On the phrase rendered as 'from this very rush', al-Hasan and Qatada take it to mean 'from this direction', while Mujahid and Ikrima take it to mean 'from this anger'. On the meaning of 'marked', views differ on the mark: wool, yellow or white turbans, piebald horses. Al-Tabari prefers the reading that makes the angels themselves the ones who marked themselves, while others hold the mark was imposed by God. The following verses state that the aim of the victory is to cut off a part of the disbelievers or humiliate them, that the Prophet has no share in the divine decision, and that it was revealed concerning his curses against some disbelievers, whose repentance God later accepted. Al-Tabari and al-Razi read the 'or' in 'or He turns to them in mercy' as coordinating with what precedes.

This verse, set in the context of the battle of Badr and its aftermath, promises the believers a reinforcement of angels on condition that they endure and fear God. According to most commentators, the meaning is that God will aid the believers with five thousand marked angels if they stand firm against the enemy and avoid disobeying their Prophet, and if the polytheists attack them straight away, 'from their very rush'. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and others link the passage to Badr: word had reached the Muslims that Kurz ibn Jabir was reinforcing the polytheists, which troubled them, and the verse came to reassure them. As for the phrase 'from their very rush', al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas explain it as 'from their direction' or 'from their journey', while Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Abu Salih take it to mean 'from their anger'. Opinions differ on how the promise was fulfilled. Some, such as al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and al-Rabi', hold that it took place at Badr, the help arriving gradually from one thousand to five thousand angels. Others, such as 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak, hold that it concerned Uhud, where the Muslims did not endure and therefore received no help. Al-Tabari notes that the verse does not decide the question clearly, but he prefers the reading 'musawwimin' with a kasra, supported by reports from the Companions. On the marks of the angels, views vary: white turbans according to Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ali, yellow turbans according to Hisham ibn 'Urwa, and wool on the manes and tails of the horses according to Mujahid and Qatada. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi consider that the angels fought only at Badr, or that their presence served mainly to strengthen hearts and sow terror, while others affirm that they actually fought. Several commentators stress that victory comes from God alone, and that the announcement of reinforcement is good news meant to calm hearts.

The commentators explain the plain meaning as follows: God made the reinforcement by angels only as good news for the believers, so that their hearts would be reassured, and victory comes only from God, the Mighty, the Wise. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi agree that the aid itself is not the true cause of victory but a means of comfort. They concur that 'victory' here means the victory of the believers, while the defeat inflicted on the disbelievers is a trial. On the occasion of the verse, opinions differ: al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link it to Badr, whereas Mujahid, al-Dahhak and 'Ikrima place it at Uhud, where the conditional promise, tied to patience and piety, was not fulfilled because the Muslims did not remain steadfast. On whether the angels actually fought, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari affirm it at Badr, while al-Alusi holds that the majority view is that they did not generally fight and that their role was mainly to strengthen hearts. Regarding the reason for the revelation of 'You have no say in the matter', the reports vary: the Prophet's curses against certain disbelievers after Uhud, or a remark that a people who wound their prophet will not prosper. Al-Razi and al-Alusi observe that the attributes of might and wisdom suit the idea that victory belongs to God alone.

This part of the verse states that God granted victory to the believers at Badr in order to cut off a part of the disbelievers, that is, to strike a decisive blow by killing and capturing them. This took place at Badr: according to al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Ishaq, about seventy of their nobles and leaders were killed and as many were taken prisoner. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the verse as referring to this battle, whereas al-Suddi applies it to the eighteen pagan dead at Uhud, a view that Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan present as a separate opinion. The word "yakbitahum" is understood by most as "to humiliate and defeat them" or "to put them to flight"; al-Khalil and Abu 'Ubayda take it to mean throwing someone to the ground on his face, while Ibn Qutayba, followed by several philologists, holds that it derives from "yukabbidahum", striking the liver with grief and rage, a view supported by verses of al-A'sha and al-Mutanabbi. "Khayba" means returning without having obtained what one hoped for. As for the preposition "li", commentators attach it either to "God helped you", to "victory comes only from God", or to an implied verb. The parenthetical phrase "you have no say in the matter" is linked by several commentators to the occasion when the Prophet invoked curses against some polytheists; Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir judge the strongest reading to be that "or He will turn to them" is coordinated with "to humiliate them".

The commentators explain that the verse means the decision belongs to God alone: the Prophet ﷺ has no share in the fate of the disbelievers. God may cut off a group of those who disbelieved or humiliate them, then pardon whom He wills by guiding them to Islam, or punish those who persist in wrongdoing. Most exegetes report that the verse was revealed at the battle of Uhud, when the Prophet's face was wounded and his tooth broken, and he said: how can a people prosper who did this to their prophet while he calls them to their Lord? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others also report that the Prophet ﷺ wanted to curse certain men and God restrained him, some of them later embracing Islam. Ibn 'Atiyya and others take 'or He will pardon them' as coordinated with 'to cut off', with 'you have no say in the matter' as a parenthetical clause. Al-Farra' and others read 'or' as meaning 'until' or 'unless', giving: you have no say in their affair until God pardons them or punishes them. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer the first reading. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi stress that God grants repentance to whom He wills and that punishment is deserved only through wrongdoing. Al-Razi holds that the verse forbids the Prophet any act or word not authorized by God, and affirms that all matters rest with God. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a reminder of what happened at Badr, with the varied outcomes for the disbelievers, and as a consolation for the Prophet. What the commentators agree on is that God alone holds the decision, that unjust disbelievers deserve punishment, and that the door of repentance remains open to whom God wills.

This verse declares that all sovereignty belongs to God alone: whatever is in the heavens and on earth is His, He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and God is Forgiving and Merciful. It comes in the context of Uhud, after the Prophet ﷺ, wounded, wished to curse the disbelievers; the verse makes clear that the decision over people's fate belongs to God and not to the Prophet. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, God has absolute disposal: He forgives and punishes by His will, and this statement concludes the preceding sentence, 'you have no part in the affair'. Most stress the general scope of the formula and the primacy of mercy, since the verse ends with 'Forgiving, Merciful'. On the extent of forgiveness, the commentators differ. Al-Zamakhshari, reporting the Mu'tazili position as Abu Hayyan also does, holds that forgiveness is conditional on repentance, and that God wills to forgive only the repentant. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi, following the Sunni view, answer that the verse imposes no such restriction and that God may forgive one who dies without repenting of a major sin; they consider repentance a condition for disbelief rather than for all sins. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite reports about the occasion of revelation, namely the Prophet's wound at Uhud and his supplications, while several commentators hold that the verse's meaning goes beyond that single event. Al-Qurtubi also notes that the verse abrogates nothing. The commentators agree that the verse affirms God's sovereignty and mercy, without settling the theological debates definitively.

This verse forbids believers from practising usury in the form common before Islam: when a debt fell due and the debtor could not pay, he was told to pay or to let the sum grow, and the term was extended again and again with the amount increased until it had multiplied many times over. Most commentators treat the phrase "multiplied manifold" as describing the prevailing practice rather than as a limit that permits smaller amounts. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan affirm that usury is forbidden in all its forms, and that the prohibition is tied to the taqwa on which success depends. Al-Mawardi and al-Razi regard usury as a major sin, and al-Razi argues that the verse shows that it cancels the chance of success, whereas al-Qurtubi notes that God singled out usury for warning because it was linked to a declaration of war, and holds that whoever deems it lawful disbelieves. On the phrase "the Fire prepared for the disbelievers," opinions differ: Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take the threat to apply to those who consider usury lawful, while al-Mawardi and al-Razi hold that the Fire also concerns sinners at varying degrees, and that naming the disbelievers does not exclude others. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari cite many traditions that repentance and asking forgiveness erase sins. Al-Qurtubi quotes Ibn 'Atiyya, who knows of no reported occasion of revelation for this passage placed within the account of Uhud. Al-Tabari, citing Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and 'Ata', explains that pre-Islamic usury meant postponing a debt in return for an increase. Overall, the commentators agree that the verse calls for piety and obedience to God and His Messenger in hope of success and mercy, and promises forgiveness to those who repent.

This verse tells the believers to guard themselves against the Fire prepared for the disbelievers, that is, to keep away from whatever leads to it. Most commentators understand it as a warning against disbelief and against imitating the disbelievers, and especially against usury (riba), which the preceding verses forbid. Al-Tabari explains that believers must not enter the abodes of the disbelievers after having believed. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the Fire is prepared for the disbelievers in the primary sense, while disobedient believers enter it secondarily. Abu Hanifa, as reported by Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and others, considered this the most frightening verse in the Quran, since it threatens believers with the Fire of the disbelievers if they do not fear God by avoiding what He has forbidden. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as a warning that believers should not deem usury lawful, and al-Zajjaj adds that one must not make lawful what God has forbidden, lest one become a disbeliever. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also relate the view that the disbelief meant is treating usury as permissible. Al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi discuss whether the Fire is a single place or has degrees, and Ibn 'Atiyya reports those who distinguish the Fire of the disbelievers from that of the disobedient. The verse ends with the command to obey God and the Messenger in hope of mercy, and al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq see in this a rebuke to those who disobeyed the Prophet at Uhud.

In this verse God commands the believers to obey Him and His Messenger, and links the hope of receiving His mercy to that obedience, so that they will not be punished for their sins. The commentators agree that obedience covers carrying out commands and avoiding prohibitions, including the ban on usury mentioned in the preceding verses. Al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq report that the verse rebukes those who disobeyed the Prophet at Uhud by leaving their posts, while most exegetes take it in a general sense without limiting it to that event. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur see the verse as moving from warning to promise, to deter disobedience and encourage obedience, and they note that the word 'perhaps' signals how hard mercy is to attain, a point also made by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi stress that, for one who has faith, sin does not fully remove a person from mercy, and Ibn Kathir reports that the mercy meant is God's mercy in this world and the next. Ibn Uthaymin holds that the mercy intended is the special mercy that secures happiness in both abodes, and that the command to obey implies obligation. Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi emphasise the legislative and social dimension of the verse, presenting obedience as the path to salvation both in this life and the next.

This verse calls believers to hasten toward forgiveness from their Lord and toward a Garden whose breadth is like the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing. The commentators explain that forgiveness is what covers sins and removes their punishment, and that one hastens toward it through the deeds that bring it about. Ibn Abbas, Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ikrima take it to mean Islam, repentance and the performance of obligations; Anas ibn Malik means the opening takbir of prayer; Abu al-Aliya means emigration, al-Dahhak means jihad, Sa'id ibn Jubayr means obedience, and Muqatil means good deeds. Al-Kalbi and al-Shawkani note that these answers are examples rather than a closed list. On the breadth of the Garden, Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and most scholars, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya, understand it as the heavens and earth joined together like cloth; others take it as a figure of vast expanse, with the Garden above the heavens beneath the Throne. The Mu'tazilites hold that it is not yet created, while the majority hold that it already exists. The commentaries also recount the Jewish questioner who asked Umar ibn al-Khattab where Hell is, and the Prophet's reply to Heraclius's envoy, asking where the night goes when the day comes. The verses then describe the God-fearing: those who spend in ease and hardship, who restrain their anger and pardon people, and God loves the good-doers. Those who commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember God, seek forgiveness and do not persist in what they did, receive forgiveness and gardens beneath which rivers flow. Ibn Kathir defines persistence as remaining silent about sin and not seeking forgiveness, al-Hasan as repeating the sin, and Qatada as continuing in it.

This verse praises the God-fearing, who are prepared for Paradise, and describes their qualities: they spend their wealth in ease and in hardship, they restrain their anger although they could act on it, and they pardon people. God loves those who do good in this way. The commentators explain that the times of ease and hardship mean prosperity and adversity, or joy and sorrow. Some add that they never stop giving, even a little: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Aisha gave a single grape and that an early pious man gave an onion. Restraining anger means holding it in while full of it, and Ibn Kathir cites hadiths promising inner security and faith to whoever does so, though some scholars questioned their soundness. There is general agreement that pardon extends to anyone who wronged you. Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi and Abu al-Aliya took it first of masters forgiving their slaves, while Zayd ibn Aslam and Muqatil took it as general. Al-Razi and Ibn Atiyya see the verse as covering every form of kindness to others. Commentators stress that praiseworthy pardon is that given by one who could retaliate, not that of the powerless. Most affirm that God loves the doers of good, in a manner befitting Him.

This verse describes a group of the God-conscious who, when they commit a fault, repent. When they commit an indecency, meaning a grave sin, or wrong themselves with a lesser offence, they remember God, His threat and His greatness, and ask Him for forgiveness, since none but God forgives sins. They do not persist in disobedience, knowing it to be disobedience. The commentators agree that this group ranks below the first, yet they are counted among the God-conscious when they repent. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the indecency means adultery for Jabir, al-Suddi and Muqatil, while others take it to be any major sin, with wronging oneself meaning minor sins. Al-Nakha'i holds the two terms to overlap, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi read them as two categories. On remembering God, al-Tabari and al-Razi understand recalling His warning and punishment, others understand asking forgiveness with the tongue, and Ibn Kathir combines heart, tongue and deeds. On persistence, Qatada takes it as continuing in the sin, al-Hasan as committing the sin until repentance, Mujahid as going on, and al-Suddi as failing to seek forgiveness. Al-Tabari concludes it means persisting in sin without repentance. Several cite the hadith that one who seeks forgiveness does not persist, even if he returns to the sin seventy times a day, though al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi differ on the soundness of its chain. As for 'while they know', most take it to mean they know it is disobedience, while others take it to mean they know God accepts repentance.

This part of the verse states that the reward for those who are mindful of God and do good, including those who repent without persisting in their sins, is forgiveness from their Lord and gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever, an excellent wage for those who act. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that forgiveness means pardon from punishment for past sins, and that the gardens are orchards with rivers flowing through them as a reward for righteous deeds. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the word 'wage' after 'reward' signals that the recompense is owed for the deed performed, while Ibn Atiyya holds that God obliged Himself through His true report to accept repentance, though reason imposes no duty on Him. Ibn Kathir also relates the comparison of Paradise's breadth to the heavens and the earth, which he reads as an image of vastness. Most commentators understand persistence (israr) as continuing in sin without repentance, while Ibn al-Jawzi and others give several meanings for indecency (fahisha), sometimes adultery and sometimes any grave sin. The exegetes agree on the value of repentance but differ on the fate of those who persist: al-Zamakhshari excludes them from Paradise, whereas al-Alusi refuses to draw that conclusion from the silence of the text. In short, the verse combines divine mercy with the principle that good deeds are the cause of a generous reward.

God addresses the believers after the setback at Uhud: ways (sunan) of past nations have already passed, in which victory went to the prophets and their followers and ruin to the deniers. He therefore orders them to travel the earth and look at the ruins of those destroyed, so that they may take warning. The commentators agree that the verse is both consolation and warning. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the sunan are the punishments God inflicted on disbelieving peoples such as Noah's people, 'Ad, Thamud and Lot's people, and that the respite given to the unbelievers is only a delay until a fixed term. Ibn Zayd takes them as examples, while Mujahid links them to the divine law that applies to believers and unbelievers alike. Al-Zajjaj suggests an implied phrase meaning people of ways, that is, peoples who followed a good or bad path. Al-Razi, Ibn Qayyim and Ibn 'Ashur note that the journey may be physical or intellectual, since seeing the remains is more powerful than hearing a report. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that such travel is valuable only when it aims at reflection, and that one should weep when passing the dwellings of Thamud, following the Prophet's example. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take the verb 'look' mainly as seeing, though some read it as reflection. All agree on the grim end of the deniers and on the lesson of steadfastness for the believers.

The commentators agree on the general meaning of the verse: the Qur'an is a clear explanation for mankind, and a guidance and admonition for the God-fearing. They differ, however, on what the demonstrative "this" refers to. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, al-Rabi' and Muqatil take it to mean the Qur'an itself. Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari and others link it to the preceding statement that ways have passed before you, meaning that this account is an explanation for people if they accept it. Al-Tabari prefers this second reading, since the demonstrative points to something heard in the preceding verses. Others consider the Qur'an the broader reference, and some hold that both meanings are valid.

The three key terms are explained fairly consistently. Bayan means clarification and making things evident; al-Sha'bi says it removes blindness. Huda is the indication of the right path, and mawi'za is exhortation through encouragement and warning that drives away ignorance.

Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi note that only the God-fearing benefit from guidance and admonition, so these are specified for them, while the clarification is general to all people. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di likewise hold that the pious are the ones who benefit, and that the clarification establishes proof for everyone. Ibn 'Atiyya observes that the Qur'an is not fittingly attributed to those whose hearts are blinded by disbelief. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the clarification is general while guidance and admonition are for the pious.

Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the passage as a warning to unbelievers to reflect on the fate of their predecessors, and as added insight and firmness for believers. Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin see it as preparing the believers for consolation after Uhud. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the God-fearing benefit from the Qur'an, and that whoever is not moved by it should examine himself.

God comforts the believers after the defeat at Uhud. He forbids them to weaken or give way in fighting their enemy, and tells them not to grieve over the dead and wounded, promising that they are the superior ones and that victory will be theirs if they are believers. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi explain it as: do not lose heart in jihad and do not lament those who fell, for the outcome and victory are yours. Most commentators take “you are the superior” as a statement that the word of Islam will rise, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read a higher rank: your fighting is for God and your dead go to Paradise, whereas your enemies fight for Satan and their dead go to Hell. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the verse belongs to the alternation of days, which tests and purifies the believers. Al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan link the condition “if you are believers” to the prohibition: true faith gives firmness of heart and trust in God. Al-Razi offers several readings, attaching the condition either to the superiority or to belief in God’s promise. Ibn 'Atiyya distinguishes the forbidden weakness from the gentleness proper to believers. Ibn Kathir and the narratives cited by al-Baghawi and al-Tha'alibi connect the verse to the events of the battle and the pursuit of the enemy. Ibn 'Ashur sees a warning against weakness of resolve. The commentaries do not choose between these views, which largely complement one another.

After the defeat at Uhud, God consoles the believers: the wounds and deaths they suffered were matched by their enemies' losses at Badr, and the days are turns of fortune that God alternates among people, so the believers should neither weaken nor grieve. Commentators explain that qarh, with a fatha on the qaf, means the wound and, with a damma, the pain of it; many treat the two readings as synonyms, while al-Farra' and others see a difference in meaning. All agree that 'the days' means the periods of victory and domination, which God alternates to distinguish the sincere believer from the hypocrite and to honour some of them with martyrdom. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the Muslims had asked God for a day like Badr in which to fight and win martyrdom, and the 'martyrs' are those slain at Uhud. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir note that without this trial, people would enter Islam without truly wanting it. As for 'God does not love the wrongdoers', al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq take it to mean the hypocrites who withdrew from the fighting, while Ibn Abbas and others take it to mean the polytheists. Al-Razi holds that God grants the unbelievers victory not out of love for them but for the benefits it brings the believers. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the trial purifies the believers and destroys the unbelievers, and al-Alusi adds that God does not truly support the disbelievers but lets them prevail at times as a test for the believers or a respite that leads to their ruin.

The commentators explain that this verse refers to the battle of Uhud and the trial that the believers underwent. God states that the days are alternated among people, sometimes in favour of the believers and sometimes of the disbelievers, and that the purpose is to separate and purify the believers while destroying the disbelievers. Al-Tabari reports from Mujahid and Ibn Abi Najih that tamhis means testing, and from al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq that it means testing the patience and certainty of the believers so that the sincere are distinguished from the hypocrites. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir understand mahq as diminishing and annihilating. Al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad take tamhis to mean purification and sifting, that is, cleansing the believers of their sins. Ibn Atiyya, al-Baghawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the trial erases sins and that victory over the disbelievers wipes them out. Al-Razi gives several wisdoms for the alternation of fortunes, among them that faith must not become a compelling certainty, which would nullify moral responsibility. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin combine both meanings: the believer is purified of sins and of hypocrites, while the disbeliever may be destroyed by his arrogance after victory. Ibn Kathir adds that martyrdom itself expiates sins. Al-Jalalayn simply says that tamhis purifies the believers from sins through what befalls them, and that mahq means the destruction of the disbelievers.

This verse rebukes the believers after the Battle of Uhud, who thought they would enter Paradise without being tested by fighting and hardship. The commentators explain that God has not yet made manifest, by a knowledge of visible occurrence, those among them who strove and those who endured patiently. Most read the question as a rebuke, with the particle 'am' understood as disjunctive, meaning roughly 'rather', as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan note. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir see it as a reproach to those who fled at Uhud after having longed to meet the enemy as at Badr. The meaning of 'lamma' is discussed: it stands for 'lam' while implying an expectation of future fulfilment, according to al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi. Al-Razi draws from it that love of the world cannot coexist with the happiness of the Hereafter. The readings of 'wa-ya'lama' differ: a subjunctive with an implied particle according to the Basrans, a waw of accompaniment or of exception according to the Kufans, a jussive by coordination in al-Hasan's reading, and an indicative in Abu 'Amr's reading as a new clause or circumstantial phrase. Ibn Kathir and others report that the wish for death refers to the wish for fighting and martyrdom, and a tradition forbids wishing to meet the enemy. Ibn 'Uthaymin distinguishes God's eternal knowledge from the knowledge that becomes actual and entails reward or punishment. Several commentators conclude from this verse that struggle and patience are the path to Paradise, and that wishing alone is not enough.

God addresses the believers who had missed the Battle of Badr and had longed to fight and win martyrdom, saying that they used to wish for death before meeting it, meaning they wished for the battle that causes it, and now they have seen its signs with their own eyes. The commentators generally take the address to refer to those who had pressed to go out at Uhud and then fled in the defeat, which is why the verse rebukes them. They agree that by death is meant martyrdom or its causes such as fighting, and that wishing for martyrdom is not in itself blameworthy; the reproach falls on turning back when steadfastness was required. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that these men wished to match the companions of Badr, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya stress their insistence that the Prophet go out. They differ on the purpose of the repetition in « while you were looking »: al-Akhfash sees emphasis, al-Zajjaj means « while you could see clearly », and others read it as a call to reflect on your own conduct. On the word « seen », some take it as knowledge, others as direct observation. Many link the verse to the rumour of the Prophet's death and the revelation that followed. The overall meaning is a reproach, a reminder of the pledge made, and an acknowledgement that the wish for martyrdom is legitimate when joined with patience and steadfastness.

This verse reminds the believers that Muhammad ﷺ is a messenger like the messengers before him, a mortal who will die as they did, and that his presence among his community is not a condition for the survival of the faith. According to the reports cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, it was revealed after Uhud, when a rumour spread that the Prophet had been killed; some Muslims faltered, and some hypocrites urged a return to their former religion, and God rebukes them. The commentators read the interrogative particle as a reproach, and understand turning back on one's heels as apostasy, though some, such as al-Zamakhshari, take it to mean fleeing the battle. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the Prophet was not in fact killed, and that mentioning death or killing addressed what the hearers considered possible. The phrase that one will not harm God in any way means the harm falls on the apostate himself. Al-Tabari reports from Ali that the grateful are those who stayed firm, Abu Bakr and his companions, and Ibn Kathir relates that Abu Bakr recited this verse at the Prophet's death, which steadied the people. The scholars agree on the rebuke, the warning and the praise of the steadfast, but differ on the precise meaning of turning back and on who the grateful are.

This verse states that no soul dies except by God's permission, and that every life has a fixed, written term that can neither be advanced nor delayed. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir note that fear does not lengthen life and courage does not shorten it. Most commentators report that the verse was revealed after Uhud, when the rumour spread that the Prophet had been killed, to steady the believers. They differ on the meaning of 'permission': Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jurayj take it as command or divine decree, Muqatil as permission itself, Abu Muslim as an order to the Angel of Death, al-Razi as allowing something to happen, and some as knowledge. Most explain the 'written term' as the record of appointed times, and al-Razi links it to the Preserved Tablet. In the second part, al-Tabari, Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Kathir explain that whoever desires the rewards of this world receives what was allotted to him, and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter receives it. Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi and al-Baydawi read this as a rebuke to those who left their posts for booty at Uhud, while those who stood firm with Abd Allah ibn Jubayr desired the Hereafter. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it as a general principle for all deeds, since intention matters more than outward action. Commentators agree that God will reward the grateful, and some specify those who remained steadfast in faith.

The commentators explain that the verse reminds believers that many prophets fought alongside large bodies of followers who, despite wounds or death in God's cause, did not weaken, falter, or submit to the enemy; God loves the patient. They differ over the reading qātala versus qutila. Al-Tabari and those who follow him prefer qutila, meaning the prophet himself was killed along with some companions, which fits the rumour of the Prophet's death at Uhud. Al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr hold that no prophet was ever killed in battle, and make the verb refer to the rabbiyyun. Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn 'Atiyya consider qātala more comprehensive in praise, since it includes both those who died and those who survived. On the meaning of rabbiyyun, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Farra' say thousands, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada say large companies, al-Hasan says patient scholars, and Ibn Zayd says followers, with the rabbaniyyun being the rulers. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain wahn, da'f and istikana as discouragement, weakness and submission to the enemy, while Qatada and al-Rabi' take istikana to mean apostasy. Ibn Kathir also notes that the Companions recalled this verse after the Prophet's death. The next verse shows their prayer was for forgiveness and steadfastness, and God gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the next, a model for believers to follow.

This verse describes the words of the believers who stood firm alongside their prophets in battle. The commentators explain that their only speech was supplication and seeking forgiveness. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that they asked God to forgive their sins and their excesses, to make their feet firm in the battles, and to grant them victory over the disbelieving people. The commentators differ on the meaning of the words for sins and excesses. Ibn 'Abbas and several others take sins to mean minor offences and excesses to mean major ones, while al-Dahhak holds that sins are general and that excess refers only to grave sins. Others say the two words have the same meaning and are repeated for emphasis. As for making the feet firm, Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars understand it as steadfastness in combat, whereas al-Zajjaj understands it as steadfastness in faith, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that both readings are possible. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that forgiveness is requested before victory because victory requires purity from sin. Al-Zamakhshari adds that this order makes the supplication more likely to be answered. The scholars agree that God gave them the reward of this world, namely victory and spoils, and the good reward of the Hereafter, which is Paradise. Several commentators also see in the verse a reproach to those who fled at Uhud, and an invitation for the believers to imitate these steadfast people in their supplication and their firmness.

This verse describes the reward given to those who persevered in fighting alongside their prophets and remained steadfast after they were killed, asking God for forgiveness of their sins and their excesses in their affairs, for their feet to be made firm, and for victory over the disbelievers. The commentators explain that God gave them two rewards: the reward of this world, which is victory, triumph over the enemy and honour, and the good reward of the Hereafter, which is Paradise and its bliss, together with God's love for the good-doers. Nearly all agree that the worldly reward is victory over the enemy and the otherworldly reward is Paradise, as stated by Qatada, al-Rabi', Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and others. Ibn Jurayj, al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud add spoils of war and a good name. Regarding the good reward of the Hereafter, Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Sam'ani, describes tents of pearl and ruby in which God settles the Prophet and his companions, Ibn Jurayj understands it as God's good pleasure and mercy, while Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Wahidi understand it as recompense and forgiveness. Al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the attribute 'good' is reserved for the future reward to highlight its greatness, since worldly reward is fleeting and mixed with harm. Al-Razi also observes that God calls them 'good-doers' after they confessed their sins. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a lesson for believers who remained firm after the death of their prophet.

This verse forbids believers to obey the disbelievers, because obeying them would turn them back into disbelief after faith, and they would lose both this world and the next. It then reminds them that God is their protector and the best of helpers. The commentators differ on who the disbelievers are. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and al-Suddi say they were the hypocrites who, after the defeat at Uhud, told the believers to return to their ancestors' religion, arguing that had Muhammad been a prophet he would not have been killed; al-Suddi also names Abu Sufyan and his companions. Ibn Jurayj and al-Hasan take them to be the Jews and Christians, who cast doubts into the hearts of Muslims. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that the wording is general and covers every disbeliever, since the occasion of revelation does not restrict the scope of the text. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan add that the prohibition extends to consulting them and seeking their advice, while Abu Bakr al-Razi makes an exception for someone whose sincerity is reliable, such as a spy or a guide. For the next verse, nearly all report that it refers to the polytheists' decision after Uhud to return and attack Medina, and to God casting terror into their hearts so that they turned back. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith in which the Prophet says he was aided by terror over a month's distance. The commentators agree that these verses remind believers that victory comes from God alone.

In this verse God addresses the believers: do not obey the disbelievers, lest they turn you back on your heels and you become losers; God is your protector and helper, and He is the best of helpers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that "mawlakum" means your helper and guardian, so the believers should rely on His support rather than on anyone else's. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan read "bal" as a turn away from what the condition implies: the disbelievers are not your allies to be obeyed, rather God is. Al-Hasan read the divine name in the accusative, meaning "obey God instead", a reading considered irregular since the conditional already carries a prohibition. On who the "disbelievers" are, opinions differ: Ali and those who follow him identify them as the hypocrites who told the believers at the defeat to return to their former religion; al-Hasan, Ibn Ishaq and al-Zamakhshari say they are Jews and Christians or those who submit to them; al-Suddi names Abu Sufyan and his men; al-Razi and most exegetes hold that the wording is general and covers every disbeliever, since a specific occasion does not restrict a general expression. Al-Razi also explains that God is the best helper because He is capable, knowing and generous, and helps in this world and the next, even before being asked. Ibn al-Qayyim develops the idea that whoever turns to God obtains victory. Contemporary commentators such as al-Jaza'iri and Ibn 'Uthaymin note that the prohibition concerns obedience in matters of worship rather than in trades or practical matters.

This verse announces that Allah will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, because they associated with Him deities for which He had sent down no authority, and that their final abode will be the Fire, the worst abode for the wrongdoers. Most commentators link the verse to the battle of Uhud. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn Ishaq and as-Suddi, reports that Abu Sufyan and the polytheists, after leaving the field, regretted not finishing off the Muslims and decided to return, but Allah cast fear into their hearts and they turned back. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir relate similar accounts, while al-Mawardi and al-Wahidi are briefer. Ibn Ishaq sees the promise as reassurance for the believers, guaranteeing victory as long as they remain obedient. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that sultan means proof or evidence, and that denying its descent implies denying its existence altogether. Al-Razi draws from the verse an argument against blind imitation (taqlid). Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that the promise covers every disbeliever in every age, citing the hadith: I was helped by terror across a distance of a month's journey. The two readings of the word al-ru'b, with and without a vowel on the middle letter, are treated as two dialects with the same meaning. Al-Razi notes that many exegetes restrict the promise to Uhud, while others extend it to all times. Ibn Ashur explains that polytheism leaves the soul unsettled and fearful, so terror is its natural consequence.

This verse recalls that God fulfilled His promise of victory at Uhud, when the believers were slaying the polytheists by His permission, meaning by His enabling. The commentators explain that this initial success depended on the archers keeping their positions as ordered. When some believers faltered, disputed what to do, and disobeyed the Prophet after seeing victory, the archers left their posts to collect booty, while a small group stayed loyal. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Wahidi agree on this account, and note that Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas reported that some companions wanted worldly gain that day. For al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, the tide turned when Khalid ibn al-Walid, leading the cavalry, circled behind the archers. The word hass is taken by most as killing, though al-Zamakhshari restricts it to a crushing slaughter. Grammarians differ on the missing answer of the conditional clause: al-Farra saw the answer in the verb 'you disobeyed' with a superfluous waw, most supposed an omitted answer, and al-Zamakhshari suggested it means 'He withheld His help from you'. Al-Razi and al-Tabari note that the majority view attributes the defeat to God's permission as a test, while the Mu'tazila attribute it to human choice. Finally, God pardoned them: according to Ibn Abbas this means pardon from punishment, according to al-Hasan pardon from total destruction, and al-Razi draws from it that a grave sin does not expel the believer from faith.

This verse describes the state of the Muslims at Uhud when they were routed and fled up the slopes and into the valley, not turning back for anyone, while the Prophet ﷺ called to them from behind, saying 'O servants of God'. God then repaid them with one grief after another: the loss of victory and spoils, the defeat, the dead and wounded, and then the rumour that the Prophet ﷺ had been killed, so that they would not grieve over what escaped them or what befell them. The commentators agree on the meaning of the ascent: 'iṣʿād' is fleeing across level ground or through valleys, while 'ṣuʿūd' is climbing hills, and the verse rebukes the fugitives while recalling God's pardon. They differ on the two griefs. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Suddi take them as the loss of spoils and victory, then Abu Sufyan appearing above them. Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Ishaq see the killing and wounds first, then the rumour of the Prophet's death. Mujahid takes the first as the initial flight and the second as a second flight when they heard he had been killed. Al-Hasan says it refers to the grief at Uhud in exchange for the grief Badr inflicted on the polytheists. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also raise the possibility that the Prophet shared their sorrow. On 'so that you would not grieve', most see it as training in patience, while al-Mufaddal holds that 'lā' is superfluous. Al-Tabari preferred the view that the first grief was the loss of victory and spoils, and the second the defeat, the dead and the rumour.

These two verses describe how God sent down a sense of security upon the sincere believers after the grief of Uhud, so that a light sleep overcame them, while another group, whom most commentators identify as the hypocrites, was preoccupied with their own selves, thought wrongly of God, and asked whether they had any say in the matter. God replies that the whole affair belongs to Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that this remark was made by Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, and that Mu'attib ibn Qushayr said it within earshot of al-Zubayr. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi note that sleep is a sign of safety, since the frightened do not sleep. The divine answer, that even had they stayed home those destined to die would have gone out to their places of death, is read by most as an affirmation that no precaution can override the decree. The purpose of the trial, according to al-Tabari and al-Baydawi, is to expose what is in the hearts and to purify them. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'their own selves had made them anxious': Qatada and Ibn Ishaq take it as fear of death, while others take it as concern only for their own safety. On 'the ignorance of the pre-Islamic period', most identify it with the thinking of idolaters, whereas al-Tabari and Qatada attribute it to the followers of Abu Sufyan. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi also cite reports that Abu Talha and others dozed during the battle. The recitations differ on 'yaghsha' and 'taghsha' and on the case of 'kulluhu', but the exegetes do not draw a decisive difference in meaning from them.

This verse states that those among the Muslims who turned their backs on the day of Uhud, when the two armies met, were led into error by Satan because of some of the sins they had committed, and that God pardoned them, for He is Forgiving and Forbearing. The commentators agree that the flight was a fault and that the pardon is an act of divine grace. They differ on who is meant. Umar, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd, and most exegetes including al-Tabari, hold that it refers to everyone who turned away from the polytheists that day. Al-Suddi restricts it to those who fled to Medina, while Ikrima reports that the verse was revealed about named men, and Ibn Ishaq names Uthman ibn Affan and his relatives. As to the cause of the slip, al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj explain that Satan reminded them of past sins, so they disliked meeting God before repenting, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi point to leaving the post the Prophet had ordered them to hold, or to greed for booty. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note that some regard the fault as minor, whereas others hold that the pardon extends even to grave sins. For most, forgiveness means the lifting of consequences in this world and the next, and Ibn Atiyya notes that fleeing from battle is counted among the major sins. Commentators understand halim as patience that does not hasten punishment.

This verse warns believers not to imitate the disbelievers and hypocrites who, when their kinsmen travelled for trade or went out to fight and died or were killed, said: had they stayed with us, they would not have died or been slain. The commentators see this as a challenge to the divine decree, since staying at home cannot advance or delay a person's appointed term. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the remark referred to Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, while Ibn Ishaq and others extend it to all the hypocrites; al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi limit it to the hypocrites, and al-Razi holds that it covers any disbeliever who speaks this way. Most understand the brotherhood mentioned as kinship, the phrase 'striking through the land' as travelling, and 'ghuzza' as the plural of 'ghazin'. On the lam in 'li-yaj'ala Allah dhalika hasratan', most take it as the lam of consequence: their words end up becoming a regret in their hearts. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi relate it instead to the utterance or to the prohibition, and they differ on what 'dhalika' refers to: the belief, the saying, or the prohibition. The exegetes stress that God alone gives life and causes death, that neither residence nor travel changes this, and that the believer submits to the decree. Some draw from it the prohibition of imitating the unbelievers in belief and speech, and the point that the duty of fighting is not lifted by fear of death. The verse closes by affirming that God sees what people do and will repay them for it.

The commentators explain that God addresses the believers: being killed in the way of God or dying in it brings forgiveness and mercy from Him, which is better than whatever people gather of worldly goods. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya read the verse as a reply to the hypocrites, who claimed that those who died while travelling or fighting would have lived had they stayed at home; God answers that death is in His hand and that each term is fixed. The commentators agree that the verse encourages jihad and belittles worldly wealth. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya set out several reasons why the reward of the hereafter is better: it endures, while worldly pleasures pass and are mixed with pain. The readers differ on the vowel of 'mutum': the Kufans and others read it with a kasra or a damma depending on whether the verb is taken as (mata yamatu) or (mata yamutu), and Abu Hayyan notes that the kasra form belongs to the Hijaz dialect. Hafs reads 'yajma'un' in the third person, so that it refers to the unbelievers, while the majority read it in the second person, addressing the believers. Killing is mentioned before dying because it is more meritorious in God's sight, according to Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan. Ibn 'Uthaymin finally holds that the way of God may include fighting, preaching and the teaching of knowledge.

This verse tells the believers that death and death in battle, whatever the cause, do not place anyone beyond God's reach: it is to Him alone that people will be gathered to be repaid for their deeds. Read against the context of the battle of Uhud, the commentators see in it an exhortation to jihad and a warning against clinging to worldly wealth. Al-Tabari explains that the believer should prefer what brings him closer to God, such as fighting and obedience, over the fleeting goods of this world, and Ibn Ishaq agrees that the world should not deceive the faithful. Al-Wahidi and al-Sam'ani add that the gathering to God applies in whatever state one leaves this life, whether remaining in jihad or falling while engaged in it. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di connect the verse to the prohibition of imitating the unbelievers who said of their dead on journeys or in raids that had they stayed home, they would not have died. God answers that life and death are in His hands, and that the forgiveness and mercy gained by dying in His cause are better than what people gather in this world, a view shared by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi. On recitation, Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'mittum' with a kasra, the Hijazi form, while the others read it with a damma, which Abu 'Ali and Ibn 'Atiyya consider the more common and more regular form. Al-Razi notes that the verse shows that divinity requires this gathering, and Ibn 'Ashur explains the order of mentioning killing before death as a matter of rhetorical balance. Al-Alusi observes that the order is reversed here because death is more common than killing, while the oath in the verse stresses that the gathering to God is certain.

This verse explains that the Prophet's gentleness toward his companions was a mercy from God, for had he been harsh and hard-hearted they would have scattered from around him. The commentators define the fazz as the coarse, ill-tempered person and ghalîz al-qalb as the hard-hearted one who does not soften; al-Tabari notes that this was not his character. God then commands him to pardon those who erred, to ask forgiveness for them, to consult them in affairs, and once resolved, to rely on God. The exegetes agree that consultation concerns matters requiring opinion, such as war. They differ on its purpose: Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Ishaq hold it was to soothe hearts and win over the companions; al-Dahhak holds it was to show its merit and set an example for the community after him; al-Hasan and Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna hold it was a sunna the community should follow, al-Hasan adding that God knew he had no need of their counsel.
