Ibn Kathir and others take it to concern matters on which no revelation came. Al-Razi and others report that some restricted consultation to war while others generalized it. The commentators agree that tawakkul does not mean abandoning the means, but acting while relying on God. For most, consultation is recommended, or obligatory in public affairs, as various reports indicate, and scholars differ on whether the command is specific to the Prophet or extends to rulers. The verse also addresses the disobedience of the archers at Uhud, whose fault God pardoned, which made pardon and consultation possible afterwards.

This verse states that victory and abandonment both belong to God alone: if God grants you His help, no one can overcome you; if He forsakes you, no one can help you after Him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi understand it first as a reference to Badr, where God gave the believers victory, and to Uhud, where He left them, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi take it as a general principle linking victory to obedience and defeat to disobedience. Ibn 'Abbas and others explain that divine help means aid against the enemy and that abandonment means withholding that aid. Al-Zamakhshari sees in the verse a reminder that all authority belongs to God and a call to place trust in Him.

Commentators agree that faith requires relying on God alone, and that the placement of "upon God" before the verb stresses exclusivity. Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Jaza'iri add that reliance on God does not dispense with lawful means: one acts and then leaves the outcome to Him. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse can also console the believers after the defeat at Uhud and urge them to seek what brings divine help.

The meaning of "after Him" is debated: for al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi it refers to God's abandonment, while others, including al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, also read it as "once you have gone beyond God." Abu Hayyan observes that the interrogative form softens the statement towards the believers, avoiding a blunt declaration that they have no helper.

This verse states that it is not for any prophet to commit ghulul, that is, to embezzle from the spoils or conceal part of them, and it warns that whoever does so will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying what he took. Then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned, without injustice. The commentators discuss the two readings. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Asim read the active yaghulla, and Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and Sa'id ibn Jubayr relate that the verse came down concerning a red cloak lost at Badr, when some said the Prophet had taken it. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil place the revelation at Uhud, when the archers left their post, while al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' mention scouts who were not given a share. The passive yughalla, read by most, is taken by al-Hasan and Qatada to mean being betrayed, and by Ibn Ishaq as referring to concealing revelation.

Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Qurtubi, regard ghulul as a grave sin, and hold that the offender must return what he took and be disciplined at the judge's discretion. Those who take the Day's image literally, such as al-Razi, say the thief will bear his theft on his back, while al-Kashshaf and al-Qasimi read it as public disgrace. Al-Qurtubi reports that the Prophet burned a man's gear in some reports, but judges that view weak; al-Shafi'i, Malik and Abu Hanifa allow only correctional punishment, whereas Ahmad, al-Awza'i and Ishaq permit burning the thief's goods.

This verse states that the one who seeks the pleasure of Allah through obedience is not equal to the one who returns with His anger through disobedience, whose refuge is Hell, a dreadful destination. The commentators offer several readings. Al-Tabari, followed by Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, takes the pursuit of Allah's pleasure to mean abstaining from embezzling booty, and returning with anger to mean committing it, a view attributed to al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and linked to the warning against embezzlement just before it. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the denial of embezzlement for the Prophet honours him, and Ibn 'Atiyya records the same reading while noting variant opinions. Others, such as al-Wahidi, al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi, widen the meaning to faith and obedience versus disbelief and disobedience, or to loyalty to the Messenger. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi note that the wording is general and not confined to one incident. According to al-Zajjaj, as cited by al-Razi and Abu Hayyan, the pleasure refers to fighting and the anger to fleeing at Uhud. On the phrase that they are degrees before Allah, the scholars differ: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Baghawi understand that the two groups differ in rank, the faithful in reward and the others in punishment, while Mujahid and Qatada take it as referring to the people of pleasure alone. Ibn Sa'di stresses that people vary in rank according to their deeds, and that Allah sees all they do.

The commentators explain that those who pursued God's good pleasure, that is, who obeyed Him and avoided embezzling the spoils, and those who earned His wrath through disobedience and treachery, are not equal in rank before God. Each has degrees or lower degrees according to his deeds. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy take the sense to be general, covering both groups: the people of Paradise differ in their degrees and the people of the Fire in their lower levels. Mujahid and al-Suddi hold instead that the pronoun refers only to those who pursued God's pleasure, who therefore have lofty and honourable ranks. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain that the verse speaks of the difference between the rewarded and the punished. Al-Razi argues that the pronoun refers to those who pursued God's pleasure, since 'degrees' usually denotes reward and 'lower degrees' punishment. Ibn 'Atiyya regards the general sense as more likely, and Abu Hayyan holds that the pronoun covers everyone. Al-Qurtubi notes that a degree is a rank and that the term 'darak' is used for the Fire. Ibn al-Jawzi cites Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, who see in the degrees differences of excellence. All agree on the closing point: God is fully aware of what people do and repays each according to his deeds.

This verse describes God's favour upon the believers in sending them a messenger from among themselves, who recites His signs to them, purifies them, teaches them the Book and wisdom, though they had been in clear error before. Al-Tabari understands wisdom as the Sunna of the Prophet and explains that purification means cleansing from sins through obedience. Qatada says the Prophet was sent to a people who did not know, and to a people without manners, and he taught and disciplined them. Most commentators agree that the Book is the Quran and wisdom is the Sunna, and that "from among themselves" means of their own kind, an Arab who speaks their language and whose honesty they knew, which made his message easier to understand and to trust, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi explain. Ibn Kathir adds that being human allowed them to speak with him and ask him questions.

Opinions differ on the scope of the verse. A'isha, as reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, holds that it refers only to the Arabs, while others take it to include all believers. Al-Razi gives several reasons for this favour, among them the honour and pride it brought to the Arabs, the ease of learning from someone of their tongue, and the Prophet's known integrity. Ibn Ashur notes that the word "favour" here means a benefit, not a reproach. Al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan record a minority reading, "min anfasihim", meaning "from among their noblest". Ibn Sa'di stresses that this is the greatest of all blessings, since it rescues people from misguidance.

This verse reproaches the believers who were struck at Uhud, where seventy of them were killed, after they had inflicted twice that loss on the enemy at Badr, with seventy killed and seventy captured. They asked in surprise how this could befall them while they were Muslims and the Prophet was among them. God tells His Messenger to answer that the cause lies within themselves. The commentators agree on the general sense: the calamity had a human cause, and God is capable of all things. They differ on which cause is meant. Al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn 'Abbas, followed by most exegetes such as al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, point to disobedience to the Prophet, either by those who insisted on going out of Medina rather than staying, or by the archers who left their post for the sake of spoils, as al-Wahidi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain. Others, including 'Umar, 'Ali, 'Ubayda al-Salmani and al-Hasan, report that the cause was accepting ransom for the prisoners of Badr, a view also recorded by Ibn Kathir. Al-Baqa'i and al-Zamakhshari tried to reconcile these views, while Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi examined them at length. Al-Razi draws theological conclusions about human acts from the verse, which the other commentators do not adopt. Some explain that the two equal losses refer to the dead and the captives, others to the defeat. Ibn Sa'di sees the verse as a consolation to the believers, showing that caution cannot repel what God has decreed.

The plain meaning of the verse is that the harm which befell the Muslims on the day of Uhud, when the two armies met, namely the wounds, the deaths and the defeat, occurred by the permission of God, that is by His decree and destiny, and that the purpose was to reveal the faith of the sincere believers and to distinguish them from the hypocrites. The commentators agree that the day of the meeting of the two hosts is the day of Uhud, and that the word permission means decree, knowledge, or allowing the enemy to prevail. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain it as God's decree and destiny, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi lean toward divine permission in the sense of leaving the matter to play out, and al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer the sense of knowledge and enabling. As for the hypocrites led by Abdullah ibn Ubayy, who withdrew from the army on the way, they were told to fight in God's cause or at least to defend by increasing the numbers, and they replied that had they known there would be fighting they would have followed. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, regard this as a pretext, since fighting was bound to happen. They differ on the meaning of defence: al-Suddi and Ibn Juraij take it as increasing the numbers, Abu 'Awn al-Ansari as garrisoning the frontier, and others as fighting to protect the homeland. The majority read their saying with their mouths what is not in their hearts as a description of their hypocrisy, the mention of the mouths serving to emphasise. Finally, to those who stayed behind saying that had they obeyed they would not have been killed, God replies that caution does not avert destiny and that death cannot be warded off by sitting at home.

This verse concerns the Battle of Uhud, when Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul withdrew on the way with about a third of the army. Some believers, including Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Haram, called on them to fight in God's cause or at least to defend their families and territory. They replied that if they knew there would be fighting they would follow, and the commentators agree that this was a pretext. On the statement that they were that day nearer to disbelief than to faith, the commentators generally explain that their withdrawal and words distanced them from the outward faith they had shown, bringing them closer to unbelief. Al-Tabari, Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi read 'or repel' as increasing the number of Muslims even without fighting, Abu Awn al-Ansari as standing guard, while Ibn Atiyya and others read it as a call to fight out of zeal. Al-Zamakhshari understands their claim 'if we knew there were fighting' as saying that what they were doing was not fighting but self-destruction, and al-Razi offers two readings. On 'God knows best what they conceal', many hold that God's knowledge is detailed while believers know only in outline from signs; most keep the comparative sense, though some take it as simply 'knowing'. Ibn Kathir notes that a person may at times be nearer to disbelief and at other times nearer to faith, and some use this to support the idea that faith increases and decreases. Al-Wahidi concludes that one who utters the testimony of faith should not be declared a disbeliever on that basis alone. Ibn Uthaymin observes that the hypocrites' lies appear in their words, and that speech uttered without intent has no legal effect.

This verse from Al-Imran describes the hypocrites who stayed behind on the day of Uhud and then said of their brothers who fought and were killed: had they obeyed us and stayed, they would not have been slain. The plain meaning, as the commentators explain it, is that these hypocrites wanted to discourage the believers from fighting by claiming that staying at home protects from death. God answers: say, ward off death from yourselves if you are truthful, meaning that if staying behind could avert what is decreed, then ward off death itself. The commentators agree that the speakers were Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his followers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu al-Su'ud take the brothers to be the martyrs of Uhud, whether kin, neighbours or men of their kind, while Ibn Uthaymin prefers the sense of outward brotherhood, since the hypocrites displayed Islam and none of them was among the martyrs.

Most exegetes draw from this that the wish to save oneself cannot avert the divine decree, that each person dies at his appointed term, and that caution does not overcome destiny, as al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi state. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi address the objection that these hypocrites did escape death by staying back: there are many causes of safety, and fighting itself can save a man. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan read the conditional phrase as mockery. Ibn Ashur sees it instead as a refutation of their excuse rather than a denial that they were spared. Commentators also note that the reading of al-Hasan and Hisham, with the doubled consonant, stresses the killing, and some report a tradition that seventy hypocrites died on the day the verse was revealed. Ibn Kathir and others recall the circumstances of the withdrawal on the road and of the ransom taken at Badr, without deciding firmly between the accounts.

This verse tells believers not to regard those killed in God's cause as dead, for they are alive with their Lord and receive provision, rejoicing in the bounty God has given them. The commentators explain that the address is to the Prophet or to anyone addressed, and that the verb for supposing means thinking here. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, take the verse to refer to the martyrs of Uhud, though some apply it to the martyrs of Badr or Bi'r Ma'una, or to every martyr. They cite the hadith transmitted from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud that the souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise and rest in golden lamps beneath the Throne. Al-Qurtubi regards this as the soundest view. The majority hold that this life is real for their souls, whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya give a figurative reading, such as the lasting remembrance of their names or their being owed the blessings of the afterlife. Al-Razi reports the view of al-Ka'bi that this life will only come on the Day of Resurrection and rejects it. Ibn Kathir suggests that the martyrs have different ranks. The martyrs also rejoice over their brothers who have not yet joined them: some say they hope these will be martyred too, others that they learn of their future. Readings vary on a few words, and Abu Hayyan considers the accusative reading of 'alive' weak. All the commentators agree that the verse honours the rank of martyrdom and consoles and encourages the living to fight.

The commentators explain that this verse teaches that those who were killed in the cause of God are not truly dead, but alive with their Lord and provided for. They rejoice in the favour God has given them, and they rejoice for their brothers who have not yet joined them, knowing that if these are also martyred they will receive the same honour. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi tie the verse to the martyrs of Uhud, while others relate it to Badr or to Bi'r Ma'una. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi affirm that the martyrs' life is real, and Ibn Kathir reports the hadith that their souls are in green birds that eat from the fruits of Paradise and rest beneath the Throne. Ibn Ashur holds that this life is of a spiritual kind distinct from worldly life. Abu Muslim and al-Zamakhshari prefer to see a joy shared among all believers, and al-Zamakhshari notes that the account of the martyrs encourages the living to strive. On the meaning of istibshar, Qatada and Ibn Juraij take it as the martyrs wishing for their brothers to be martyred too, while al-Sudi takes it as receiving a book listing those who will come. Ibn Ashur notes that the reading with inna or anna does not change the core meaning. The general sense is clear: real life, joy and peace for the martyrs and hope for their brothers.

The commentators explain that this verse continues the description of the martyrs who were killed in God's cause: they rejoice in the blessing and grace God bestows on them, beyond what their deeds alone would merit. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand this joy as the fulfilment of God's promise and the immense reward they now witness. Al-Tabari also notes that the grace is an increase in honour over the recompense, while al-Razi and al-Zajjaj separate the blessing, which is the reward, from the grace added to it. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi regard the two terms as essentially one meaning. The phrase that God does not waste the reward of the believers is read by the majority with a fatha on the alif, as a continuation of the blessing, whereas al-Kisa'i reads it with a kasra as an independent statement, a reading supported by the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. All agree that God does not lose the reward of believers; they differ on the meaning of the rejoicing. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan see it as joy at knowing that God grants a good end, since the martyrs feared a bad conclusion, while Ibn 'Atiyya stresses that the full wage is received. Most exegetes report that the verse concerns the martyrs of Uhud, some the martyrs of Bi'r Ma'una, but all retain the general scope of the wording. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir stress that it is good news for believers and an incitement to jihad.

This verse describes those who answered the call of God and His Messenger after the battle of Uhud, despite their wounds, and promises a great reward to those among them who did good and feared God. Most commentators explain that this refers to the Muslims' pursuit of Abu Sufyan as far as Hamra' al-Asad, eight miles from Medina, to frighten the enemy and show their strength. Some of them were seriously wounded, and it is reported that some carried their companions in turn. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi all connect the revelation to this episode. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi hold that the word "min" in "minhum" is explanatory rather than partitive, since all who responded were both good-doers and God-fearing. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that A'isha applied the verse to her nephew's father and grandfather, namely al-Zubayr and Abu Bakr.

Most explain the expedition by the regret of Abu Sufyan and his men at having withdrawn without finishing off the Muslims, and by the Prophet's wish to show the believers' strength. Mujahid and 'Ikrima, however, link the verse to the expedition of Badr al-Sughra, the appointment for the following year, a view that most exegetes do not adopt, according to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. The commentators differ on who the "people" who warned the believers were: Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i for some, a caravan from the tribe of Abd al-Qays for others, or the hypocrites. All agree that the believers then said "God is sufficient for us, and the best Guardian," and that their faith increased; some note in this connection that faith can grow and diminish.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the believers who, after the battle of Uhud, answered the call of God and His Messenger to pursue Abu Sufyan despite their wounds, and God praises them for their goodness and piety. It is then reported that people told them the enemy had gathered against them and that they should fear them; this only increased their faith and certainty, and they said, "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian." Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that this phrase is the one Abraham uttered when he was cast into the fire, and that the Prophet ﷺ also said it. Opinions differ on who spoke to them: for Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ishaq and others, it was a group from the tribe of Abd al-Qays who met Abu Sufyan; for Mujahid, 'Ikrima and Muqatil, it was Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i; for al-Suddi, it was the hypocrites. Al-Tabari holds that the event took place at Hamra' al-Asad, while Mujahid and others place it at the lesser Badr. On the increase in faith, most commentators understand it as growth through obedience, while others attribute it to steadfastness and trust in God. The verse concludes that Satan frightens his allies, and that believers should fear God alone.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the return of the believers who answered the call of God and His Messenger after Uhud. They came back with a blessing and grace from God, untouched by any harm, and they followed God's pleasure by obeying. They agree that the 'blessing' means well-being and safety, and that the 'grace' means the profit from trade or the reward, as Mujahid and al-Suddi say and Ibn Kathir repeats. They differ on the occasion. The majority, including Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, place it in the expedition to Hamra' al-Asad that followed Uhud, while Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq and others link it to the departure for Badr al-Sughra for the appointment with Abu Sufyan. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi take the gain from the market as the grace meant. As for who frightened the believers by announcing that Quraysh had gathered, some name Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, others a group from the tribe of Abd al-Qays, and al-Suddi the hypocrites; al-Razi notes that the word 'people' may refer to a single man. The verse closes by stressing the immensity of God's favour, which al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud read as a rebuke to those who had stayed behind. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, also discuss whether faith increases, which some tie to deeds and Ibn 'Atiyya ties to proofs and their effects.

The commentators explain that this verse establishes that whoever frightens the believers with the threat of enemy armies is none other than Satan, who makes his allies speak to spread fear. The believers should therefore not fear Satan's allies, but fear God alone if they are true believers. Opinions differ on the omitted object in the phrase "he frightens his allies". Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrima, al-Farra and al-Zajjaj hold that the meaning is "he frightens you with his allies", that is, makes you fear them; al-Tabari supports this reading with the reading attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Al-Hasan and al-Suddi, however, read it as Satan frightening his allies, the hypocrites, so that they hold back from fighting the polytheists, a view also favoured by al-Razi and al-Nasafi. As for the "people" who gathered forces, some identify them with Abu Sufyan and his companions, others with Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i, others with a caravan from the tribe of Abd al-Qays, and some take the word as referring to a single person. Most connect these verses to the expedition of Hamra' al-Asad after Uhud, when the believers said "God is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs," and returned in God's grace and bounty. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and others note that natural fear is not blameworthy, whereas praiseworthy fear is that which restrains one from what God forbids, and that faith requires preferring the fear of God to the fear of people.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ not to be grieved by those who hasten into disbelief, for they cannot harm God at all; they harm only themselves. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God's wish to give them no share in the Hereafter means that He withholds reward from them as the consequence of their disbelief, and that a great punishment awaits them. The commentators agree that hastening into disbelief means eagerly rushing into it, and that the harm falls on those who do so. They differ on who is meant. Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabari say the hypocrites, al-Dahhak says the Quraysh, while al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi mention people who renounced Islam, and al-Kalbi mentions hypocrites and Jewish leaders. Ibn Ashur widens the meaning to anyone who eagerly spreads disbelief. Al-Razi reports an explanation that God's wish here is only a judgment, which he finds weak. Readers differ on the recitation of "yahzunka" and "yusari'un". Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that mentioning the divine will shows the severity of the abandonment they deserved. Ibn Ashur sees the address to the Prophet as a precaution, since the soul can be affected by outward appearances. Several commentators hold that the following verse refers to those who exchanged faith for disbelief. Overall the passage offers consolation to the Prophet and a stern warning to opponents.

This verse states that those who exchanged faith for disbelief cannot harm God in the slightest, but only harm themselves, and a painful punishment awaits them. The commentators explain the verb "bought" (ishtaraw) as an exchange, meaning that they took disbelief in place of faith. Al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq hold that the verse refers to the hypocrites who returned from Islam after entering it, and Mujahid likewise identifies them as hypocrites. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that the verse may refer to all disbelievers, or only to the hypocrites, or to Arab apostates, and that it may repeat the previous verse to reinforce its point. Al-Razi argues that the repetition reveals the instability of their convictions and their weakness, since such a person cannot inflict harm on others. Ibn Kathir stresses that disbelief does not diminish God's dominion in any way. Ibn al-Jawzi reports only that Mujahid identifies these people as hypocrites who believed and then disbelieved. Al-Qurtubi explains that "shay'an" functions as an accusative of the infinitive, and Ibn Uthaymin notes that "alim" here means "causing pain." The commentators therefore agree on the general meaning while differing on the precise identity of those meant.

This verse warns against the illusion that the respite granted to disbelievers is good for them. The commentators explain that those who disbelieve should not suppose that prolonging their lives and delaying their punishment is to their benefit. It is a respite (imla') that only increases their sin, and they will face a humiliating punishment. Most exegetes agree that imla' means granting respite and lengthening life, and that the verse denies any true good in this delay. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi read the particle of "liyazdadu" as one of purpose, whereas al-Zamakhshari and the Mu'tazilites read it as one of consequence. Al-Razi holds that the verse supports the Sunni position on predestination and answers the Mu'tazilite objections. The commentators differ on who is addressed: Ibn Abbas names the Jews, Christians and hypocrites; Muqatil names the polytheists of Mecca; 'Ata' names the tribes of Qurayza and al-Nadir; and al-Zajjaj names people whom God knew would never believe. On reading, Hamza reads "tahsabanna" in the second person, while the others read the verb in the third person. Ibn Atiyya, al-Zajjaj and al-Qurtubi discuss the grammatical analysis that follows from these readings. Several commentators cite Ibn Mas'ud's saying that death is better for every righteous and wicked person alike.

This verse states that God does not leave the believers mixed with the hypocrites as they are, but separates the wicked from the good, that is the hypocrite from the sincere believer, through trial, hardship and demanding obligations. The commentators note that this happened at Uhud, when the hypocrites who withdrew were exposed. The unseen that God does not disclose to ordinary people means what lies in the hearts, faith or hypocrisy; yet God chooses from among His messengers whom He wills and informs him of part of the unseen by revelation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the address to be to the believers, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan extend it to both sincere believers and hypocrites, while Ibn Abbas and most exegetes direct it to the disbelievers and hypocrites. On the meaning of the wicked and the good, opinions differ: Mujahid and Ibn Juraij take the wicked to be the hypocrite, Qatada and al-Suddi the disbeliever, and Ibn Kaysan holds that the obligations themselves are what reveal the inner state. The next verse concerns miserliness. Al-Suddi and Ibn Abbas understand it as withholding zakat, or concealing what is in the scriptures; al-Tabari adopts the first reading and cites the hadith of the bald venomous serpent that encircles the miser's neck on the Day of Resurrection, which Ibn Kathir also supports with several reports. The commentators therefore agree on the call to sincere faith and piety, on God's exclusive knowledge of the unseen, and on the harm that miserliness brings to the one who practises it.

This verse warns that those who withhold what God has given them, refusing what is due from it, should not think that their stinginess is good for them. Rather it is harmful, for what they withheld will be placed upon them as a burden on the Day of Resurrection. Commentators differ on what the "collar" (yutawwaqun) means. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Wa'il, al-Sha'bi and al-Suddi, as recorded by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, understand that the withheld wealth becomes a serpent wound around the neck that bites its owner, and some rely on Abu Hurayra's report in al-Bukhari for this. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i says it is a collar of fire, while Mujahid explains it as an obligation to produce again what was withheld. Al-Razi takes stinginess to mean withholding wealth, including zakat and obligatory spending, and notes it may also apply to withholding knowledge. In a report from 'Atiyya, Ibn 'Abbas links the verse to Jewish rabbis who concealed the description of the Prophet; al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan also mention this view without deciding between them. Readers differ on whether the verb is addressed to the Prophet or the people, and al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi discuss the grammatical consequences of that choice.

All agree on the closing point: God inherits the heavens and the earth, meaning he remains the sole owner of everything after its human possessors are gone, so there is no sense in clinging to what will pass away. The verse ends by reminding the reader that God is fully aware of what people do.

This verse records the words of some Jews who said that God is poor and they are rich, when the verse about lending God a goodly loan was revealed. God declares that He has heard this saying, that He will record it and requite it, together with their unjust killing of the prophets, and that on the Day of Resurrection they will be told: taste the punishment of the burning. The commentators agree that the speakers were Jews and that the saying is grave, whether it was held as belief or uttered in mockery. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy report that the main speaker was Finhas, and that the episode with Abu Bakr is the occasion; other reports, transmitted from al-Hasan and Qatada, name Huyayy ibn Akhtab, while Mujahid speaks of a group. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that God's hearing means knowledge and a warning. Most attribute the killing of the prophets to those present because they approved of their forefathers' deeds, as al-Tabari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir note. On the recording, some take it as the angels writing in the registers, others as preservation in divine knowledge, and the recitations differ between the nun and the ya. Several see the phrase taste as a rebuke and humiliation. All affirm that God does not wrong His servants, and that the punishment is the due recompense for what their hands have sent ahead.

Verse 3:182 of Al Imran, read in the context of the verses before it that speak of those who said that God is poor and they are rich, and who killed prophets without right, is explained by the commentators to mean that this punishment is due to what their hands have committed, that is, their disbelief and sins, and that God is far from injustice and does not punish His servants without fault. The mention of hands stands for the whole person, since most actions are carried out by them. Most commentators read the phrase as an affirmation of divine justice, God recompensing every soul according to what it has earned.

The exegetes agree that the verse concludes the warning that precedes it and that the punishment is just rather than arbitrary. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that these verses were revealed about Jews who said this on hearing the verse about lending to God, with Finhas the most commonly named, while al-Kalbi, al-Suddi and Muqatil name a group of rabbis such as Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that such a statement can only come from deep rebellion in disbelief, and note that the killing of prophets is paired with it to show that these are crimes of the same kind.

The commentaries also agree on the sense of 'God is not unjust toward His servants'. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya observe that the intensive form 'zallam' may suggest a quantity; some answer that it marks attribution, meaning injustice is not ascribed to God at all, while others take it as intensity in relation to the number of servants. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud make the clause a cause of the punishment, since denying injustice implies a justice that rewards the good and punishes the wrong; al-Razi and al-Alusi reject this reading and treat the clause as a parenthetical affirmation that God does not punish without fault.

Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Sha'rawi note that 'hands' refers to all the limbs, and that tasting the punishment is an image of experiencing suffering. These points are broadly shared across the commentaries.

This verse reports the claim of the Jews that God had commanded them, in the Torah, not to believe any messenger until he brings them an offering that fire consumes. God answers that earlier messengers came with clear proofs and with exactly what they demanded, yet they were denied and killed. The commentators explain that the qurban was an offering, an animal or a gift, through which one drew near to God; if a white fire descended and consumed it, this was the sign of its acceptance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that this was a known practice among the prophets of the Children of Israel, and that spoils of war were burned in the same way before being made lawful for this community. They also mention that the verse was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Finhas and their companions, while Ibn Kathir links the immediate context to Finhas's saying that God is poor. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi judge the claim a lie against God, since the fire's consuming of an offering proves a messenger only as a miracle, like any other. Ibn 'Ashur notes that such a sign occurred in the time of Moses but was not a rule for all prophets. Al-Razi reports two views on the condition: as-Suddi holds that it had an exception for Jesus and Muhammad, while others regard it as a fabrication about the Torah. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi read the question "why did you kill them" as a rebuke addressed to the contemporaries of the Prophet, who approved of their ancestors' deeds. The verse ends by consoling the Prophet, since earlier messengers were also denied despite their clear proofs, their scriptures and the luminous Book.

This verse is a consolation from God to His Prophet ﷺ when the Jews and the idolaters denied him: if they call you a liar, messengers before you were also denied, though they came with clear proofs, scriptures and the illuminating Book. The commentators agree that these messengers brought evident signs and arguments, and that rejection is the habit of peoples toward their prophets, so the Prophet should not grieve. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the zubur are written books and that the illuminating Book refers to the Torah and the Gospel, while al-Razi holds that earlier messengers' books were not themselves miracles, the Quran alone being both book and miracle. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand the zabur as a book of restraining wisdom and the illuminating Book as a guide that clarifies the path. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that Ibn 'Amir's reading with the repeated preposition matches the Syrian codices and serves emphasis. Ibn Juzayy sees the verse as consolation that invites the Prophet to follow the example of earlier messengers. The verse answers the Jewish claim that God had commanded them not to believe any messenger until he brought an offering consumed by fire: the commentators point out that the claim is an evasion, since those same people killed messengers who had brought such proofs.

This verse states that every soul will taste death, that the full recompense for deeds will be given only on the Day of Resurrection, that whoever is kept away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed, and that the worldly life is merely the enjoyment of deception. Al-Tabari reads it as a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ regarding the denial of the Jews and the idolaters, and as a reminder that all return to God. The commentators agree that death is inescapable and that complete recompense belongs to the Last Day, though Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Alusi note that part of the reward may be felt earlier, relying on the report that the grave is either a garden of Paradise or a pit of the Fire. The word 'tasting' is, according to al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya, a metaphor for experiencing death, while al-Razi and al-Qurtubi record a variant reading with tanwin and an accusative, which keeps the same meaning. On the word 'ghurur', al-Tabari understands it as deception and rejects the view of Ibn Sabit that it means a meagre provision, which he calls a possible interpretation but not the correct one. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Qasimi list examples of what passes away: green plants, the axe and the cooking pot, and fragile glass according to Ikrima. A hadith reported by al-Tirmidhi, that a whip's length in Paradise is better than the world and all it contains, is cited by most exegetes. Sa'id ibn Jubayr adds that the deception applies to one who prefers this world over the next, while one who seeks the Hereafter through it has a provision that carries him to what is better.

God tells the believers that they will be tested in their wealth and in their persons, through calamities, losses, and the burden of religious duties such as spending, jihad, pilgrimage and fasting, and that they will hear much harm from the People of the Book and from the polytheists: mockery of their faith and insults against the Prophet ﷺ. The commentators agree that patience and God-consciousness are the way to bear this, and that they belong to the firm resolutions one must commit to. The test in wealth, they explain, covers its loss or diminishment as well as the obligations attached to it, such as zakat and required spending. The test in the person covers death, wounds, captivity, sickness and the loss of loved ones. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the harm means attacks on the religion, such as the saying of Finhas that God is poor and they are rich, or the Christian claim that the Messiah is the son of God. The accounts of the occasion of revelation differ: al-Zuhri ties it to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, who satirised the Prophet and roused the idolaters against him, while 'Ikrima ties it to Finhas and his dispute with Abu Bakr, and others give different accounts. Ibn Kathir and others hold that it came before the command to fight, whereas al-Qaffal and al-Qurtubi hold that it is not abrogated, since forbearance and gentle dealing remain recommended at all times. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that resolve means carrying a matter through after reflection, so the verse teaches that patience and piety are among the things one must firmly commit to.

This verse recalls the covenant God made with the People of the Book: to make clear to people what is in their scriptures and not conceal it. They instead cast the covenant behind their backs and sold it for a paltry worldly price, and God condemns their conduct. The commentators agree that the verse primarily concerns the Jews. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi and Ibn Juraij report that it refers to Jewish rabbis such as Finhas and Ashya', and that the covenant concerned making known the mission of Muhammad ﷺ as described in the Torah. Others, including al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, extend it to Jews and Christians alike. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and most scholars, according to al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, take it as general to anyone granted knowledge, including the scholars of this community, citing the hadith about the bridle of fire for one who withholds knowledge. They differ on what 'he shall make it clear' refers to: Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi say the Prophet ﷺ, while al-Hasan and Qatada say the Book. On the readings, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim (per Abu Bakr) read the third person, while the others read the second, and al-Tabari prefers the third person. Commentators explain that casting behind the back means neglecting and abandoning, and that the cheap price is rank, wealth or livelihood. The following verse, which forbids loving to be praised for what one has not done, is linked to this theme by Ibn 'Abbas and others, and all agree on its meaning: God does not save from punishment one who rejoices in falsehood.

This verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ, or anyone able to receive the address, forbidding him to think that those who rejoice in what they have done wrong, and love to be praised for what they did not do, will be spared punishment. Rather, they will face a painful torment. The commentators differ on who is meant. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Abbas through Ibn Ishaq, understand it as the Jewish rabbis who concealed what the Prophet ﷺ asked them about their scriptures, then made him believe they had answered, rejoicing in their concealment and seeking praise. Ibn Kathir notes that the preceding verses concern the People of the Book. Al-Tabari gives weight to those who had been bound by a covenant to make Muhammad's mission known. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn Zayd instead attribute it to the hypocrites who stayed behind from campaigns, then offered excuses and swore oaths, wanting to be praised. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan record other views, including the one that extends the verse to anyone who rejoices in a bad deed or claims virtues he lacks. As for the word «mafaza», most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur, take it to mean a place of deliverance or safety. The commentaries largely agree on the general sense: a warning against pretence and against claiming merits one does not possess. They also note that loving praise for a genuine deed is not in itself condemned.

The plain meaning of the verse is that the dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, and that He is capable of all things. Most commentators read it as a rebuttal of those who said that God is poor and they are rich. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that the One who owns everything in the heavens and the earth cannot be called poor, and that His power allows Him to punish such claims and to hasten the punishment if He wills. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi connect the verse to the following verses that call for reflection on the creation of the heavens and the earth and on the alternation of night and day, as signs for people of understanding. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya link it to the preceding passage about those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they did not do: God, who owns all things, is able to seize them. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that the phrase "all things" is general, yet it refers to what is possible, since God is not capable of the impossible. Ibn Ashur sees it as a concluding statement that nothing the people conceal is hidden from God, while al-Sa'di stresses that none can escape His control. The commentators agree on the core meaning; they differ mainly over how closely the verse belongs to its context.

The commentators explain that this verse calls attention to the creation of the heavens and the earth and to the alternation of night and day, which offer clear signs of God's existence, power, wisdom and oneness, signs that only people of sound intellect grasp fully. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir agree that these signs are proofs that reveal the greatness of the Creator, and that mentioning the heavens, the earth, and the night and day is enough for the argument, even though other verses in al-Baqara list more numerous proofs. Al-Razi holds that the choice here of only celestial signs and the alternation of night and day is because they are more striking and lift the heart more strongly toward God's majesty. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir explain that "people of understanding" are those who open their insight to reflection and contemplation, not those who look without seeing.

The following verses describe these people as those who remember God standing, sitting and lying on their sides. Most commentators take this as constant remembrance in every condition, while Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali and others understand this remembrance as prayer, performed standing, sitting or lying according to one's ability. Al-Alusi and Ibn 'Ashur note that reflecting on creation is an important act of worship, accompanied by the acknowledgement that God has not created all this in vain. Some, such as Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, specify that the reflection is on created things and not on the divine essence itself.

The verses then contain the believers' prayer: seeking protection from the Fire, forgiveness, the erasure of their misdeeds, death among the righteous, and the fulfilment of what God promised through His messengers. Commentators have asked why they make this request when they know God keeps His promises. Al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and others offer several answers: supplication is itself an act of submission, or the believers desire that victory come quickly.

This verse describes people of understanding as those who remember God in every state, standing, sitting and lying on their sides, and who reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth, saying: Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire. The commentators explain that these three postures cover nearly all of a person's states, so that remembrance fills his whole life. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take this general reading, while Ibn Abbas, Ali, Qatada and al-Nakha'i, as reported by al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, understand the remembrance as prayer, performed standing, then sitting, then lying if one cannot do better. Other exegetes see it as constant invocation. Several stress the value of reflection, citing Ibn Abbas and Abu al-Darda' that an hour of contemplation is better than a night of prayer. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi note that remembrance and thought complete each other, and that supplication follows the glorifying of God. As for the words that God did not create this in vain, the commentators take them to affirm that creation has a purpose, even if some of its wisdom escapes human minds. The Mu'tazilites see here proof that God acts with wisdom, while others read in it that all of creation is wise. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi explain that disgrace means humiliation and shame, and that wrongdoers have no helper. The following verses record the believers' prayer for forgiveness, the erasing of their bad deeds, and to die among the righteous, then their request for what was promised through the messengers. God answers that He does not waste the work of any worker, male or female.

This part of the verse records the supplication of people of understanding who reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: 'Our Lord, whomever You admit to the Fire, You have indeed disgraced; and the wrongdoers will have no helpers.' The commentators agree on the basic meaning: the Fire is the punishment reserved for sinners, and 'disgrace' (khizy) means humiliation and exposure. They differ on how far this disgrace reaches. Anas, Qatada, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Ibn Jurayj hold that it concerns those who will remain in the Fire forever, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab specifies that the verse applies only to those who never come out. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, by contrast, holds that everyone who enters the Fire is disgraced even if he later leaves it, since a lesser disgrace remains for him. Al-Tabari prefers this view, and Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi follow it. Ibn 'Abbas says the wrongdoers are the polytheists, the view of most exegetes. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by the Mu'tazila, concludes that the damned will have no intercessor, whereas al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan reply that 'helper' means one who defends by force, so intercession remains possible. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also note that khizy can mean shame or embarrassment, so the disgrace of believers is their modesty before God and the disgrace of unbelievers is abasement and eternal punishment.

The commentators present this verse as the supplication of believers who, reflecting on the creation of the heavens and the earth, understood that God did not create them in vain. They glorify Him and ask to be spared the Fire, acknowledging that whoever He admits to the Fire is disgraced and that the wrongdoers have no helpers. The passage then recounts that they heard a caller to faith, believed, and ask for forgiveness of their sins, the expiation of their evil deeds, and to be counted among the righteous at death. Most exegetes, including Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and al-Razi, identify the caller as the Prophet Muhammad; Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and Qatada take it to be the Qur'an. Al-Tabari favours the latter, arguing that many believers never saw or heard the Prophet, while others compare it with the passage on the jinn. On the distinction between sins and evil deeds, Ibn 'Abbas and most commentators take the first to mean major sins and the second minor ones, whereas some hold that forgiveness and expiation mean the same and that the repetition serves emphasis. Regarding the promise made through the messengers, al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as what was promised through the prophets, al-Zamakhshari as a reward for affirming them, and others as a request for speedy victory or reward. Ibn Kathir and others report that the Prophet recited the last ten verses of the sura during the night prayer, and that he warned whoever recites them without reflecting upon them.

In this verse, people of understanding ask their Lord to grant them what He promised through His messengers, and not to disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection, affirming that He never breaks His promise. The commentators asked why such a prayer is needed when God cannot fail His promise. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, Ibn Kathir and others see it as an expression of humility, submission and dependence on God rather than doubt. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the wording may be a statement given in the form of a request, or a plea to be counted among those who deserve the reward, without claiming that merit for themselves, since that would be self-praise. Al-Tabari adds that the verse concerns the emigrants who wanted a swift victory over their enemies, and he supports this with the following verse in which God answers them. Al-Mawardi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir specify that the promise is reward or victory, and that "through Your messengers" means through their words or by believing in them. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qurtubi note that the repetition of "our Lord" reflects insistence in supplication, and Ibn Kathir cites traditions on reciting these verses at night. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir observe that disgrace on the Day of Resurrection means humiliation and exposure, and that according to some it also means eternal dwelling in the Fire.

The verse « Their Lord answered them » means that God accepted the prayer of the people of understanding who reflected on the creation of the heavens and the earth and called upon Him. He assured them that He does not waste the work of any doer, male or female, and that all are equal in reward. He then described the deeds that earned this promise: emigration, expulsion from their homes, suffering for God's sake, fighting, and being killed. He promised to remove their misdeeds and admit them to gardens with rivers flowing beneath, as a reward from Him. The commentators agree that the promise covers women as well as men regarding the reward, and that the passage primarily addresses the emigrants driven out of Mecca by the polytheists. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that leaving one's homeland and wealth seeking God's pleasure belongs to the highest ranks, and al-Qurtubi states that fighting and death are the highest forms of jihad. Al-Tabari understands the expiation as erasure and pardon. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi broaden emigration to anyone who leaves polytheism or his homeland, and extend the verse to anyone harmed for God who migrates toward Him. The recitations differ: Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read the verb with doubling, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the passive first. Al-Tabari accepts the transmitted readings of Medina, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr. Al-Alusi notes that the conjunction waw does not imply order, so some were killed while others fought. According to a report in Tirmidhi and al-Hakim, Umm Salama asked why only men were mentioned in emigration, and the revelation came in reply.

This verse is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, but the commentators agree that its real audience is his community: believers must not be misled by the free movement and prosperity of the disbelievers who travel the land for trade and gain. Their enjoyment is a brief profit, followed by Hell, which is a wretched resting place. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as a warning and a corrective, while al-Razi holds that it addresses every listener. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the prohibition is aimed at the cause, since the wandering itself is what could deceive the reader. The commentators differ on who the disbelievers are: Ibn Abbas names the people of Mecca, others name the Jews. Ibn Abbas, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba understand the word taqallub as trading, while Ikrima and Muqatil take it to mean the daily blessings they enjoy. The occasion of revelation, often reported, is that some believers who were suffering hunger envied the wealth of the unbelievers. The next verse sets against this short-lived prosperity the gardens of the God-fearing, with rivers flowing beneath them, a lodging from God. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya note that what is with God is better for the righteous, some reading this as better than worldly life, others as better than the pleasures of the unbelievers. Ibn Mas'ud holds that death is better for both believer and unbeliever. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi stress the consolation the passage offers.

The commentators explain that this verse warns the Prophet ﷺ, and through him his community, not to be deceived by the movements of the disbelievers through the lands, their trade and their comfortable living. It is a brief enjoyment, after which their refuge is Hell, an evil resting-place. Al-Tabari, Qatada and al-Razi hold that the address is to the Prophet but the intended audience is others; al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see it as a reinforcement of steadfastness, while al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya add that it may address any listener. On the occasion of revelation, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that some believers, seeing the prosperity of the polytheists while they themselves suffered hunger, complained; Ibn 'Abbas and others instead identify the Jews who travelled the lands for profit. Most read the word taqallub as commercial activity, whereas 'Ikrima and Muqatil take it as the blessings that befall them day and night. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the enjoyment is called small because it perishes, and al-Razi adds that a small favour that leads to great punishment is not counted as a favour. The scholars differ on whether the disbelievers receive a genuine blessing in this life: al-Ash'ari denies it, while al-Qadi Abu Bakr affirms it. The word mihad means bed or resting place, and al-Zamakhshari understands it as what they have prepared for themselves.

The commentators explain that this verse follows a warning to believers not to be deceived by the movements of the disbelievers through the land, their trade and gains, which are a fleeting enjoyment leading to Hell. It then turns to contrast: those who are mindful of their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever, as a welcome from God, and what is with God is better for the righteous. Most, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, agree that nuzul means what is prepared for a guest, that is, honour and reward, and that the good refers to the reward of the Hereafter being superior to the passing goods of this world. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that Ibn Mas'ud explained that death is good for every soul, and Ibn Kathir considers this report authentic. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that piety includes avoiding what is forbidden and performing what is obligatory. On who is addressed by 'do not be deceived', al-Mawardi, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it as addressed to the Prophet, meaning his community or any listener, while others identify the disbelievers as Arab polytheists or Jews according to different reports. Al-Razi argues that the word nuzul can support the vision of God, a view the other commentators do not adopt. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that the righteous are called such because they are kind to parents and children, or because they harm no one. The variant readings of the particle and of nuzul carry no notable effect on the meaning, according to the commentators.

The commentators read this verse as stating that some People of the Book believe in God, in what was revealed to the Muslims and in what was revealed to them, that they are humble before God, that they do not trade God's signs for a small price, and that their reward is with their Lord, for God is swift in reckoning. Most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baydawi, hold that these qualities describe those among them who embraced Islam, though they differ on who they were. Jabir, Ibn 'Abbas, Anas and Qatada report that it was revealed about the Negus, when the Prophet prayed over him and the hypocrites mocked. Ibn Juraij, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil name 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, while Mujahid extends it to all believing People of the Book. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi prefer this last view. 'Ata' also mentions forty men from Najran, thirty-two from Abyssinia and eight Romans.

The commentators agree that khushu' means humility and submission before God, and that not trading God's signs means not concealing or distorting them for status or gain, as some of their rabbis did. Al-Tabari understands khushu' as fear and humbleness, while Ibn Kathir notes that such qualities were rare among the Jews but more common among the Christians. The following verse, which commands patience, perseverance and guarding the frontiers, is read in different ways. The most common meaning of ribat is staying on the frontiers and preparing horses. Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman takes it to mean waiting for prayer after prayer, but Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir reject this reading and cite many hadiths on the merit of ribat.

The verse calls believers to patience, to steadfastness against the enemy, to guarding the frontiers and to the fear of God, so that they may prosper. Commentators differ on the three terms. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Juraij and al-Dahhak take it to mean: be patient in obedience to God and in the religion, be more steadfast than the enemy in battle, and guard the borders, a reading al-Tabari also favours. Zayd ibn Aslam understands patience as perseverance in jihad, while Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi understands steadfastness as patiently awaiting God's promised victory. Ribat originally meant tethering horses for war, then residing on the frontier to guard the Muslims; Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir note that permanent residents of a frontier town are not, strictly speaking, murabitun. Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, reported by al-Razi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, relates from Abu Hurayra that the verse refers to waiting for prayer after prayer, since there was no frontier campaign in the Prophet's time, citing the hadith that counts a perfect ablution in cold weather, walking to the mosques and waiting for prayer as ribat. Ibn Kathir also allows the meaning of fighting on the frontier. Al-Razi shows that the verse covers patience in acts, in trials and against the passions, and that all these readings may be held together. Taqwa extends to the whole of conduct, and la'alla is read by several as expressing purpose rather than hope. Falah means attaining what is desired and being saved from what is feared.
